exp20v2-pm.role:
What a Product Manager Does

A case-style explainer on scope, boundaries and the four things a product manager is answerable for.

1. Opening: a backlog of fourteen requests

On Tuesday, 3 March 2026, Meenal Deshpande walked into the Pune office of Taraazu Pantry Works for her third day as the company's first product manager. Taraazu sold monthly grocery subscriptions through a mobile app, competing for the same households as BigBasket and the quick-commerce players. It handled 1,45,000 orders a month at an average order value of ₹640. Its founder, Hrishikesh Joshi, had written a single line on the whiteboard: "30,000 more orders a month by the end of June."

Beneath it hung a printed backlog of fourteen requests. Sales wanted loyalty tiers. Operations wanted a delivery slot picker. The two engineers in Toronto, who had built the original ordering flow, wanted three weeks to rewrite the checkout. Hrishikesh himself wanted recipe bundles because a competitor had launched them.

The engineering team had six engineers and a twelve-week quarter. That is 72 engineer-weeks, an engineer-week being one engineer working for one week. Support and maintenance consumed about 25 per cent, or 18 engineer-weeks, leaving 54 to spend. If she simply passed the requests on in the order shouted, Taraazu would burn the quarter and learn nothing. This page follows what she did and uses it to define the role.

2. The idea

A product manager (PM) is the person accountable for deciding which problems a team solves, for whom, in what order, and whether the result worked. The role is usually dated to Neil McElroy, a Procter & Gamble executive who wrote a 1931 memo proposing that each brand have a dedicated manager responsible for it end to end. Software companies adopted the idea in the following decades because a team of engineers, designers and analysts has plenty of skill but no natural owner of the question "what should we build, and why".

The role is best remembered as four words: problem, people, priorities, outcomes. The PM owns a clear statement of the customer problem; understands the people involved, meaning customers and the colleagues who must act; sets the order of work; and answers for outcomes, the measurable change in customer behaviour that follows, rather than for outputs, the features shipped.

The sentence Meenal could repeat in any meeting without sounding glib was this: "My job is to make sure we are solving the right problem, in the right order, and to find out afterwards whether it worked; how we solve it is the team's job." The sentence concedes authority over method to engineers and designers, and claims authority over purpose. That trade is the heart of the role.

3. How it actually works

Meenal's first step was one the job description never mentions: she refused to open the backlog. The benchmark programmes at Harvard and Stanford warn against starting from a backlog rather than a customer problem, because a backlog is a record of other people's solutions. Instead she spent her first nine days on discovery, the structured work of learning what customers actually experience. She listened to 22 support calls, read 300 cancellation reasons, and rode along on two deliveries.

Second, she wrote the problem down in a form a stranger could dispute. Her finding was that 61 per cent of cancellation reasons mentioned a missing or substituted item. Customers were not leaving for lack of loyalty tiers; they were leaving because the tin of mustard oil they ordered was replaced with a brand they distrusted. Writing this as a plain paragraph forced a decision about what Taraazu would not work on this quarter.

Third, she converted each backlog request into a hypothesis, a claim about customers that could be proven wrong: "if we build X, then Y more orders will occur each month, because Z." She also asked the engineers for their cost estimates before anything else, a step practitioners usually leave implicit. A PM who prioritises on benefit alone is only half-prioritising.

Fourth, she ranked by benefit per unit of scarce resource, here orders per engineer-week, and checked the ranking with the people who would live with it. Fifth, she wrote down what the team would explicitly not do, and who had been told. Sixth, she defined in advance how success would be read: orders per month, measured eight weeks after launch. The last step is the one most often skipped, and it is the reason the role is about outcomes.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

Meenal shortlisted five of the fourteen requests, the ones that addressed the cancellation finding or the order-growth goal directly. Table 1 shows her estimates.

Table 1. Five shortlisted requests, ranked by expected orders per engineer-week
RequestCost (engineer-weeks)Expected extra orders per monthOrders per engineer-weekCumulative cost
Substitution preferences86,4008008
Loyalty tiers147,00050022
Delivery slot picker125,40045034
Referral credits103,00030044
Recipe bundles164,80030060
Total6026,600——

Each rate is the orders column divided by the cost column, for example 6,400 / 8 = 800. The rate column is not summed because a sum of rates has no meaning.

Line by line: the capacity is 54 engineer-weeks. Substitution preferences cost 8 and lead the ranking. Adding loyalty tiers brings the cumulative cost to 22, the slot picker to 34, and referral credits to 44, all within 54. Recipe bundles would take the total to 60, which exceeds 54 by 6, so they are not funded. The funded set therefore yields 6,400 + 7,000 + 5,400 + 3,000 = 21,800 extra orders a month, leaving 54 − 44 = 10 engineer-weeks as reserve. At ₹640 an order, that is 21,800 × 640 = ₹1,39,52,000, about ₹1.40 crore of extra monthly order value.

Notice what the arithmetic also says. The target was 30,000 extra orders; the funded set reaches 21,800, which is 15.0 per cent growth on 1,45,000 against the 20.7 per cent the founder wanted. The plan is 8,200 orders short. Meenal had to say so to Hrishikesh in the second week, because an honest shortfall in March is a conversation, while the same shortfall in June is a failure.

Second pass. Now change one input. Suppose the sizing proves optimistic and the real capacity is 40 engineer-weeks, because two engineers are pulled into a payments-compliance task after a notice from the Reserve Bank of India affecting the UPI mandate flow. The ranking is unchanged, but the cut moves. Substitution (8), loyalty (22) and slot picker (34) fit; referral credits would reach 44, which is over 40 by 4, and recipe bundles are further out. The funded set yields 6,400 + 7,000 + 5,400 = 18,800 orders, leaving 6 engineer-weeks. A single changed input removed 3,000 orders and a whole request from the plan. The ranking is robust; the cut line is not.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Accountable is not the same as in charge

The PM usually has no direct reports among the people building the product. Authority comes from clarity and credibility, not rank. A PM who issues instructions to engineers has mistaken accountability for command, and the engineers will comply minimally and stop volunteering information.

Outputs, outcomes and impact are different things

An output is something shipped; an outcome is a change in customer behaviour; impact is the effect on the business. Shipping substitution preferences is an output. Fewer cancellations is an outcome. Higher monthly revenue is impact. The PM answers for the middle term, which is the hardest to influence and the easiest to avoid measuring.

The estimates are guesses with a decimal point

The 6,400 orders figure was a judgement from 22 calls and some data, not a measurement. Treat every benefit estimate as a range, and ask what would have to be true for the ranking to flip. In the worked example, substitution would fall to second place only if its benefit dropped below 4,000 orders, since 7,000 / 14 = 500 and 500 × 8 = 4,000.

The role is not a mini-CEO

The phrase is popular and misleading. A CEO hires, fires, sets compensation and owns the budget. A PM owns none of these. The accurate comparison is a person who is accountable for outcomes while depending on others for nearly every input.

It is not project management, and not the founder's job either

A project manager is accountable for delivering a defined scope on time. A PM is accountable for whether the scope was worth defining. A product marketing manager owns positioning and launch; a technical programme manager coordinates dependencies across teams. In small companies one person may do two of these, but the questions remain distinct.

Prioritisation cannot tell you what to want

The ranking method assumes the goal is orders. If Hrishikesh's real goal were profit per order, or customer trust, the ranking would differ. No method supplies the objective; the PM must secure it from leadership before ranking anything.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early stage and large

In a consumer product such as Taraazu's app, customers number in the lakhs, feedback is statistical, and the PM leans on behavioural data and experiments. In a B2B product, customers number in the dozens, each contract matters, and the PM must separate the buyer who signs from the user who struggles; a request from one large account can masquerade as a market need. In a marketplace, which connects two sides such as shoppers and sellers, every decision helps one side at the other's expense, so the PM balances supply against demand and works with two sets of customers at once.

Company stage changes the job as much as product type. At a start-up of twenty people, the PM writes the spec, queries the database, answers support tickets and often runs the launch. At a firm with thousands of employees, the PM owns a narrower slice, spends more time on alignment with other teams, and writes for audiences who will never meet the customer.

7. Common mistakes

Becoming a backlog clerk. The symptom is a team that ships steadily while the key metric stays flat. The misunderstanding is that listening to requests is the same as understanding the problem. The cheapest diagnostic: ask the PM to state, in two sentences and without naming a feature, the customer problem the quarter addresses.

Declaring victory on release. The symptom is a launch announcement followed by silence. The misunderstanding is confusing output with outcome. The diagnostic: look for a calendar entry eight weeks after launch where results are reviewed. If none exists, nobody is measuring.

Avoiding the no. The symptom is a roadmap of thirty items for a team that can finish eight. The misunderstanding is that saying no is unfriendly. The diagnostic: ask who was told that their request would not be done, and when.

8. What good looks like

Well handled, Meenal's first month leaves four artefacts: a one-paragraph problem statement that cites the 61 per cent finding, a ranked table with its assumptions visible, a list of what is not being done with names beside it, and a measurement plan with dates. Hrishikesh has been told on day eleven that 21,800 is not 30,000. The engineers have seen their own estimates in the table and corrected two of them. Operations knows the slot picker is third, and why. No one is surprised in June because the shortfall was visible in March.

9. Closing: what Meenal decided

Meenal took the five-row table to Hrishikesh on 13 March. She proposed funding substitution preferences, loyalty tiers, the slot picker and referral credits, holding the 10-week reserve against compliance work, declining recipe bundles for the quarter, and revisiting the 8,200-order gap through a separate discovery effort on the checkout rewrite the Toronto engineers wanted. Her reasoning was that the funded set addressed the largest cancellation cause first, that the reserve protected the plan against exactly the risk shown in the second pass, and that a visible shortfall was cheaper than a hidden one. Hrishikesh agreed to the plan and asked for a review in eight weeks.

To go further, read next about the distinctions between a PM, a product marketing manager, a programme manager and a founder, and then about outputs, outcomes and impact; the first sharpens where the role stops, the second sharpens what it answers for.

Two questions to sit with. First, if Meenal's substitution estimate were wrong by half, which of her four funded items would you still defend, and what evidence would you want within the first four weeks? Second, which part of your current work is a decision about purpose, and which part is a decision about method that you might be holding on to?
exp40v2-pm.role:
What a Product Manager Does

A case-style treatment of the role's scope — problem, people, priorities, outcomes — and of the boundaries practitioners draw differently from one another.

1. Two desks, one week in September

On Thursday, 3 September 2026, Nandita Iyer sat above the shop floor of Yantrika Machine Works in Coimbatore with a spreadsheet she did not want to circulate. Yantrika sold a retrofit kit — a sensor box clamped to an existing CNC machine, firmware, a cloud dashboard — to the small machine shops supplying the auto-component chain around Coimbatore and Rajkot. Hardware went out at ₹38,000 a machine, the software subscription at ₹9,600 per machine per year, and the installed base stood at 4,100 machines across 266 shops: recurring software revenue of ₹3.94 crore a year. Nandita had six engineers for the quarter and four candidate bets. One, a vibration-based spindle-failure predictor, needed a new sensor in the bill of materials — which froze for the Q4 build on Thursday, 29 October 2026, eight weeks to the day. The sensor carried an eighteen-week lead time from a Pune supplier, so an order placed at the freeze would land in the week of 4 March 2027. If she was wrong, she would be wrong for a year.

Four days later, on Monday, 7 September 2026, Arnav Bhatnagar opened a different problem in Raipur. Vyapaar Metals Exchange matched 1,900 registered buyers — re-rollers, foundries, induction-furnace units — against 640 scrap aggregators and yards. In August it listed 9,400 lots, of which 5,640 drew at least one bid and 2,538 transacted at an average lot value of ₹6,80,000: ₹172.58 crore of monthly gross merchandise value, which is ₹17,258.40 lakh, on which Vyapaar charged the buyer one per cent — ₹172.58 lakh of revenue. Arnav had eleven engineers and no capacity problem; he had two customer bases asking for opposite things. Buyers wanted third-party grading, because scrap described as HMS 1 arrived closer to HMS 2. Sellers wanted a published settled-price index, believing the top forty buyers, 62 per cent of GMV between them, coordinated on price.

Both hold the same title, and neither faces the textbook capacity problem. Nandita's constraint is irreversibility; Arnav's is two customers whose interests are opposed.

2. The idea, and who refuses to sign it

A product manager is the person accountable for deciding which customer problems a team solves, for whom, in what sequence, and for establishing afterwards whether the result changed customer behaviour. Four nouns compress it: problem, people, priorities, outcomes. The lineage is traced to a memo written in May 1931 by Neil McElroy at Procter & Gamble proposing a "brand man" responsible end to end for one brand's commercial fate. The problem was organisational: a functional firm had marketing, manufacturing and sales, each excellent, and nobody whose bonus depended on whether Camay sold. Software imported the role half a century later for the same reason — a team of engineers, designers and analysts has abundant skill and no natural owner of "what should we build, and why".

Agreement ends there. Four positions are held by people who have run successful product organisations. The discovery school, visible in the empowered-team literature and in how the Stanford and HBS courses frame day one, gives the PM value and viability risk and outcome-level objectives rather than features; it signs a team given a feature list has no product manager, only a coordinator, and refuses the PM is accountable for a committed quarterly scope. The throughput school, lean-agile in origin, gives the PM a ranked backlog to maximise flow, value being realised only on release; it signs a PM who cannot commit to a quarter's scope cannot be planned around by sales, support or manufacturing, and refuses the team may change what it builds mid-quarter on new evidence. The general-manager school, McElroy's descendant, gives the PM a P&L-shaped scope in which features sit beside price, packaging and channel; it signs a PM who cannot state the product's unit economics is not managing it, and refuses the PM's accountability stops at customer behaviour. The technologist school, loudest in AI-native firms, makes the central artefact an evaluation set; it signs the quality bar is a dataset, and refuses the PM should stay out of implementation.

Neither situation is neutral between these. A bill-of-materials freeze is a committed-scope world: manufacturing cannot be told in week ten that the team learned something. And no eval set tells Arnav whose side to take.

3. Mechanics in depth: what Nandita actually did

The published method is discover, define, prioritise, ship, measure. The practised version has steps left implicit, and those decide the outcome. Nandita's first was to obtain the cost estimates before circulating any benefit estimates; a PM who publishes benefits first has anchored the room, and engineers estimate against a number they know is wanted. Her second was to require each bet as a falsifiable claim carrying a probability of technical success, set by the engineering leads. Her third was one currency: as annual rupees her four bets are commensurable, as "delight" and "platform hygiene" they are not.

Every derivation behind Table 1 is disputable, which is why each is written down. The customer-facing OEE report — overall equipment effectiveness, the metric a tier-1 supplier must show its own customer — would, sales believed, unlock ten tier-1 shops averaging 35 machines each: 350 machines at ₹9,600 is ₹33.60 lakh of new annual recurring revenue. The firmware pipeline addressed 1,180 field visits a year at ₹2,500 each, ₹29.50 lakh of cost, of which it would remove 60 per cent — 708 visits, ₹17.70 lakh. Reason-code capture addressed lapsing: 440 machines went dark in FY2025-26, 10.7 per cent of the 4,100 installed, and better capture was thought to retain a quarter, 110 machines, ₹10.56 lakh. The spindle predictor would sell as a tier at ₹4,500 per machine per year to the 1,040 machines with high enough spindle loads to matter, at 65 per cent attach: 676 machines, ₹30.42 lakh.

An expert does not, for two reasons. The first is that the engineer-week is a fiction of fungibility: Yantrika's six engineers were three cloud, two firmware and one mobile, and each bet drew on them in fixed proportions.

The second reason is that the ranking priced engineering cost and ignored manufacturing cost. The new sensor added ₹1,240 to the bill of materials of every kit, not only those whose owners bought the predictive tier. At 1,450 kits a year that is ₹17.98 lakh of added annual cost against ₹30.42 lakh of gross uplift — a net ₹12.44 lakh if the bet works, an expected ₹6.22 lakh at a probability of 0.5. Against ₹46 lakh of tooling, the expected payback is 7.4 years. On the Table 1 ranking bet A is merely last; on the binding economics it is a capital decision belonging with the managing director.

4. When the frame applies, and when it misleads

The account rests on three testable conditions. First: the work is reversible enough that evidence gathered after a decision can change it. True for Arnav, whose grading rules can be rewritten in a fortnight; false for Nandita on the BOM line and true elsewhere. Second: one customer's behaviour is what the outcome measures. True for Nandita; false for Arnav, where improving one side provably degrades the other. Third: the PM holds enough information asymmetry to add value by choosing. Here the frame misleads — when a contract has already specified two quarters of work, when a regulator has set a compliance date, or when a founder's domain intuition is still the best judge. A PM who insists on owning the problem choice there is litigating the role, not exercising it.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product companies the scarce resource is not engineering but the attention of shared functions: one sales team, one support queue, one brand. The argument runs between PMs and is settled by whoever holds the portfolio view — often a chief product officer whose existence quietly removes the problem choice from each PM. In two-sided businesses the outcome metric must be a system metric; a buyer-side and a seller-side PM measured separately optimise each other into the ground. In regulated products the compliance date is a boundary condition, carved out of capacity before anything is ranked.

In hardware plus software the seam is the freeze, handled as manufacturers actually do rather than as their process documents say: the quality head held the pen on the BOM, and the PM's influence ran through the eight weeks before 29 October. In AI-native products, where behaviour emerges from a model rather than code, "what should we build" splits into "what should the system do" and "how good is good enough" — and the second is answered by a dataset with a threshold. A PM who cannot build that dataset has delegated the specification.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Accountability is not authority, and the gap is the job. The competent reading is that a PM should acquire more authority. The expert reading is that the gap is load-bearing: it forces persuasion, which forces the reasoning onto paper and makes the decision auditable later. The tell of missing this is a roadmap no engineer can explain without reading it aloud.

Outputs, outcomes and impact are three columns, and the PM lives in the middle. Shipping the OEE report is an output; ten tier-1 shops subscribing is an outcome; ₹33.60 lakh of recurring revenue is impact. The obvious reading — own impact, since that is what the business cares about — fails because impact has too many authors. The tell: revenue reported but not traceable to a behaviour change.

The probability column is where the real argument lives. Benefit estimates get scrutinised; probabilities get waved through. Yet moving bet A's probability from 0.50 to 0.80 lifts its expected benefit to ₹24.34 lakh and its rate to 0.579 per engineer-week — still below bet D's 0.708. An expert tests whether any defensible probability flips the ranking.

A ranking is robust; a cut line is not. The order in Table 1 survives most plausible revisions. What gets funded does not: it moves with capacity, staffing mix and whatever the warranty queue consumes. Experts publish the ranking and keep the cut line provisional.

Benefit per unit of scarce resource requires knowing which resource is scarce. Nandita's scarce resource was firmware weeks; Arnav's was buyer trust, not engineering. The tell is a framework applied with a denominator inherited from the last company.

Reversibility deserves a column of its own. Two bets with identical expected value are not equivalent if one can be undone in a sprint and the other is a tooling order. Expert practice splits an irreversible bet into a cheap evidence stage and an expensive commitment.

The hardest output is the written no, with a name attached. Declining a bet is not the same as not funding it; the first means telling the person who asked. The diagnostic is who was told, and when — sharp at Yantrika, where sales had already shown two prospects the spindle predictor.

Proxy metrics are how competent PMs destroy value. A proxy is adopted because the real outcome reads slowly, and the team then optimises it with discipline. In a two-sided product the same error appears as "the customer": the competent practitioner picks a side and calls it customer obsession; the expert models the other side, because the other side responds.

7. How the job differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products feedback is statistical and the PM leans on experiments; in B2B and enterprise the population is small, the buyer is not the user, and one large account's request masquerades as a market need. Nandita sits between: 266 shops is too few for clean experiments, too many to visit. In platform products the customer is a developer and the PM's influence is documentary. In marketplaces the PM owns a balance, not a funnel. In hardware the freeze dominates. In AI products the PM owns an eval set and a threshold.

By stage the differences are narrower than folklore suggests. At twenty people the PM writes the spec, queries the database and runs the launch; at two thousand the PM owns a slice and spends the difference on alignment. The four nouns do not change; how much of the problem choice was already made upstream does.

8. Three worked examples

Arnav's two-sided arithmetic

Arnav modelled both requests through one funnel. Buyer-side assurance — mandatory third-party grading on lots above ₹5 lakh, the fee borne by the seller — would cost 20 per cent of listings as fee-averse sellers withdrew, but raise the bid rate from 60.0 to 75.0 per cent and conversion from 45.0 to 50.0 per cent. Seller-side transparency — a weekly settled-price index by grade and region — would raise listings 25 per cent, hold conversion at 45.0 per cent, cut the bid rate to 56.0 per cent, and lift the average lot value 4 per cent to ₹7,07,200 as sellers held out.

He computed the crossover: Option 2 stays ahead only while buyer-side volume erodes by less than 8.4 per cent, since 209.40 × 0.916 is 191.81, barely above 191.76. A ten per cent erosion takes Option 2 to ₹188.46 lakh, below Option 1 — so the decision rested on one unmeasured quantity, the elasticity of forty buyers.

Nandita's reframing

Having seen Figure 2 and the 7.4-year payback, Nandita reframed the spindle predictor from a bet to rank into a question she could buy an answer to. She proposed funding bets C, D and B at 56 engineer-weeks, and spending the two remaining engineer-weeks plus ₹3.4 lakh of non-engineering budget on instrumenting twelve customer machines with a borrowed sensor, to establish whether spindle failure was predictable at her existing sampling rate at all.

Where it failed: Yauvan Skincare Industries

Yauvan sold skincare direct to consumers in Mumbai through an app and a subscription. In the first half of 2026 its product manager, Sneha Barman, delivered 11 of 12 planned features — 91.7 per cent against plan — and raised her chosen metric, sessions per user per month, from 4.2 to 6.1. In July her growth analyst in Melbourne flagged that something else had moved.

The cause was a gamified daily skin-log card at the top of the home screen. It did what it was built to do — sessions rose 45.2 per cent — and it displaced the reorder prompt below the fold, where clicks fell 45.7 per cent. At roughly 60,000 first-time buyers a month, ₹60.90 lakh a cohort is ₹7.31 crore a year. Recovery took a quarter: Sneha made the 90-day repeat rate the single outcome metric, moved the skin-log to a separate tab, and the September 2026 cohort came in at 28.5 per cent — 17,100 repeat buyers, ₹247.95 lakh, recovering ₹39.15 lakh, or 64.3 per cent of the loss. She had never written down what would make her stop believing in sessions.

9. Failure modes, with their early warnings

Backlog clerking. Early sign: the team ships on cadence while the headline metric stays flat for two quarters. Diagnostic: ask the PM to state the quarter's customer problem in two sentences without naming a feature. Late cost: a year of capacity, and a team that no longer expects its work to matter.

Proxy capture. Early sign: a metric that only ever goes up. Diagnostic: ask what reading would falsify it. Yauvan's cost was ₹60.90 lakh a cohort.

Ranking on the wrong denominator. Early sign: a prioritisation table with one cost column. Diagnostic: name the binding constraint and re-check the table against it. At Yantrika, late detection would have cost a tooling order and a year of lead time.

Side-taking in a two-sided product. Early sign: one side's satisfaction rising while liquidity falls. Diagnostic: ask for the system metric — here fill rate — not either side's. Cost: a thinning market that reads as a pricing problem for quarters before anyone names it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should the PM own a number or a problem? The number position at its strongest: accountability is meaningless unless measurable, and PMs given problems rather than targets drift into research; the evidence is the reliability of metric-owning teams in mature consumer businesses. It is wrong when the metrics available are proxies, because the frame then guarantees the Yauvan failure. The problem position: durable accountability is for having chosen correctly, and metrics follow the problem. It is wrong where the organisation cannot tell a well-chosen problem from an interesting one.

Is the general-manager framing useful or corrosive? Steelmanned: a PM who does not own price, margin and channel will optimise features in a business whose constraint is distribution — Nandita's spindle bet is that error, and only the BOM arithmetic caught it. Against: the framing invites PMs to act as though they held authority they do not, and where the founder is the general manager it produces permanent conflict. What would settle it is evidence on whether PMs with pricing authority outperform; none of quality exists.

Can one person be accountable for outcomes they do not control? The single-owner position rests on jointly owned outcomes being unowned, and on the value of having someone to ask. The triad position — PM, design lead and engineering lead jointly accountable — rests on outcome quality depending on all three, and on singling out the PM producing a dictator or a scapegoat. Both camps contain people who have shipped well. The field has not settled it; the answer appears to depend on whether the three leads trust each other, which is not a property of the operating model.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised the role rather than studied it behaves differently in four ways. They ask for cost estimates before publishing benefit estimates. They can name, unprepared, the quantity on which their plan most depends — for Arnav the elasticity of forty buyers, for Nandita whether spindle failure is detectable at her sampling rate. They describe what they are not doing as specifically as what they are. And they separate a decision about purpose, which is theirs, from one about method, which they hand over even knowing the answer.

12. What each of them decided

Nandita took Tables 1 and 2 to the managing director on 17 September 2026 and asked for two things: funding for bets C, D and B at 56 engineer-weeks, and a decision from him, not her, on whether to spend ₹46 lakh of tooling against an expected ₹6.22 lakh a year. She also asked that the spindle sensor be left out of the 29 October freeze and reconsidered at the next, on the twelve-machine evidence. The bet was not badly ranked but wrongly classified: a capital decision dressed as a feature.

Arnav chose Option 1, buyer assurance, on 21 September 2026, giving up ₹17.64 lakh of modelled monthly revenue. His argument: fill rate is the only number describing whether an exchange is an exchange, Option 1 was the only option in which it rose — from 27.0 to 37.5 per cent — and an untestable assumption about forty buyers' elasticity was not defensible. The same memo committed him to publishing the index the following quarter.

Three questions. First: Nandita escalated the tooling decision rather than making it. Did she exercise the role or abdicate it, and what would have to be true about Yantrika for the other answer to be right? Second: Arnav gave up measurable revenue for an unmeasured systemic benefit. What evidence within ninety days would show him wrong, and what would you build to produce it? Third: Sneha satisfied every delivery commitment Yauvan had made to her. Who was accountable for the ₹60.90 lakh, and what single artefact written in January would have prevented it?

13. Going deeper

PM myths vs reality dismantles the mini-CEO story. Origins of product management follows the McElroy memo forward. PM vs PMM vs TPM vs project manager vs founder sharpens the boundaries Figure 1 maps. Outputs vs outcomes vs impact is the sequel to the Yauvan failure. The product triad and Empowered teams vs feature teams take up section 10's open argument. How the PM job changes by company stage turns section 7 into a calendar. Hypothesis-driven product development formalises the probability column. Decision rights and escalation paths is what Nandita used. How AI is reshaping the PM role tests the technologist claim.
case20v1-pm.role:
Gaddi Billing Works: Whose Quarter Is It?

A teaching case on what a product manager is, and is not, responsible for

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday, 13 October 2026, Tanishka Pol sat in the Pune office of Gaddi Billing Works with a blank planning document and a deadline. The company's thirteen-week quarter would begin on Monday, 19 October, and the plan had to be locked by Friday, 16 October; the quarter would run to Friday, 15 January 2027. She had been the company's product manager for exactly nineteen days.

Four people had already told her what the quarter was for. The chief executive wanted a WhatsApp ordering assistant. The sales head wanted a custom module for a large prospect who would sign only if it went live by 18 December. The customer-success lead wanted the onboarding fixed. The engineering lead wanted to rewrite the mobile app. Together they added up to more engineering time than the team owned. Nobody had said who was supposed to choose, and Tanishka had begun to suspect that the unspoken answer was her.

2. Company background

Gaddi Billing Works sells billing, stock and credit-ledger software to wholesale distributors in India, the small businesses that carry products from companies such as Amul, Asian Paints and Tata Consumer Products to the neighbourhood shop. The name comes from the gaddi, the cushioned seat from which a traditional trader runs his accounts. Founded in 2018 by Parag Lele, a former FMCG salesman, it grew through resellers across Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka.

The competition is crowded. Established desktop accounting packages such as Tally, Busy and Marg hold the habits of older accountants. Vyapar and Khatabook are strong with the smallest shops, and Zoho Books attracts the more formal buyers. Gaddi's pitch is narrower: GST-ready invoicing, scheme and discount tracking that distributors need and general accounting tools handle poorly, and a retailer credit ledger that works on a phone.

Exhibit 1 shows the customer base at the start of October 2026. The business has three kinds of customer, and they behave very differently.

Account losses of 264 out of 1,506 are 17.5 per cent; in rupees, ₹115.2 lakh of ₹882.0 lakh is 13.1 per cent. The gap between those two figures is the story of the company: the accounts that leave are mostly the cheap ones. Yet the small segment alone loses 240 of its 1,200 accounts, a rate of 20 per cent, against 8 per cent among mid-sized distributors (24 of 300).

3. The situation

Tanishka joined from a payments company where she had owned a merchant-onboarding flow. In her first nineteen days she sat in on sales calls and listened to forty support recordings. She concluded that small distributors were not leaving for a competitor but within their first ninety days, after a messy setup in which stock opening balances were entered wrongly and payment reminders to retailers never went out. The product worked; the first month did not.

The four requests reached her desk by different routes, and each was framed in the language of its sender. Exhibit 2 puts them side by side, with engineering effort estimated by Anirudh Prabhu, the engineering lead in Bengaluru. The team has four engineers. Over the thirteen weeks that is 52 engineer-weeks gross; Diwali on 8 November and planned leave take out 4, leaving 48 deliverable.

Exhibit 3 draws the same comparison as bars against the 48-week line. Two points stand out. The customer-success request is the smallest and the only one whose value rests on evidence the company already owns. And the largest request, the WhatsApp assistant, is also the one with the least evidence behind it.

The global team saw the problem from where it sat. Marlene Dekker, the contract designer in Amsterdam, had already mocked up the WhatsApp flows and was impatient to see them built. Ewan Mackie, a data scientist working from Melbourne on a part-time contract, had run the cohort analysis behind the ninety-day finding but had not been asked to present it. Neither had been in the room when the requests were made.

4. The people

Parag Lele, chief executive, Mumbai. He built the company and still thinks like its first salesman. He believes that WhatsApp is where Indian small business now lives and that Gaddi must be there before a larger rival is. He has said twice that the quarter "should have a big thing in it".

Mehul Karve, head of sales, Hyderabad. He has courted the large chain for eight months. If the module is late, the deal goes to a competitor.

Rutuja Chhabra, customer-success lead, Jaipur. She reads the exit notes every Monday and has seen the same pattern for a year. She has asked for the onboarding fix in three consecutive planning cycles and lost each time to a request with a bigger name attached.

Anirudh Prabhu, engineering lead, Bengaluru. He is candid that the mobile app is brittle and will cost more each quarter to patch. He will build whatever is prioritised but wants the choice made once and not reopened in week five.

5. The options

Option A: Back the strongest voices. Take the custom module (14 weeks) and the WhatsApp assistant (20 weeks), 34 weeks in all, leaving 14 for support and bugs. The upside is concrete: a ₹40 lakh first-year contract, a satisfied chief executive and a visible launch. The cost is that nothing addresses the 240 small accounts that leave each year, which represent ₹86.4 lakh of annual fees, and the choice is made by who asked loudest rather than by any stated problem.

Option B: Promise everything and manage delivery. Accept all 59 weeks and close the 11-week gap with contract engineers at an assumed ₹1.5 lakh per engineer-week, which is ₹16.5 lakh. Nobody is told no, and Tanishka becomes the person who tracks the plan. The cost is not only the money. Contractors need onboarding, the Diwali weeks are already thin, and the plan still has no view about what matters most. If anything slips, all four stakeholders are disappointed at once.

Option C: Choose the problem for the quarter. Name one outcome, keeping small distributors past their first ninety days, and build the plan around it. Fund the onboarding fix (9 weeks), do a scoped single-warehouse version of the custom module that Mehul can take to the chain (10 weeks), spend 8 weeks on discovery for the WhatsApp idea, and hold the remaining 21 weeks for bugs and carry-over. Defer the app rewrite with a written date for revisiting it. The upside is a plan with a reason. The cost is that two senior people will be told no or not yet, and the chain may refuse a reduced scope.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, which customers is Gaddi losing, and why does the 17.5 per cent account loss rate understate how much the pattern matters for the small segment?

2. Of the four requests in Exhibit 2, which carries evidence of customer value that a reader could check, and which carries only an opinion? What would it take to turn an opinion into evidence?

3. Who should decide what the team builds: the chief executive, the sales head, engineering, or the product manager? Which decisions in this case are Tanishka's to make, and which does she only inform?

4. Which option would you recommend on Friday, how would you explain it to each of the four stakeholders, and what would make you change your mind?

7. A note for the learner

This case is about the boundary of the product manager's job. A PM is responsible for four things: understanding the customer problem, aligning the people who can solve it, setting priorities among competing uses of scarce effort, and being accountable for outcomes rather than output. Equally important is what the PM is not: the PM is not the order-taker for the loudest executive, not the project manager who tracks other people's plans, and not the author of every solution.

Through that lens, Option A has no organising problem, and Option B treats prioritisation as a scheduling puzzle: it solves the 11-week gap with ₹16.5 lakh instead of a decision. Option C is the defensible path. The outcome it names, keeping small distributors past ninety days, rests on the one request supported by evidence the company already holds: 20 per cent annual loss in a segment of 1,200 accounts, and a cost of 9 weeks against a potential ₹21.6 lakh of annual fees kept. The plan uses 9 + 10 + 8 = 27 weeks and holds 21 in reserve, which accounts for the full 48.

Option C is not an evasion. The scoped module honours the real ₹40 lakh opportunity, and the discovery weeks give the chief executive's idea a fair test, with a promise to bring evidence on WhatsApp ordering to the next planning cycle. A good answer also sets out the conversations to have before Friday: Tanishka should show Parag the ninety-day analysis, ask Mehul to test the reduced scope with the chain this week, and tell Anirudh that the rewrite is deferred, not rejected. If the chain insists on the full module, the plan should be re-cut openly, taking weeks from the reserve rather than quietly dropping the onboarding fix. What the PM must not do is let the quarter's priorities be set by default.
case40v1-pm.role:
Kadi Lift Systems: The Slide Nobody Owns

An ambiguous case, set in Chennai, Pune and Doha, November 2026

1. Sunday night, 22 November 2026

The board pack was due at nine the next morning, and Sravanthi Addanki had written one slide eleven times. The brief from the chair had been four words long: who is our customer. Under it a second line asked for the one number Kadi Lift Systems would be held to in the financial year beginning April 2027.

She was working from the Pune office, empty but for a security guard and the hum of a test rig in the corner — a half-height lift shaft with a Kadi Pulse box bolted to its controller. She had joined one hundred and eighteen days earlier, on Monday 27 July, as the company's first product manager. Nobody had explained what that meant, and she had spent the first month assuming the ambiguity was trust rather than indecision.

Four answers were live inside the company, each supported by data she had helped produce, each held by someone more senior than she was. The founder wanted the slide to say India's lifts; the co-founder who ran field operations, the maintenance contractors; the customer-success lead, the housing societies; the investor director, whichever answer would produce a clean compounding number.

What troubled her more than the disagreement was smaller. The two lines in her offer letter that described her job read: own the product roadmap and the release calendar. Neither mentioned a customer. Neither mentioned a number.

2. The company, and a signature from 2022

Kadi Lift Systems was founded in Chennai in April 2019 by Hariharan Ramaswami, who had spent fourteen years as a service engineer in the lift industry, and Baljeet Chadha, who had run a facilities contracting firm in Coimbatore. The kadi of the name is the link of a chain. The product is a retrofit: a sensor-and-modem box the size of a lunch tin that clamps onto an existing lift controller and reports door cycles, overloads, power cuts and stoppages over an NB-IoT SIM. It does not move lifts. It tells someone when a lift has stopped moving.

The first box shipped in October 2020. The economics are legible: it costs ₹4,100 to build, of which ₹1,850 is a sensor module from Tenma Sensor Trading in Osaka on a sixteen-week lead time; it sells installed for ₹6,900 before GST, a gross margin of ₹2,800 a unit; and the subscription that follows is the business.

The decision that still shapes everything was taken in August 2022. Selling to committee-run societies one at a time was burning cash, so Hariharan signed a five-year exclusive channel agreement with Sambhal Lift Care Services, a Coimbatore federation of maintenance-contract firms with some eleven hundred technicians across nine states. Sambhal would sell and fit Kadi boxes into the buildings it serviced; Kadi agreed not to solicit, price to or contract directly with any society under a Sambhal member's contract. The agreement runs to 31 July 2027 and renews automatically for three more years unless a party gives written notice by 31 January 2027.

It worked: by September 2026 the contractor channel held 15,500 of the company's 20,000 installed units. It also meant that for four years the product was shaped by what a technician on a ladder needed, and that Kadi had no relationship with the people who ride lifts.

3. The industry

India is among the world's largest lift markets by annual installation; industry estimates put the installed stock at roughly ten lakh passenger lifts, growing by some seventy thousand a year as mid-rise housing spreads through Pune, Hyderabad and Ahmedabad. Almost all of it is unmonitored. New lifts from Otis, Kone, Schindler and Johnson Lifts increasingly arrive with the maker's own connected-service offering, but that covers the maker's own equipment under warranty, and does not touch a twenty-year-old geared machine in a 1998 co-operative society in Dadar.

Regulation is state-level and uneven. Maharashtra's Lifts, Escalators and Moving Walks Act of 2017 and the older Tamil Nadu statute require registration, inspection and licensed maintenance through state electrical inspectorates; the Bureau of Indian Standards code IS 14665 governs installation and safety. None of it requires telemetry, which is Kadi's central commercial problem: it sells a voluntary good into a market that complies by paper. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 bites at the edges — a door sensor is not personal data, but a camera in a lift car is, and a society's managing committee is an awkward data fiduciary. Demand-side attention already belongs to MyGate, NoBrokerHood, ApnaComplex and ADDA.

Kadi's exposure abroad is narrow and heavy. In March 2024 it signed a ₹6.40 crore contract with Mashriq Facilities Group, which manages towers in Doha. Export of services is zero-rated under GST, the per-lift price is five times the Indian contractor rate, and the money has paid for two years of engineering. It has also produced a second firmware variant, a second certification regime and a March 2027 milestone that India does not want.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The channel strategy was never chosen so much as accreted. Of the four routes in Exhibit 1, three began as somebody's experiment: the builder pilot, 800 units for a Hyderabad developer, because a sales manager knew the project head; the direct business from April 2023, sited in Pune and later Nashik because neither lay in Sambhal territory; and the Gulf business, from an inbound email.

Three beliefs held the company together through 2025; Sravanthi had found evidence against all three.

The first was that an installed box is a monitored lift; the board deck says so in those words. Of 20,000 installed units, only 10,300 reported telemetry in the thirty days to 30 September 2026. In the contractor channel it is 6,200 of 15,500, an activation rate of exactly 40 per cent, leaving 9,300 boxes dark. Since Sambhal is billed only for active units, that is a revenue gap too: billed contractor subscription revenue is ₹111.60 lakh a year against ₹279.00 lakh if every installed unit in the channel were active and billed — a difference of ₹167.40 lakh.

The second was that the dark boxes were a demand problem: contractors sold the box and societies would not pay to keep it alive. Baljeet's field audit, Exhibit 2, says the opposite — dormancy traces mostly to installation and provisioning. Sravanthi thought the audit substantially right and unable to carry the weight placed on it.

The third was that safety outcomes were improving, the story behind the Series A deck. Exhibit 6 shows entrapment alerts per thousand active lifts rising from a mean of 3.36 a month over January to May 2026 to 8.30 over June to September, a factor of 2.47. On 1 June, firmware 4.2 redefined an entrapment alert from a door-open failure over ninety seconds with a load detected to any door-cycle fault over forty-five seconds, load or no load. Meghashree Hiremath had approved it as a noise fix; no release note recorded it. The October sales pack reports alerts up 184 per cent since January, which is arithmetically correct — 3.1 to 8.8 — and means nothing. What Sravanthi could not settle was whose job it had been to notice.

5. Exhibits

Two readings are available and the case does not settle between them. Read the activation column and the contractor channel is a four-year detour: three-fifths of the units ever shipped through it are silent. Read the ARR column and it is still Kadi's largest line of recurring revenue — while Doha, six per cent of the base, yields ₹103.50 lakh from a customer whose milestones, not whose renewals, pay the salaries.

Exhibit 3 is the strongest card in the building and weaker than it looks: the FY26 window closed early, the cohorts are small, and every unit sits in Pune or Nashik, where Kadi's own team does the fitting, so it confounds customer type with installation quality. Beside Exhibit 2 the two describe different companies — in one the society is the loyal customer the channel kept Kadi from reaching; in the other the channel is fine and the screwdriver is the problem.

Cash at 30 September 2026 was ₹4.93 crore. At the ₹29.00 lakh a month of Exhibit 5 that is exactly seventeen months. The ₹12.00 lakh of monthly enterprise revenue is the straight-line accrual of M4's ₹168 lakh in Exhibit 4, over the fourteen-month schedule agreed in January 2026; abandon M4 and the outflow becomes ₹41.00 lakh and the runway a little over twelve months.

6. The people

Hariharan Ramaswami, founder and chief executive, Chennai. Kadi is a safety company, he holds; the slide should read: the people who ride India's lifts. His incentive is a Series A at ₹180 crore pre-money, sold on 20,000 lifts monitored. Unsaid: he signed both the Sambhal exclusivity and the M4 scope without engineering review, and the term sheet he calls close has not moved since 2 October.

Baljeet Chadha, co-founder and head of field operations, Chennai, sixty-one people. Dormancy is a workmanship problem with a workmanship fix: thirty engineer-weeks for an installer application with photographic proof-of-fitting and a provisioning checklist, and the base lights up. His technicians are paid on installations completed. He says a quarter of the installed base has never once reported, which his own audit does not support. Unsaid: he has been costing a Kadi-run maintenance business, which the 2022 agreement would not survive.

Meghashree Hiremath, engineering lead, Bengaluru, fourteen engineers across Bengaluru and Pune. The India and Gulf firmware lines must converge before anything else, and she wants one written priority, signed, not four spoken ones. Her incentive is to stop losing people: two of her six firmware engineers hold offers. Unsaid: firmware 4.2 carried the alert-definition change, and she is no longer sure she noticed.

Anjana Pisharody, customer-success lead, Kochi. She owns Exhibit 3 and reads it as proof that the society is the customer. She is measured on renewal rate, and direct societies renew easily. Unsaid: she and a colleague have for eight months supported some forty societies inside Sambhal territory over WhatsApp — a quiet breach of the agreement.

Sudeep Thota, data scientist, Austin, on a twenty-hour weekly contract. The contractor channel is structurally unprofitable: 60 per cent dormancy, the lowest fee, the highest service cost. He is paid in dollars and wants a full-time offer; the direct business is where his models matter. Unsaid: his dormancy test is no telemetry in thirty days, which also marks dark the units in buildings that shut lifts for monsoon repairs; and he has never visited an Indian lift shaft.

Agnieszka Romanek, product designer, Warsaw, on contract since 2024. She has a society-app concept complete to the resident's lock-screen notification, and calls the installer application not a product. Her incentive is billable hours on work she can show. Unsaid: she walked the investor director through it at a conference in September, before Sravanthi saw it.

Indumathi Varadan, investor director for Vindhya Growth Partners, Chennai, and chair of Monday's meeting. One customer, one number; the choice matters more than which choice it is. Her fund sets reserves in December. Unsaid: she has told Hariharan that the Doha revenue is not venture revenue, and another company in the fund's portfolio, a lift component maker, has begun looking at retrofit monitoring.

7. Voices

"Twenty thousand lifts is true. We shipped twenty thousand boxes. Say ten thousand three hundred in a fundraising deck and we are telling the market the product is broken. It is not. We have a channel that fits antennas badly."Hariharan Ramaswami, management meeting, Chennai, 11 November 2026
"With respect, the audit is mine and I would not bet the company on it. Four hundred units, six cities, coded by my own supervisors."Baljeet Chadha, same meeting, five minutes later
"I can deliver M4 or I can deliver the direct rebuild, not both, and I will not be the one who discovers in February that the answer was both. Sravanthi, I am asking you in writing: which one."Meghashree Hiremath, chat to Sravanthi, 17 November 2026, 11.52 p.m. IST
"Please do not put the 85.6 per cent beside the other two without the asterisk. Half that cohort has not reached its date and someone will read it as a decline."Anjana Pisharody, email to Sravanthi, 19 November 2026
"Dormancy in the contractor base is 60 per cent. At ₹1,800 a lift it cannot carry its own service cost. I have said so in three decks since March and have never been asked what I would do instead."Sudeep Thota, comment on the board pack draft, 21 November 2026, 09.14 CDT
"Decide who the customer is and I will fund the quarter. Keep three and the fund will mark you a services business. I am not asking for a strategy, Sravanthi. I am asking whether anyone at Kadi has the authority to choose."Indumathi Varadan, call with Hariharan and Sravanthi, Friday 20 November 2026

8. The options as Sravanthi sees them

Option A: the society is the customer. Give notice on the Sambhal agreement by 31 January 2027, fund Agnieszka's society application at an estimated sixty-four engineer-weeks, and rebuild around the buyer who renews at 88.8 per cent. The ₹111.60 lakh of contractor ARR goes at risk, as does the fitting labour of eleven hundred technicians Kadi does not employ, and the direct business has only been proved in Pune and Nashik with Kadi's own fitters.

Option B: the contractor is the customer. Accept that Kadi sells to the trade, spend thirty engineer-weeks on the installer application and a certification scheme, and go after activation. Lift contractor activation from 40 to 70 per cent and 6,200 active units become 10,850, worth 10,850 at ₹1,800, or ₹195.30 lakh — an uplift of ₹83.70 lakh on the same base with no new hardware. It rests on Exhibit 2, which Baljeet distrusts, and on a partner whose contract renews if nobody acts.

Option C: the enterprise is the customer. Finish M4, collect ₹168 lakh, and sell the Gulf product as the product. Export fees of ₹9,000 a lift are five times the contractor rate and two and a half times the direct rate, and the buyer is one professional operator, not ten thousand committees. India becomes a reference market and the company's fate rests on a market it has one customer in.

All three sat on the eleventh version of the slide, and then three things unsettled the frame. A channel is not a customer: in Options A and B the person riding the lift is the same, and what changes is who sells and who fits. None of the three names an owner for the activation rate, which Figure 2 suggests is nobody's. And she had been hired to own a roadmap and a release calendar, and was now asked at seventy-two hours' notice for the choice that would decide the company.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 9.30 a.m. on Monday 23 November 2026 in Chennai. Cash is ₹4.93 crore against a net outflow of ₹29.00 lakh a month: seventeen months at the current shape, a little over twelve if M4 stops. The Sambhal notice window closes on 31 January 2027; miss it and the exclusivity runs to July 2030. M4 is due 31 March 2027, with ₹2.52 lakh a week of penalty to a cap of ₹16.80 lakh, and needs in-car video, which in India brings the DPDP Act, a consent architecture and an argument about who the data fiduciary is in a society. Engineering has fourteen people and, across the seventeen working weeks from 1 December to 31 March, 238 engineer-weeks less 26 of planned leave, or 212; the tabled demands are M4 at 100, the installer application at 30, the direct rebuild at 64, DPDP consent work at 18 and run-the-business at 60, which is 272 — sixty engineer-weeks more than exist. Four hires were approved conditional on a signed Series A. Any hardware change needs 2,000 Tenma modules at ₹1,850, ₹37.00 lakh, half on order, on a sixteen-week lead time.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, what is Kadi's installed base actually worth, and which reading of the activation column would you defend to the board?

2. Exhibits 2 and 3 are each produced by the person whose performance they describe. What would each have to show before you treated it as evidence rather than advocacy?

3. Hariharan's 20,000 and Sudeep's 10,300 describe the same base. Is either wrong, and whose job is it to decide which number goes on the slide?

4. Exhibit 6 was used in a sales pack to claim a 184 per cent rise in alerts, and the arithmetic is right. Who should have caught it, and what does that imply about the job?

5. Options A, B and C differ in channel but not in who rides the lift. Construct a fourth option the case has not offered, and state the number you would be held to under it.

6. It is Monday morning. What goes on the slide, what does Sravanthi say when the chair asks for the one number, and what — if anything — does she say about whether this was hers to decide?

Some time after midnight she deleted the three options and typed a single line at the top of the slide, read it twice, and could not tell whether it was the bravest thing she had written in four months or a resignation. The cursor sat at the end of it. Outside, the test rig cycled, stopped, and reported nothing to anyone.
exp20v2-pm.outcomes:
Outputs, outcomes and impact

How a product manager tells whether shipping the feature changed anything

1. The review that nobody wanted to open

On the morning of 14 July 2026, Meenal Joshi, head of product at Madhuban Grocery Exchange, a Pune-based platform that lets neighbourhood kirana stores order stock from wholesalers, opened a slide that her team was proud of. It read: "One-tap Reorder: shipped 3 March, on time, on budget." Underneath were four green ticks: design complete, built in 11 sprints, launched to all 80,000 active retailers, rated 4.6 out of 5 by the 1,900 retailers who had bothered to leave a rating.

The board would meet on 21 July. Nitin Bhargava, the chief executive, had already told her what he would ask: whether the ₹54 lakh the company spent building the feature had returned anything. Meenal realised that nothing on her slide answered him. Every tick described something her team had done. None described something a retailer had done differently.

The stakes were practical. A second feature, a credit-limit upgrade, waited for the same engineers, and the board would fund it on the same logic. If the team told itself a flattering story and it was wrong, it would repeat the error on a larger bet.

2. The idea: three different kinds of "done"

An output is something the team produces: a feature, a release, a redesigned screen, a document. Outputs are countable and entirely within the team's control, which is why organisations love them. An outcome is a change in the behaviour of the people who use the product, and that change is what makes any business result possible. Impact is the lasting result of that behaviour change for the business or for users' lives: revenue, retention, cost saved, harm avoided. The three form a chain, and each link is less controllable than the one before it.

The vocabulary has two ancestors. Programme evaluators from the 1970s used "logic models" separating outputs, outcomes and long-term impact, because governments confused clinics built with people healed. Melissa Perri's 2018 "build trap" and Josh Seiden's 2019 Outcomes Over Output brought it to product work: an outcome is a change in human behaviour that drives business results.

The sentence Meenal could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib is this: "We shipped it; now let us find out whether retailers behave differently because of it, and whether that difference pays for itself." It concedes the output, which was real work, and refuses to treat it as the answer.

Moving from output to outcome requires the belief that users will notice and prefer the feature; moving from outcome to impact requires the belief that the new behaviour is worth money. Each can fail independently.

3. How it works, step by step

Consider what Meenal's team did, including the steps they left unwritten. First, someone had a problem statement: kirana owners re-keyed nearly identical orders every week, and many forgot items. That problem statement was the origin of the feature, and it contains the outcome in embryo, since it says what should change: retailers should place complete orders with less effort.

Second, the team shipped One-tap Reorder, which copies a retailer's last order into the cart. That is the output. Third, retailers encountered it. The step usually left implicit is exposure and trial: a feature that fewer people try than hoped has no chance of an outcome. Fourth, some tried it, and a smaller group kept using it, which is adoption. A retailer who taps the button and then orders exactly as often as before has adopted the feature and changed nothing that matters.

Fifth, a subset changed the thing the team cared about: how often they ordered. This is the outcome, and Meenal's team had chosen "orders per active retailer per month" as the metric. Sixth, extra orders earned Madhuban a margin, and the margin is set against the cost of building the feature. That is impact. The implicit step that most teams skip sits between the fifth and sixth: working out what would have happened without the feature. Without that comparison you cannot assign any of the change to your work.

4. A worked example, line by line

Madhuban had, wisely, held back 10 per cent of its retailers from the feature when it launched. This holdout group is a randomly chosen set of users who do not receive the change, so that they show what would have happened anyway.

GroupRetailersShare of baseOrders per retailer per month, beforeOrders per retailer per month, 3 March to 28 April

Table 1. The measurement window is eight weeks, 3 March to 28 April 2026. The holdout rose by 0.1 because of the Holi and wedding-season stocking that lifted every retailer.

The analyst's first draft compared the exposed group with itself: 4.5 minus 4.0 is 0.5 extra orders per retailer, and 0.5 times 72,000 retailers is 36,000 extra orders a month. That is a before-and-after comparison, and it credits the feature with the seasonal lift. The correct comparison puts the exposed group against the holdout over the same weeks: 4.5 minus 4.1 is 0.4 extra orders per retailer, and 0.4 times 72,000 is 28,800 incremental orders a month. The naive method overstated the effect by 7,200 orders, which is 25 per cent of the true figure (7,200 divided by 28,800).
