Of the 72,000 retailers, 30 per cent adopted, yet the lift is measured across all 72,000. The 28,800 extra orders, multiplied by the margin, earn ₹46.8 lakh each month, so the ₹54 lakh build cost is recovered in about 1.2 months. This required a holdout.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose Madhuban's wholesalers, irritated by the volume of one-tap orders, negotiate the margin on reorder-driven orders down from 2.5 per cent to 2.0 per cent. Orders are unchanged at 28,800 a month, but margin per order falls to ₹130 (2.0 per cent of ₹6,500). Monthly margin becomes 28,800 x ₹130, which is ₹37.44 lakh, and the ₹54 lakh is recovered in about 1.4 months. The outcome did not move, yet the impact did, which is the clearest demonstration that they are different things. A team that reported only orders would have missed the change entirely.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Adoption is not outcome

The most common blur. Trial and repeat use are signals that the feature is being noticed, so track them, but name them as adoption. Here 30 per cent adopted and the exposed group still ordered only 0.4 more per retailer. Adoption without behaviour change means the feature is a comfort, not a lever.

An outcome needs a counterfactual

A counterfactual is an estimate of what would have happened without your change. Before-and-after comparisons fold seasonality, marketing campaigns and competitor moves into your credit. A holdout is the strongest tool; where one is impossible, a staggered rollout or comparison with similar unaffected cities is a weaker substitute. State which you used.

Outcomes arrive late, so pick leading signals

Twelve-month retention is the real impact of a reorder feature, but nobody can wait a year. Teams therefore choose leading indicators, early measures believed to predict the slow ones. The belief itself must be checked: if retailers who reorder more in month two do not in fact stay longer, the indicator is decoration.

Impact is shared, so ownership is partial

A product manager is accountable for outcomes, since the team can influence behaviour directly. Impact depends on pricing, supply, sales and the economy as well. The discipline is to say what share you can defend, and the holdout arithmetic above is the model.

A metric that becomes a target gets gamed

If the team is rewarded for orders per retailer, someone will make reordering so frictionless that retailers accidentally duplicate orders. The orders count rises while returns and complaints rise too. Pair every outcome metric with a guardrail, a number that must not worsen, such as the rate of cancelled orders.

What the method cannot tell you

It does not tell you why the lift happened, whether a different feature would have done better, or whether the lift will last once novelty fades. Treat the number as evidence for a decision, never as the decision.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

In a consumer product, such as a music or food app, outcomes show quickly because behaviour is frequent and the user is one person. Holdouts are easy and the sample is large, so the discipline is mainly about resisting vanity numbers like downloads. In a B2B product, a decision may involve a buyer, an administrator and twenty end users, and contracts renew annually. The outcome of interest, say a finance team closing its books in four days instead of seven, may take two quarters to appear and sample sizes are small, so qualitative evidence carries more weight. Madhuban sits between the two: a business customer who behaves like a consumer, ordering weekly.

In a marketplace, one side's outcome can be the other side's cost. A feature that gives retailers more orders may crowd wholesalers' dispatch capacity, so outcomes have to be read on both sides at once. Madhuban's wholesaler negotiation in the second pass is exactly this.

7. Common mistakes

Celebrating the launch

Symptom: a launch email, a party, and no follow-up review. Misunderstanding: that done means shipped. Cheapest diagnostic: ask for the date on the calendar, set before launch, when the outcome will be read.

Quoting adoption as proof

Symptom: "40,000 people used it". Misunderstanding: that use equals benefit. Diagnostic: ask what the same people did before, and what similar non-users did during the same weeks.

Crediting the feature with the tide

Symptom: a chart with one steep line and no comparison. Misunderstanding: that any improvement after launch belongs to the launch. Diagnostic: overlay the holdout or an unaffected segment, and see how much of the rise it shares.

8. What good looks like

Before building, Meenal's team writes one page: the retailer problem, the target behaviour (orders per active retailer per month), a minimum worthwhile lift of 0.3 orders, the guardrail (cancellation rate not to rise), a 10 per cent random holdout and a review date of 28 April. They ship, they watch trial and repeat use weekly, and on 28 April they read the result against a bar they set in advance. The lift of 0.4 clears the bar of 0.3; the guardrail holds; the margin arithmetic recovers the ₹54 lakh in about 1.2 months. The credit-limit upgrade is proposed with the same one-page structure. Nothing in this is sophisticated. It is simply honest in sequence: claim first, measure second, judge third.

9. What Meenal decided

She rebuilt the slide. The ticks stayed, relabelled as outputs, but the first line now read: "Exposed retailers placed 0.4 more orders a month than the holdout, 28,800 extra orders, worth ₹46.8 lakh of monthly margin." She also disclosed what she did not know: the lift had been measured over eight weeks, during a season; the retention effect was unmeasured; and the wholesaler margin could erode the result, with ₹37.44 lakh a month as the downside case. The board funded the credit-limit upgrade, conditional on a holdout and a stated review date. Nitin Bhargava's only comment was that he would rather hear an honest 1.2 months than a confident "success".

What to learn next is the product manager's responsibility for outcomes, because this page showed how to measure a result without saying who answers for it; and then velocity illusions, which explore how a team can ship faster and still deliver less because the bottleneck moved somewhere the output count cannot see.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of the last feature your own team shipped: what did you say in the launch announcement, and what would the holdout have said? Second, if the margin had fallen to 1.5 per cent and the board still wanted the feature, what would you want to know about retailers before agreeing?
case40v1-pm.outcomes:
Tolaai Leaf Works: Twenty-Five Crore Kilos and Ninety-One Corrections

Jorhat, Assam — Sunday, 11 October 2026

1. The night before

The last flight to Guwahati had gone, so Tanvi Chaliha stayed in Jorhat, in the company's field office behind the civil hospital. Outside, the first cold night of the season was settling over the gardens along the Dhansiri road. On her laptop were two documents that did not agree.

The first was the board pre-read her co-founder and chief executive, Tridib Saikia, had circulated on 2 October, opening with a slide headed Six months of grower product. Nine releases. Twenty-three thousand eight hundred installs. Eleven districts. Two dialect voice prompts. A price page carrying the Tea Board's notified green-leaf price within two hours. Every line was true.

The second was a memo from Mercy Chepkoech, the data scientist in Nairobi whose hours overlapped with Assam only in the late afternoon. Of the 68,000 grower records in the platform's factory ledgers, 5,712 had opened the Tolaai Patti app in the previous thirty days. The dispute feature had produced 91 corrected weighing slips, worth ₹63,973 — ₹0.64 lakh — returned to growers. The work had cost ₹150.60 lakh.

Next morning, Monday 12 October, Tanvi had to tell the board what her team would be asked to move before the year ended. She had three options drafted and a suspicion that all three answered the wrong question. Assam's leaf would stop flowing in about five weeks.

2. How Tolaai came to be shaped this way

Tolaai Leaf Works was founded in March 2022 by Tridib Saikia, a mechanical engineer who had spent nine years on withering troughs and rolling machinery in Sivasagar, and Hiranya Kakoty, a chartered accountant from Guwahati. Their first product was not software for farmers. It was a ruggedised Bluetooth weighing terminal and an app called Tolaai Slip, sold to bought-leaf factories — processors that buy green leaf from small growers rather than owning gardens.

The pitch worked. Leaf arrived through agents who weighed it on spring balances and wrote figures in carbon-copy books; it was deducted for coarseness, re-weighed after shrinkage, and paid for weeks later. Tolaai Slip put a timestamped slip in the grower's hand and the same record in the factory's system.

In January 2023, needing volume, Tolaai made the decision that shaped everything after it: a four-year exclusive supply agreement with the terminal manufacturer — cheaper hardware against a minimum annual purchase, expiring 31 January 2027 — and, more consequentially, a master services agreement under which each factory owns all grower records and Tolaai merely processes them. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the factory is the data fiduciary and Tolaai the processor. The grower is not Tolaai's user. The grower is a row in somebody else's ledger.

By March 2026 Tolaai served 42 factories across Jorhat, Golaghat, Sivasagar, Dibrugarh and Tinsukia, with 1,260 terminals in the field, thirty per factory. Annual recurring revenue stood at ₹252.00 lakh: ₹176.40 lakh of platform fees at ₹4.20 lakh per factory, and ₹75.60 lakh of terminal rental at ₹500 a month each. The Series A of ₹26 crore raised in September 2024 from Tipam Capital Partners had left ₹6.40 crore in the bank against a burn of ₹52 lakh a month.

3. The industry around it

Assam produces roughly half of India's tea, and the change of the last two decades has been the rise of the small grower: a hectare or two, often on former paddy land, supplying a large share of the state's crop through several hundred bought-leaf factories. A grower sells green leaf by the kilo; a factory sells made tea, at auction through the Guwahati Tea Auction Centre or privately. Roughly 4.5 kilos of green leaf make one kilo of made tea.

What a grower receives is governed by the Tea Board of India's price-sharing formula, which notifies a minimum green-leaf price each month from the previous period's auction averages. For September 2026 the notified district price was ₹18.90 a kilo; across Tolaai's 42 factories the realised average was ₹18.50, the difference arising from deductions on leaf that failed the fine-leaf standard. On the 2,520 lakh kilos of green leaf that moved through the platform in the preceding twelve months, that forty paise is ₹10.08 crore — a figure Tanvi had never put in a deck, because she did not know whether it described underpayment, poor plucking, or the arithmetic of a quality standard.

The buying end is consolidating and particular. Tata Consumer Products, Hindustan Unilever's Brooke Bond, Wagh Bakri and Girnar compete on blend consistency; European Union buyers enforce residue limits stricter than domestic thresholds, and one failed consignment can shut a factory out of a buyer's list for a season. Kenyan tea, auctioned at Mombasa, sets the floor for plainer grades. UPI has meanwhile made it trivial to pay a grower in seconds.

4. What happened, and what has since looked different

In January 2026, at a Guwahati Tea Auction Centre seminar, Tridib heard small growers described as the least informed participants in the chain, and came away convinced Tolaai held the answer: it already had every weighing slip. If growers could see their slips, the district price and their payment status, the asymmetry would close. The board sanctioned ₹1.50 crore for two quarters.

Tolaai Patti version one shipped on 14 April 2026, a fortnight after Rongali Bihu, in Assamese and Hindi. On 22 June the price page went live. Forty-two days later, on 3 August, came the feature everyone had argued about: a button letting a grower query a weight or deduction, opening a ticket in the factory's console.

Three beliefs have since turned out differently. First, that installs would become use: Exhibit 2 shows how thin the chain became. Second, that field evidence and analytics would agree: Exhibit 3, presented eleven days after Mercy's memo, says close to the opposite. Third, that the factory and the grower wanted the same thing. On 3 September, Surjya Mahanta of Moran Leaf Works, Tolaai's largest customer by volume, telephoned Tridib to ask why he paid ₹4.20 lakh a year for software that taught his suppliers to argue with his agents.

Then on 26 September came a letter of intent from Warsaw. Tomasz Zielinski of Wisla Blending House wanted 11.20 lakh kilos of made tea a year, traceable to the plot and tested against EU residue limits, at ₹14 a kilo above his usual contract price. The volume is small — 50.40 lakh kilos of green leaf, two per cent of what Tolaai sees — but it would be Tolaai's first revenue that was not a licence fee.

5. The people

Tanvi Chaliha, vice-president of product, Jorhat. Position: no fourth quarter of shipping without naming the change it should make. Incentive: options vesting on the Series B. Not saying: she wrote the Patti specification, and Exhibit 2 is a verdict on it.

Tridib Saikia, co-founder and chief executive, Guwahati. Position: take Warsaw, make traceability the story, scale Patti alongside, since the installs prove growers want it. Not saying: he has told Tomasz informally that Tolaai can begin in January, and has not read Exhibit 6b.

Hiranya Kakoty, co-founder and chief financial officer, Guwahati. Position: Patti consumed ₹150.60 lakh and returned ₹0.64 lakh of measurable value; the factory product pays the salaries. Not saying: he thinks the honest move is to stop Patti, but not in front of Tridib.

Tarulata Phukan, head of field operations, Dibrugarh. Position: growers love Patti; the analytics measure the wrong thing, because growers share handsets. Incentive: her thirty-one field officers earn a bonus with an activation component, and they administered her survey face to face.

Trishala Mhaskar, engineering lead, Pune. Position: the architecture treats the factory as tenant and the grower as a record inside it, so a grower-first product means a new identity layer, ten engineer-weeks and a renegotiation with every factory. Not saying: the untouched user with most value is the agent.

Mercy Chepkoech, data scientist, Nairobi. Position: nothing in the data licenses a claim about outcomes, because the 68,000 denominator is not a count of growers. She wants a holdout design before any further build. Not saying: Exhibit 5's gap is the only number here that is both large and real.

Surjya Mahanta, managing partner, Moran Leaf Works, Golaghat. Position: he will pay for anything that brings leaf to his gate, not for a grievance channel. Incentive: his working capital, and agents who can move to a rival in a week. Not saying: his cycle is long because his own buyers pay him in 45 days.

Tomasz Zielinski, sourcing and quality director, Wisla Blending House, Warsaw. Position: he needs plot-level traceability and residue testing he can show retail customers. Not saying: his letter of intent rests on a twelve-week audit he has not scheduled, and is talking to Kenya in parallel.

6. Exhibits

Source: release log and analytics. The district line counts any district with one or more installs, not coverage: growers sell across district lines, so installs reached eleven districts although the 42 factories sit in five.

Every line of Exhibit 1 describes something Tolaai did; Exhibit 2, circulated on 7 September, describes what growers did.

Event logs joined to factory ledgers on mobile number. The 68,000 records are not de-duplicated: a grower selling to three factories appears three times, and field estimates of the overlap run from twelve to thirty per cent, so the last column is a loose bound. The query button existed only from 3 August, so all 357 queries arose in the 29 days to 31 August. The 91 revisions averaged 38 kilos; at ₹18.50 a kilo they returned ₹63,973.

Eleven days later Tarulata presented Exhibit 3, and the mood in the room changed.

Administered face to face by field officers in eight of the 42 catchments, on days they chose; their bonus includes an activation component. If 71.0% held across the ledger it implies roughly 48,280 weekly users against Exhibit 2's 5,712 thirty-day actives.

Exhibit 4 is the cost, and the one Hiranya reads aloud.

Fully loaded. The Melbourne contract runs to 31 December 2026, over thirteen times the Dibrugarh trainer rate per head. Excludes Tanvi, the 31 field officers and factory-side support, so the true figure is higher. Sanction: ₹1.50 crore.

Exhibit 5 exists because Mercy could not reconcile the factories' payment reports with what growers told field officers, and rebuilt the journey from bank and agent books.

"Ledger days": delivery date to the date the factory releases payment to the agent, the factory system's own measure. "Reconstructed days": delivery to the date the grower is credited or handed cash, from UPI timestamps and, for 31% of the sample, agents' books. The columns do not measure the same event. On the ₹466.20 crore of green leaf the platform carries in a year, the 12.9-day difference is about ₹16.48 crore of float at any moment.

Exhibits 6a and 6b are the Warsaw proposition, from the letter of intent and two calls.

From the letter of intent of 26 September 2026, subject to a twelve-week audit not yet scheduled. The premium is contracted to the factory, not to Tolaai or the grower, and no share for Tolaai is agreed; Tridib assumes 20%, or ₹31.36 lakh.

Tanvi's estimates from the 2025 pilot in two Golaghat clusters. No line says who bears the ₹55.00 lakh: the letter of intent is silent and the master services agreements do not contemplate it.

7. Voices

"Nine releases in six months and nearly 24,000 growers on the app. The fastest adoption of anything we have built. Why re-litigate it the week of the board?"Tridib Saikia, product review, 21 September
"23,800 installs. 14,280 verified. 5,712 opened it once in a month. 1,428 looked at a slip while it still mattered. Which of those do you mean when you say adoption?"Mercy Chepkoech, same review, joining at 4.30 p.m. Assam time
"Fourteen rupees a kilo more. On twenty-five crore kilos that is — " / "It is fourteen rupees on made tea, Tridib, and eleven lakh kilos of it. Three rupees eleven on green leaf, on two per cent of our volume."Tridib Saikia and Hiranya Kakoty, board pre-read call, 2 October
"Sir, the app is good. But if I raise a query on Thursday, on Friday the agent asks whether I still want the advance for my daughter's admission. I have taken ₹40,000 from him this year at no interest. Nobody in Jorhat has ever offered me that."Ajit Chetia, secretary of a growers' society near Teok, to Tarulata Phukan, 14 September
"My staff spent eleven hours last month answering queries your app generated. Eleven of the ninety-one corrections were mine. I do not mind paying for scales. I mind paying for a tribunal."Surjya Mahanta, email to Tridib Saikia and Hiranya Kakoty, 3 September
"Every option on this list adds a screen for the grower. Not one touches the agent, and the agent decides whose leaf gets on the truck."Trishala Mhaskar, engineering channel, 9 October

8. The options as Tanvi sees them

Option A — carry on and widen. Eighteen more factories sit in the pipeline across Nagaon and Udalguri; the drafted plan adds eight districts, a Bodo-language build and an offline mode. It keeps the delivery record intact, gives Tridib his slide, and costs about what the last two quarters did. It also assumes the 2.1% who looked at a slip in time will grow as a share if only there are more of them, which is the one thing Exhibit 2 does not support.

Option B — make one number the quarter's target. Freeze new districts and take on Exhibit 5's 12.9-day gap: UPI payment at the terminal, a payment status grower and factory both see, and a facility letting a factory pay in seven days without waiting for its own buyers. The prize is the largest number in the case; the risk is that it puts Tolaai between the factory and the agent whose advances hold the arrangement together, and asks factories to accept a definition of "paid" that is not theirs.

Option C — build for the buyer. Take the Warsaw letter of intent, stand up plot mapping and residue testing for 1,250 growers, and sell traceability. It is the first non-licence revenue and makes Tolaai legible to a Series B. It also needs the master services agreement reopened, since plot and spray records are grower data under a factory's fiduciary duty, and rests on an audit not yet scheduled by a buyer who is also talking to Kenya.

Tanvi had written all three on one page, then added in the margin two sentences she had shown nobody. All three assume the grower's problem is information. Ajit's problem is a ₹40,000 advance. If that is right, the customer may not be the grower at all, or the product may have to buy out the agent's credit before any screen matters — and neither is on her page.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board meets at eleven on Monday 12 October and will approve or refuse the next tranche of product spend. ₹6.40 crore of cash against ₹52 lakh a month gives 12.3 months, and Tipam says a Series B needs a second revenue line visible by March. Revenue today is ₹252.00 lakh a year from 42 factories who can leave on ninety days' notice.

Three hard edges constrain the choice. The terminal exclusivity expires on 31 January 2027, 111 days after the board meeting, and renewal carries a ₹1.05 crore minimum purchase Hiranya will not sign without knowing which product it serves. The master services agreements make every factory the data fiduciary under the DPDP Act, so grower-facing or buyer-facing uses of plot and payment data need consent architecture Tolaai does not have. And the leaf: plucking falls away through November and stops until April, so a field experiment has roughly five weeks — 11 October to about 15 November — before the only evidence is a survey.

Tanvi closed the laptop at a quarter to one. The pre-read was still open behind it, nine releases in green. She had been asked, six months ago, to make growers better informed, and had done exactly that: 23,800 installs, 41,900 price-page views, 91 corrected slips, ₹63,973. Somewhere in the same six months, ₹16.48 crore had sat in a gap between two definitions of the word paid, and nobody had been asked to move it.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Classify each line of Exhibit 1 as an output, an outcome or an impact. Which could rise while nothing changed for a single grower?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 cannot both describe the same population. Give three explanations for the gap, and say what evidence would separate them before 15 November.
  3. Exhibit 5's two columns measure different events. Which is the outcome Tolaai should be accountable for, and what does your answer imply about who its customer is?
  4. Using Exhibits 4, 6a and 6b, was Patti worth ₹150.60 lakh? Say which inputs are measured and which assumed, including the ₹55.00 lakh and the unagreed revenue share.
  5. Tridib wants Warsaw to be the story; Surjya Mahanta pays the bills and does not want a grievance channel; Ajit Chetia's constraint is an interest-free advance. Can one product serve all three? If not, whose outcome does Tolaai choose, and what does it stop doing?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Tanvi put on one slide, what single measure does she ask the team to own until April, and what does she say to Tipam when they ask why nine releases were not the answer?
exp40v2-pm.outcomes:
Outputs, outcomes and impact

A case treatment for practitioners who must referee the argument, not recite it

1. Two rooms, six weeks apart

On Monday 20 July 2026, Devyani Kulkarni, vice-president of product at Panghat Water Works, sat in an Ahmedabad mill office with a page written for the board meeting of 3 August. Panghat builds solar-powered community water ATMs — a resident taps a prepaid card and draws twenty litres of treated water for ₹5 — sold on service contracts to municipal corporations across Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana. The page said 1,240 units were live in nine municipalities, uptime held at 97.4 per cent, firmware v4 had shipped chlorination telemetry in February, and the ward-engineer app had replaced paper logbooks. Girish Vaidya, the founder, wanted ₹7.40 crore for 400 more units at ₹1.85 lakh of capital each. Every line described something Panghat had done, not what a household did differently, or whether the ₹7.40 crore would come back.

Six weeks earlier, on Tuesday 9 June, Hemant Bhide, head of product at Praroop Document Systems in Mumbai, took a harder call. Praroop extracts structured fields from trade-finance paperwork — letters of credit, bills of lading, insurance certificates — for banks working under RBI and DGFT rules. Eight weeks after the v6 model shipped on 14 April, Lalita Ranganathan, head of trade operations at Praroop's largest client — a private-sector bank processing 1,42,000 documents a month — opened the renewal conversation ahead of 30 September with one sentence: "Your accuracy went up and my headcount did not go down." Praroop's release note was true: field accuracy had risen from 91.4 to 96.2 per cent, earned by an engineering pod in Kraków and verified by Wanjiru Kamau, the data-science lead in Nairobi. Lalita was also right.

Panghat's outcomes are invisible without fieldwork; Praroop's sit inside someone else's standard operating procedure.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

An output is an artefact the team produces and controls: a release, 1,240 installed units, a model with a stated accuracy. An outcome is a change in the behaviour of people outside the team — a household drawing water elsewhere, a checker clicking "accept" instead of re-keying twelve fields. An impact is the durable consequence: margin, contracts retained, cost removed, illness avoided. Controllability falls at each step and latency rises — outputs are known on ship day, outcomes in weeks, impact in quarters.

The vocabulary is borrowed. Programme evaluation built it first — United Way's 1996 Measuring Program Outcomes and the Kellogg Foundation logic model separated inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact because donors kept being shown clinics built rather than patients treated, and Carol Weiss insisted each arrow be a falsifiable belief. Management ran a parallel line from Drucker's objectives to Grove's High Output Management (1983), where "output" means a whole organisation's output — nearer to today's outcome. The current framing is Ries's "vanity metrics" (2011), Perri's build trap (2018), Seiden's outcome as "a change in human behaviour that drives business results" (2019), Torres's split between product and business outcomes (2021), and Cagan's insistence that teams be given problems rather than features.

It would be comfortable to stop there. Four positions disagree, and each signs some propositions and refuses others. The outcome-accountability school signs that a feature roadmap is a liability and a team should be judged on a behaviour change it was asked to produce; it will not sign that a team can be held to a revenue number shaped by pricing, supply and the monsoon. The controllable-input school, clearest in Amazon's weekly business review as described by Bryar and Carr, signs the reverse: lagging outcomes are not actionable, so management should name the few inputs it owns. It will not sign that outcome metrics belong in an operating review at all, since a number nobody can move this week produces discussion rather than action. The causal-inference school (Rubin; Kohavi, Tang and Xu) signs that no outcome claim is admissible without a counterfactual, and refuses a before-and-after chart as evidence. The craft-and-appetite school, sharpest in Basecamp's Shape Up, signs that in small products measurement noise exceeds the effect and fixed appetite is the honest unit; it will not sign that every piece of work must carry a metric.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice has five moves; the third and fifth are usually left implicit. The first writes the chain as a sentence naming a behaviour: households within walking distance will take their drinking water from the jal point instead of an untreated borewell or a tanker, every week. The second instruments exposure, trial and habit separately: a product nobody meets cannot produce an outcome. Devyani's team metered 240 of the 1,240 units and surveyed their catchments in June 2026.

Table 1. Panghat exposure-to-habit funnel, mean of 240 metered units, June 2026. Each row is a subset of the one above.

The third move, almost always skipped, decomposes the outcome by what it displaced. Of the 57 primary-source households, 31 had drunk untreated borewell or tanker water, 14 had boiled at home and 12 had bought twenty-litre jars; the subsets sum to 57. Only the first group — 54.4 per cent of the 57, or 31 × 1,240 = 38,440 households fleet-wide — is a health effect Panghat can claim; the other 26 are a transfer between safe sources. Reporting "70,680 households now rely on Panghat" is true and lets the listener infer something false.

The fourth move converts behaviour to money. A ₹5 vend splits into ₹1.80 to the kiosk operator, ₹0.90 of electricity and consumables, and ₹2.30 of contribution. The fleet averaged 105 vends per unit per day in June, so a mean unit contributes 105 × ₹2.30 × 30 = ₹7,245 a month and repays ₹1.85 lakh in 185,000 ÷ 7,245 = 25.5 months. Praroop's mechanics turn on composition. A document is touchless only if all twelve critical fields are correct, so if field errors are independent, 91.4 per cent field accuracy implies a pass rate of 0.91412 = 34.0 per cent and 96.2 per cent implies 0.96212 = 62.8 per cent. A 4.8-point gain in the output nearly doubles the modelled outcome — an argument in Praroop's favour Hemant had never made, because he had never computed it.

The observed touchless rate moved only from 31 to 38 per cent, because of bank policy: documents above USD 50,000 of face value get mandatory four-eye review whatever the machine says, and those are 36 per cent of volume. Only 64 per cent are eligible, so the ceiling is 0.64 × 62.8 = 40.2 per cent, and 38 is 94.5 per cent of what was available. On the eligible denominator the rate is 38 ÷ 64 = 59.4 per cent, within 3.4 points of the modelled 62.8. The rest sits behind a threshold the bank sets.

Of that, ₹2.75 crore came from v5 and the platform and the v6 release added ₹62.03 lakh. A further ₹2.20 crore a year — ₹18.31 lakh a month — needs the bank to change its own threshold. The output was Praroop's; the largest remaining slice of the outcome is Lalita's.

4. When the framing applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions are testable claims. The behaviour must be observable at a cadence shorter than the decision. Panghat passes for the second arrow — vend telemetry arrives nightly — but the displacement question needed a quarterly door survey; Praroop passes fully. A credible counterfactual must be constructible. Praroop fails: it cannot withhold extraction from a random tenth of a bank's regulated documents, so it relies on staggered branch rollouts. Panghat partly passes: installation is sequenced across wards, so difference-in-differences against not-yet-installed wards is available. The behaviour must be monotonically linked to value. Both pass; section 8 shows a company where it did not.

The framing misleads in three cases: where the product is a legal obligation, such as Praroop's audit trail for RBI inspection, so the justification is compliance; where the effect is smaller than the measurement noise, so the review manufactures false precision; and where two or three teams jointly produce an outcome, so per-team targets invite each to claim the same movement.

5. Hard edges

Panghat's hardest seam is organisational: municipal engineers choose where each unit is bolted, and the 248 stranded units are mostly sites picked for political visibility near ward offices rather than foot traffic. Panghat owns the output and the telemetry; a third party owns the largest determinant of the outcome. Mature firms here rarely demand control — they re-price, charging less where the municipality accepts Panghat's siting model, converting an uncontrollable outcome into a contractual input.

Multi-product organisations hit the double-count. Panghat's four product pods claimed FY26 annual impacts of ₹2.1 crore, ₹1.4 crore, ₹0.9 crore and ₹1.2 crore, totalling ₹5.6 crore, while company gross contribution rose ₹3.1 crore — an over-claim of 1.81 times. Nobody lied: each pod used a defensible local counterfactual and overlapping effects were double-counted. The unpopular fix treats the P&L movement as a budget constraint and makes pods argue about shares.

Two-sided dynamics bite here too: a stranded unit's operator earns ₹1.80 × 25 = ₹45 a day, ₹1,350 a month, against ₹387 a day, ₹11,610 a month in the top band, so attrition at stranded sites depresses vends further and the distribution widens by itself. The AI-native equivalent is drift: Praroop's accuracy decays as banks change templates, so a constant outcome needs continuous output.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert

The average is a composition, not a fact. The tell is a headline rate quoted without a distribution; a mean of 25.5 months formed from 12.5 and 107.2 supports no decision. The obvious reading, that the average describes a typical unit, fails whenever the variable is multiplicative, as utilisation is.

Component quality compounds against you. The tell is accuracy quoted per field when the user's unit of work is a whole document. Twelve fields at 96.2 per cent give 62.8 per cent of documents; the intuition that a 96 per cent model yields a 96 per cent experience is the most expensive arithmetic error in AI product work.

The denominator is a political choice. The tell is a rate whose denominator is never named in the same sentence. Praroop's 38 and 59.4 per cent are the same reality; the first invites a renewal fight, the second a joint policy conversation. State both, and say which bears on the decision.

A ceiling is more informative than a gap. The tell is a target set by ambition, not by what is attainable. Knowing the ceiling is 40.2 per cent reframes 38 per cent from failure to 94.5 per cent of the available, and moves the next investment from the model to the threshold. Adoption, substitution and incrementality are also three things: Panghat's 57 primary-source households hold only 31 substitutions away from unsafe water.

Counterfactuals form a ladder, and you must name your rung. Before-and-after is the bottom, a randomised holdout the top; staggered rollout, matched wards and difference-in-differences lie between. The tell is a chart with one line, and an expert never says "we cannot experiment here" without naming the rung climbed instead.

The measurable outcome drifts from the one you care about. Panghat measures litres and cares about waterborne illness, which it cannot see at unit level; the tell is a proxy nobody re-validates. The same mismatch governs timing: a 90-day dashboard cannot judge a 96-month asset, and penalises wards where trust in treated water takes a monsoon to build.

Every rewarded outcome metric becomes a target and then a lie. Goodhart's law is a prediction, not a caution; the tell is a metric rising while its natural companion goes unreported. Pair each outcome with a guardrail that must not worsen: for Panghat, chlorine-residual compliance to IS 10500; for Praroop, touchless documents later found wrong in audit.

Impact is shared, so claim a share and say so. The tell is a team claiming a round P&L number with no mention of the pricing or policy changes that ran concurrently. Praroop's defensible claim is ₹62.03 lakh a year for v6 within ₹3.37 crore of realised saving, with a further ₹2.20 crore available only if the client lifts its own threshold. Small claims that survive scrutiny compound into credibility; large ones do not survive the second meeting.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products behaviour is frequent and individual, holdouts are cheap, and the discipline is refusing vanity numbers. In B2B and enterprise the buyer, administrator and end user differ, and the outcome may be gated by the client's own policy, so the product manager's real work is often helping a customer change a procedure. In platform and marketplace products one side's outcome is often the other side's cost, as the operator-income arithmetic shows. In hardware the asset life sets the measurement window and placement dominates, and in AI-native products composition and drift are the structural facts, with the outcome mediated by a reviewer's trust, which moves slower than the model.

By stage the honest statement is narrow. A pre-product-market-fit team has too little traffic for credible counterfactuals and should lean on qualitative evidence and fast output cycles; the craft school is right at that size. At scale, experimentation is cheap and the constraint becomes attribution across teams. "Early-stage companies should not care about outcomes" is false: the instrument changes, not the question.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Panghat's siting rule. If the 400 new units land in the distribution of the top two bands — a mean of (372 × 120 + 248 × 215) ÷ 620 = 158 vends a day — each contributes 158 × ₹2.30 × 30 = ₹10,902 a month and repays ₹1.85 lakh in 17.0 months, against 25.5 months in the current fleet distribution. That difference, not the ₹7.40 crore, is the subject of the 3 August meeting.

Praroop's renewal. Hemant's proposal held the licence at ₹1.42 crore and added a joint objective: if the bank lifts the four-eye gate from USD 50,000 to USD 250,000 for documents Praroop scores above a confidence threshold, the modelled saving rises by ₹18.31 lakh a month, a quarter of it payable as a success fee.

A failure. Rangrez Apparel Industries, a Bengaluru direct-to-consumer label, decided in January 2026 that its outcome metric would be weekly sessions per active user, then 2.4, and shipped a personalised feed and notification engine on 3 March. By July sessions reached 3.6, a 50 per cent gain, and the team was congratulated.

The notification engine had pulled users into impulse purchases of ill-fitting garments; sessions were an engagement proxy with no validated link to a purchase that stuck. The failure was definitional, not statistical: sessions are a behaviour, so they met Seiden's test, and were the wrong behaviour.

The recovery was unglamorous. By September sessions had fallen to 3.0 and net contribution recovered to ₹407.19 lakh — 71.7 per cent of the ₹73.39 lakh loss reclaimed, leaving ₹20.79 lakh a month, 4.9 per cent of the baseline, gone with the churned customers. An outcome metric must be paired with the economic quantity it is believed to drive.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Launch as conclusion. Sign: no review date set before the ship date. Diagnostic: "On what date, and against what number, will we decide this worked?" Caught late, the next quarter is already committed. Adoption quoted as benefit. Sign: the deck leads with users touched. Diagnostic: "What did these same people do before, and what did comparable untouched people do in the same weeks?"

Proxy gaming. Sign: the metric rises faster than any plausible mechanism. Diagnostic: "Which companion number would deteriorate if we were gaming this?" Rangrez's cost of late detection was ₹20.79 lakh a month. Impact double-counting. Sign: team claims exceed the P&L movement. Diagnostic: "Reconcile these claims against the gross-margin line." Caught late, it destroys the credibility of every future claim.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should a team be accountable for an outcome it does not control? The outcome school at its strongest: accountability for outputs reliably produces busy teams building unwanted things, and the only cure is to hold teams to a behaviour change and let them choose the means; the evidence is a long record of feature factories with healthy velocity and flat retention. The input school at its strongest: an uncontrollable target produces learned helplessness or creative accounting, and managing a small set of owned inputs has scaled further than any outcome-OKR system. For the first to be wrong, teams held to outcomes would have to game or despair systematically; for the second, input-managed firms would drift into local optima invisible to the chosen inputs. Both patterns are observed, and Devyani cannot control siting.

Is a holdout always worth its cost? The experimentation school holds that without one you are guessing, and at Praroop's volumes the statistics are trivial. The opposing case is not laziness: withholding a compliance control from a random tenth of regulated documents is not permissible, and withholding safe drinking water from a random tenth of wards is not defensible.

Can the frame price long-horizon craft? Trust, accessibility and architectural quality surface over years. The craft school says the frame underfunds them; the metrics school answers that "it will pay off later" is unfalsifiable and has funded much waste, and neither has a measurement the other accepts. And who owns impact? Some firms assign impact to finance and outcomes to product, arguing that a product manager modelling margin will model it favourably; others insist the product manager own the whole chain. Panghat's ₹5.6 crore against ₹3.1 crore is the best evidence for the first view and the best argument for the second, which is why the question stays open.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this says "outcomes, not outputs" and renames the roadmap columns. Someone who has internalised it states the behaviour change in a sentence a user would recognise, before the work starts, with a minimum worthwhile effect attached; names the rung of the counterfactual ladder they stand on, unprompted; brings a distribution, not an average; and volunteers the number that weakens their case — the 248 stranded units, the ₹62.03 lakh of a ₹3.37 crore saving that is genuinely theirs. A disconfirmed chain is a result, because it was written down as a belief.

12. What each protagonist decided

Devyani went to the 3 August board with the band table rather than the fleet average, asking for the ₹7.40 crore on two conditions: Panghat's footfall model governs siting, with the tiered contract as the fallback where a municipality insists on choosing, and the 248 stranded units are assessed for relocation before any new installation. She also disclosed the uncomfortable figure — only 31 of 57 primary-source households per unit represent a displaced unsafe source — because the health claim appears in Panghat's municipal tenders, and she preferred to narrow it herself than have a procurement officer do it later.

Hemant reframed the renewal into a joint design problem, showing Lalita the composition curve, the 40.2 per cent ceiling, the 94.5 per cent attainment against it, and the ₹18.31 lakh a month behind her own threshold. He claimed ₹62.03 lakh of annual value for v6, not ₹3.37 crore. The licence renewed at ₹1.42 crore, with a success fee attached to a threshold change the bank's risk committee would decide in November.

  1. Panghat's customers buy units installed, not litres consumed. If the contract rewards the output and Devyani manages to the outcome, who absorbs the cost of the 248 stranded units?
  2. Praroop's defensible v6 claim is ₹62.03 lakh a year against a ₹1.42 crore licence. Is a vendor reporting its true marginal contribution disadvantaged against one reporting the full ₹3.37 crore?
  3. Rangrez's sessions metric met the formal definition of an outcome and still destroyed ₹73.39 lakh a month. What pre-ship test would have caught it?

13. Going deeper

What a product manager does supplies the job description this page prices: outcomes are the accountability, outputs the instrument. The PM's responsibility for outcomes takes up the question section 10 leaves open — who answers for a number they influence but cannot command. Velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved explains why faster output can lower outcomes, as Rangrez found. PM myths vs reality dismantles the mini-CEO story that makes shared impact feel like personal failure, and origins of product management traces the brand-manager inheritance that put outputs on the roadmap. PM vs PMM vs TPM vs project manager vs founder matters because each role's natural metric sits at a different link, and PM archetypes shows who over-trusts the output end. How the PM job changes by company stage develops section 7's claim; the end-to-end product lifecycle places the measurement window inside the arc from discovery to sunset.
case20v1-pm.outcomes:
Navachar Systems: Eleven Features and a Question

A case on outputs, outcomes and impact

1. Opening

On the morning of Friday, 9 October 2026, Neha Nambisan, head of product at Navachar Systems, opened a slide that her own team had built and could not decide whether to be proud of it. It was titled "Q2 delivery" and it was mostly green. Eleven of twelve planned items had shipped. Twenty-four lakh WhatsApp fee reminders had gone out to parents. Three hundred of 420 schools had switched the feature on. The board pack and the October to December roadmap were both due on 16 October.

Nothing on the slide said whether a single additional parent had paid on time because of any of it. Neha had to decide what the next quarter's team would be asked to move: things shipped, parent behaviour, or school finances.

2. Company background

Navachar Systems, headquartered in Pune, sells a fee-collection and parent-communication app to private schools in Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns, including Nashik, Nagpur and Warangal. Navachar charges the school a flat ₹60 per enrolled student per year. With 3,50,000 students on the platform, annual revenue is ₹2.10 crore (₹210 lakh).

Large school-ERP vendors bundle fee modules into expensive suites, while many schools simply use a UPI QR code or Razorpay payment links and chase parents by phone. Navachar sits between the two. Parents pay through UPI under NPCI rules, and because the platform holds guardians' contact details, every decision also sits under the DPDP Act, 2023.

School principals kept telling the founder-CEO, Nitin Awasthi, that parents paid late. So on 3 August 2026 Navachar launched Smart Reminders, a scheduled WhatsApp message with a UPI payment link, sent before and after each fee due date.

3. The situation

Term-2 fees were due on 15 September, just over six weeks after launch. Neha's team shipped steadily throughout the quarter. By the end of September it had delivered eleven roadmap items against twelve planned. Exhibit 1 shows the scorecard Nitin liked to read aloud. Every line is something Navachar did or built; none is something a parent did differently.

Source: Navachar product analytics. "Read" means the WhatsApp read receipt was returned.

Nuno Castro, the data scientist in Lisbon, was the first to ask the uncomfortable question. He had noticed that on-time payment rose in every school during the autumn term, whether or not reminders were on. He proposed comparing the 300 enabled schools with the 120 that had not switched the feature on. Exhibit 2 is that comparison.

"On time" means paid on or before the due date. The blended rates are student-weighted. Schools opted in themselves, so the groups are not randomly assigned.

The gain in reminder schools was six percentage points, which looked like a triumph. The gain in schools without reminders was three. Nuno's reading was that the first three points would have arrived anyway. Had the enabled schools followed the other group's trend, 58% of their 2,70,000 students, or 1,56,600, would have paid on time. They actually reached 1,64,700, so the feature's attributable effect was 8,100 more students paying on time, three points rather than six. He cautioned that schools opted in themselves, which could flatter the estimate.

From Osaka, Naoki Mori, the lead designer, had a different worry. Support tickets showed that 5,400 families, 2.0% of the 2,70,000 students in reminder schools, had complained about reminder tone or frequency. Naoki feared the product was producing irritation faster than payment.

4. The people

Neha Nambisan, head of product, Pune. She owns the roadmap and the quarterly metrics.

Nitin Awasthi, founder and CEO, Pune. He wants the board to see momentum and a story about scale. He favours the largest ambition on the table.

Nimesh Parekh, head of sales, Ahmedabad. Paid on new schools signed, he wants more channels to show prospects.

Nuno Castro, data scientist, Lisbon, and Naoki Mori, lead designer, Osaka. Nuno wants a clean measurement before any further build. Naoki wants the experience fixed before volume rises.

5. The value chain, and what the evidence shows

Diagram. The three levels, with this case's figures. Schematic only; the figures are from Exhibits 1 to 3.

Exhibit 3 follows the chain from Exhibit 1's output through Exhibit 2's outcome to the impact on schools, and sets it against what Navachar spent. WhatsApp business messages cost Navachar roughly ₹0.50 each, so 24,00,000 messages cost ₹12,00,000, or ₹12 lakh. The 8,100 additional on-time payers, at an average term fee of ₹9,000, mean ₹7.29 crore collected by the due date.

The ₹7.29 crore is cash brought forward, not new revenue to schools or to Navachar. The renewal figures are early: the difference rests on 25 schools, so it is a weak signal, and renewals are not due until December.

Read together, the exhibits show an awkward but useful pattern. The output was large; the outcome was real but half the headline. And the impact that matters most to Navachar, whether schools renew and tell other principals, is still invisible, because the renewal comparison is too small to carry any weight yet.

6. The options

Option A: Keep shipping against the plan. The Q3 roadmap lists twelve items, including voice-call reminders in Hindi and Marathi, a Telugu template set and a principal dashboard. Nimesh would have more to show prospects, and the team's delivery record stays strong. The cost: no item is tied to a change in parent behaviour, and complaints would scale with volume.

Option B: Make on-time payment the quarter's target and learn what moves it. The team would freeze new channels, fix duplicate messages to families who have already paid, and run a randomised test in the 120 schools yet to switch on and in new schools. Timing, tone and a split-payment link would be tested against a held-out group. The success measure would be the percentage of students paying on time, with complaints as a guardrail. The board pack would show fewer shipped items.

Option C: Aim directly at impact. Nitin's preference is to partner with a lender and offer parents instalment fee loans, so that schools receive money at the start of each term regardless of parents' cash flow. This would be the most valuable outcome for schools and could add new revenue. But it needs regulatory work with the RBI's digital lending rules, takes more than two quarters and rests on an unproven assumption that late payment is a cash-flow problem, not a forgetfulness problem.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Classify each line of Exhibit 1 as an output, an outcome or an impact.
  2. In Exhibit 2, why is the six-point rise in reminder schools an unreliable estimate of the feature's effect? What would you need to know about how schools came to switch the feature on?
  3. Using Exhibit 3, is Smart Reminders worth its cost? Which parts of your answer rest on assumptions?
  4. Which option would you choose, what single metric would the team own, and what would make you change your mind before the December renewals?

8. A note for the learner

This case is about the three levels at which a product team can claim success. An output is what the team produced: a feature, a message, a release. An outcome is a change in what users do because of it. An impact is a change in the health of the user's or the company's situation that follows. A product manager is accountable for outcomes: outputs can be delivered perfectly while nothing changes, and impact arrives too late to steer by. State every piece of work as a chain, and ask at each link what evidence shows it held.

A well-reasoned answer notices three things. First, Exhibit 1 measures effort, not change. Second, a naive reading of Exhibit 2 would overclaim by a factor of two, and Third, Exhibit 3 looks favourable, about ₹148 per additional on-time payer against ₹9,000 of fee, but its renewal evidence is thin and its schools self-selected.

One defensible path is Option B, with a defined route towards C. The reasoning runs as follows. Reminders work modestly and irritate noticeably, so the cheapest learning is how to message, not which channels to add. A randomised holdout removes the self-selection problem that limits the current estimate. On-time payment is an outcome the team can move within a term, whereas renewals are an impact that lags by a year. If the test shows that split-payment links lift on-time payment materially, that is evidence for the cash-flow hypothesis behind Option C, and Navachar could then approach a lender with data rather than a hope. Option A makes velocity the goal; Option C is a solution still looking for evidence.

If Neha reports the quarter to the board as "24 lakh reminders sent, 8,100 more families paying on time, ₹7.29 crore collected earlier, 2.0% complaining," she turns a delivery review into a conversation about change.
exp40v2-pm.ethics.intro:
The PM's responsibility for outcomes

Own what the product does to people, not only for them. Foundations › The PM Role & Foundations.

1. Two rooms in one October

On Monday 5 October 2026, Omkar Vaishampayan put one scatter on the screen at Pathik Mobility Network, a Bengaluru last-mile two-wheeler delivery network operating in seven cities. Prerna Barve, group product manager for rider earnings, had shipped Peak Pay in June: an evening bonus paying ₹180 for twelve trips between 7 p.m. and 11 p.m., ₹320 for sixteen and ₹520 for twenty. Over the twenty-five peak evenings from Monday 31 August to Friday 2 October, Pathik logged 50,000 rider-evenings in Bengaluru and paid ₹75.80 lakh. By the only measures set, it worked.

Omkar's scatter showed what nobody had measured. He flagged every rider-evening in which a rider sat one or two trips short of a tier with forty-five minutes or less left, then closed the gap: sprints, 6,750 of the 27,000 tiered rider-evenings, 25.0 per cent. On sprint evenings the handset's accelerometer recorded 11.2 risk events per 100 kilometres — hard braking, overspeed, phone handling while rolling — against 4.0 elsewhere. Of Pathik's 140 accident claims in the window, 49 of the 140, 35.0 per cent, came from sprint evenings. Osheen Talreja, who ran rider support, already heard it: riders calling at 10:50 p.m. to ask whether an order counted. Rituraj Kanitkar, the chief operating officer, wanted a decision by 16 October.

Rupali Dandekar had eighteen days. On Friday 2 October, Pushkar Nene handed her the pilot read-out for Padav Flow, the bed-and-discharge planning module her team sells at Padav Clinical Systems in Pune. Flow scores each medical inpatient every morning for discharge readiness and ranks a worklist. At Parijat Hospitals Group's 560-bed Nagpur hospital, the ninety days from 1 July to Monday 28 September read as the best slide Padav had owned: average length of stay down from 4.6 days to 4.1, and 8,100 discharges against 7,200 in the ninety days to 30 June. Thirty-day unplanned readmissions, on the same page, ran at 11.0 per cent against 9.0 at baseline. Padav's contract covers Parijat's 2,400 beds at ₹310 a bed a month, ₹89.28 lakh a year, and a twelve-hospital rollout decision was due on Tuesday 20 October.

2. The idea, and who refuses to sign it

State the proposition precisely, because its force lies in its boundaries. A product manager is accountable for the changes in people's circumstances that the product causes — including changes nobody intended and nobody measured — to the extent that the mechanism was foreseeable from what the team knew, or detectable by instruments the team could reasonably have built. Causes includes effects routed through someone else's choice, because designing an incentive causes the behaviour it rewards. The last clause is the one practitioners resist: it makes not looking a decision you answer for.

The vocabulary predates product management. Avedis Donabedian's 1966 framework split quality into structure, process and outcome and insisted outcome be measured on the patient, not the clinic. Herbert Simon established that organisations choose not what is true but what to attend to. Goodhart and Campbell supplied the failure mechanism: a measure pressed into service as a target distorts what it measures. Helen Nissenbaum named the organisational obstacle in 1996 as the problem of many hands: where harm emerges from many correct local decisions, no one hand holds it.

Four positions divide practitioners. The fiduciary school holds that the duty runs to the firm and externalities are the legislature's business: it signs “do not deceive and do not break the law” and refuses “forgo lawful profit to avoid a foreseeable harm.” The stakeholder school, after R. Edward Freeman and Donald Berwick's Triple Aim, signs “a product with an uninstrumented harm channel is not fit to ship.” The systems school, Deming's heirs, treats responsibility as instrumentation and blame as noise: it signs “if nobody is looking, nobody is responsible” but never “Prerna is culpable.” The procedural school, how most risk functions think, signs only “follow a reasonable process and record it.”

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice is a sequence, and most of it is measurement design rather than ethics. Write the intended outcome as a claim about a person with a named mechanism: not “raise peak supply” but “a rider who would stop at 8 p.m. stays out until 11 because the marginal hour pays better, and earns more without riding harder.” The italicised clause is the testable one, and the one Peak Pay broke. Enumerate the parties, including non-users: at Padav, the patient, the carer at home, the nurse whose discharge-coordination minutes a ranked list rations, and the payer. Compute each proxy's base rate before the change, choose the measurement design — denominator, sampling frame, response mechanism — and pre-register both the trade rule and the decision right. Then segment, and price the harm in two ledgers, expecting them to disagree.

Two quantities travel well. The concentration ratio is a segment's share of the excess harm divided by its share of the population: 1 means evenly spread, above 2 means an average is lying to you. Pathik's sprint evenings are 13.5 per cent of all 50,000 rider-evenings and carry 35.0 per cent of the claims, a ratio of 2.59. Harm-adjusted contribution is margin less a priced estimate of the harm, taken once for what lands on the firm and once for what lands on everyone.

Read Exhibit 1 as a redistribution, not a saving. Design R costs ₹1.31 lakh less in total, but moves ₹17.94 lakh towards the 23,000 evenings that earn nothing today and takes ₹10.65 lakh from the 4,500 highest-output evenings — ₹236.60 an evening from the riders best at the job. That transfer is itself an outcome Prerna would own. The cliff also does work: Rituraj's objection was that a flat rate leaves restaurants short.

4. Conditions, stated as tests

An expert states the conditions as claims that can fail. First: the product changes behaviour rather than serving a stated request. Peak Pay exists to change when and how fast riders ride; Flow changes a clinician's sequencing. A product that renders an invoice when asked fails this test, and treating it as a site of moral hazard wastes attention. Second: the affected party is not the deciding party. At Padav the hospital buys and the patient bears; at Pathik the rider chooses inside a payoff curve Prerna drew. Third: the harm is detectable at acceptable cost. Omkar's classifier took four engineer-days; where detection costs more than the product earns, narrow the claims instead.

The idea misleads twice over. Where the causal chain is long and crowded — a payroll product held to household budgeting three steps downstream — a PM who accepts the frame drowns. And where the contested behaviour is the purpose, “unintended” is a dodge.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Padav is the regulated, enterprise and AI-native case at once. Flow is clinical decision support, so under India's device rules and the Clinical Establishments Act the accountable party is the discharging physician, not the vendor. Legally Rupali is clear. Practically the vendor chose the features, the ranking and the default, and nobody at Parijat Nagpur can inspect any of them: Dr Padmaja Vanjari, the medical superintendent, signs a discharge policy she did not design. In two-sided markets the seam runs between sides: cutting rider risk is paid for in restaurant service levels, and whoever owns that side has no metric rewarding it. With hardware the harm channel outlives the release.

What mature firms do, as distinct from what their principles pages say, is run two systems: a formal one — risk committees, launch sign-offs, model cards — good against known harms and useless against novel ones, and an informal one, a senior person or two who ask unwelcome questions and are tolerated because they have been right before. Patrícia Loureiro, a clinical-safety consultant in Porto retained two days a month, was that system at Padav, and her value was having no delivery commitment to protect.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert

Foreseeability is a property of your instruments, and your instruments are your choice. The tell-tale is a team that describes a harm fluently but cannot state its denominator. Pathik's riders had complained for months; what was missing was a rate. The decision not to build Omkar's classifier was taken implicitly at every sprint planning for four months.

Averages conceal concentrated harm, and concentration is measurable. The tell-tale is a flat rate with no segment cut: “readmissions went from 9.0 to 11.0 per cent.” At Parijat the rise was almost entirely one group, concentration ratio 5.4. Ask whose two points.

Sometimes the harm is revenue. The tell-tale is a harm that enters the profit-and-loss account with a plus sign. Parijat's excess readmissions consumed 939.6 bed-days and billed roughly ₹46.04 lakh of contribution, so no financial report would flag them. An expert hunts the cases where the incentive runs the wrong way.

A proxy has a false-positive rate, and acting on it is itself an intervention. Some of Omkar's sprinters are fast riders finishing a nearby cluster, and Design R takes ₹236.60 an evening from the top band, part of it from people never at risk. A conservative proxy relocates harm rather than removing it.

Measurement design dominates metric choice. The tell-tale is a harm number from a voluntary channel. Rozana's survey, below, asked the right question and read 6.4 per cent, because the people who answer a wellness survey are the people the product is working for. The frame was broken, not the metric.

A harm rate without a control is a number, not evidence. Figure 1's gap is consistent with Peak Pay causing risky riding and equally consistent with risk-tolerant riders selecting into sprints. Pathik launched in all seven cities at once, destroying that comparison.

The counterfactual belongs in the accounting but is not a licence. The tell-tale is “they would have done it anyway.” Riders chased daily targets before Peak Pay; patients were discharged on judgement before Flow ranked them. Both change the magnitude attributed to the product without dissolving the duty, and Pathik's estimate of 1,500 residual sprint evenings carries Exhibit 2.

Pre-commitment beats conviction. The tell-tale is a threshold that moves, because the mind reading a good revenue figure is not the mind that wrote the guardrail. Padav had the readmission metric in the read-out; what it lacked was a June note saying which reading would stop the rollout.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the user and the affected party coincide, harms are behavioural, and the data already sits in the event stream; the constraint is willingness to look. In B2B and enterprise the buyer and the bearer diverge, and the hard part is contractual — Padav's agreement says nothing about readmissions, so Rupali cannot demand the data she needs. On platforms every outcome is distributive, and the honest decision says which side pays. In hardware the channel persists after release and recall is expensive, so pre-launch instrumentation earns a premium. In AI products the mechanism is opaque even to its builders, which makes segment cuts non-negotiable.

By stage the duty is constant and the mechanism is not. At twenty people the enemy is survival pressure, which makes looking feel like a luxury. At Pathik's 1,400 it is diffusion: four teams each own a correct slice and the harm lives between them. At enterprise scale it is believing someone else owns it.

8. Three worked cases

Parijat Nagpur: a real gain with a concentrated cost

Ask what the pilot cohort's 8,100 discharges would have consumed at 4.6 days: 37,260 bed-days against 33,210 used, so 4,050 were released. Of the 891 readmissions, 729 would have occurred at the baseline rate of 9.0 per cent, leaving 162 excess, which at an average readmitted stay of 5.8 days consumed 939.6 bed-days. The net release is 3,110.4 bed-days, 76.8 per cent of the gross. Because readmitted bed-days also bill, nothing in Parijat's accounts said so.

Exhibit 4 is the finding. Patients living alone are 1,000 of the 8,100 discharges, 12.3 per cent, and 108 of the 162 excess readmissions, 66.7 per cent — a concentration ratio of 5.4. Their rate rose 10.8 points, from 20.3 to 31.1 per cent, a relative rise of 53.2 per cent, while every other segment moved 0.5 to 1.0 points. Neither cause was a model defect. Flow's features described the body and nothing about who would be at home, and the ranked worklist rationed the ward's scarce discharge-coordination minutes towards the top of the list, so those needing most planning got least.

Rupali's remedy was a gate, not a model change: a patient flagged as living alone requires a twenty-minute discharge-planning call and a day-three teleconsultation before Flow will rank them. At ₹640 a patient the gate costs ₹6.40 lakh per hospital per 90 days. Removing the whole 108-readmission excess would free 626.4 bed-days worth ₹46.35 lakh of fresh-admission contribution while forgoing ₹30.69 lakh of readmission billing: net ₹9.26 lakh. Removing half leaves ₹1.43 lakh, so the gate breaks even at 40.9 per cent of the excess.

Rozana Wellness Works: the approach followed, and failing anyway

Rozana sells a sleep-and-activity ring with a subscription app from Hyderabad and had 3,40,000 active users at 31 March 2026. Prabuddha Lotlikar's team had done what this page recommends: named the harm, anxiety about the sleep score, set a guardrail at 8 per cent of users reporting it, and reviewed it quarterly. For three quarters it read 6.4 per cent. It was not ignored. It was wrong.

What forced the issue was support volume: 2,460 tickets in the quarter to March 2026 mentioned checking the app at night — 0.72 per cent of the base, a small number that happened to be reliable. Oorvi Nadkarni ran a mandatory single question to a 1-in-20 sample, and 21.4 per cent said yes. The recovery retired the voluntary instrument, built the behavioural proxy, hid the sleep score until 7 a.m. local time and removed the streak counter. Night-time checkers fell from 41,820 to 23,120 the following quarter, a fall of 18,700 users and 44.7 per cent. Daily active users fell 4.1 per cent, from 1,98,900 to 1,90,700, and quarterly renewal fell 1.9 points on a base of 1,12,000 — at ₹399 a renewal, 2,128 renewals and ₹8.49 lakh. Rozana had bought the vocabulary of outcome ownership and none of the measurement.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Compliance as the finish line. Sign: the review ends at legal sign-off with no post-launch number named. Diagnostic: which reading, read by whom, would make us pull this? Caught late, a regulator sets the threshold.

Instrumenting only the intended branch. Sign: fourteen adoption metrics and none about regret. Diagnostic: finish “the worst thing a user could truthfully say is…” and check a number exists for it. Caught late, a journalist's figure is the first credible one.

Measuring harm through a volunteer channel. Sign: a guardrail fed by a survey with single-digit response. Diagnostic: who is systematically absent from this denominator? Caught late, green readings become evidence of negligence.

Setting the trade rule after the result. Sign: a threshold that drifts across decks, and a simultaneous rollout that left no market to compare against. Diagnostic: show me the guardrail with the date it was written. Caught late, guardrails become decoration.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The sharpest disagreement is about the locus of the duty. The fiduciary position, steelmanned: a product manager has neither the mandate nor the information to make distributive judgements for society, and a firm in which every PM trades revenue against diffuse harm by private conviction is ungovernable. The harms that did fall, in vehicle safety and drug labelling, fell to rules binding everyone at once. It is wrong where the regulator is slower than the product and the firm holds data no regulator can obtain — Omkar's accelerometer, exactly.

The stakeholder position, steelmanned: the firm alone holds the data, moves first and profits from the harm, so the duty must sit where the knowledge and the causal power sit. Its evidence is the pattern in which internal data revealed a harm years before any outside party could have. It is wrong if teams cannot reliably tell harm from noise, and Figure 1's confound is a point for that objection.

A second disagreement: whether unmeasured harm counts as zero or as unknown-and-therefore-blocking. The first is the only tractable rule for a shipping organisation, and is also how every harm on this page survived long enough to be discovered. The second, applied literally, stops all shipping; most teams run an unprincipled middle they cannot defend.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this says “we should think about second-order effects,” is agreed with, and changes nothing. Someone who has internalised it arrives with a denominator. They spend the cheap instrumentation money before launch; buy a holdback when it costs nothing; ask for the segment cut before the average; write the trade rule in a dated document; and convert their own conviction into somebody else's decision, on the record, by a date. They are less moralistic than the novice, having learned that the binding constraint is almost never willingness to do right. It is a denominator nobody built.

12. What they decided

On Friday 16 October, Prerna took Exhibits 1 and 2 to the operating review and did not ask for Design R. She asked for three things: Design R in Bengaluru and Nagpur only, the other five cities held back as a control so the 3.45× claim-rate gap could be read causally; a floor under the top band funded from the ₹17.94 lakh moving to low-trip evenings, so the riders losing ₹236.60 an evening did not pay for the fix; and a dated guardrail at no more than 15 per cent of tiered rider-evenings classified as sprints, read weekly by Omkar. Exhibit 2's ₹11.57 lakh advantage, she said, rested on an assumption only the holdback could settle. Rituraj approved the holdback and the guardrail and deferred the floor.

On Tuesday 20 October, Rupali recommended the twelve-hospital rollout proceed with the living-alone gate as a default rather than a configurable option, and the readmission segment cut added to Flow's standard monthly report, visible to the hospital and to Padav. The price, she told Padav's commercial lead: the headline length-of-stay claim falls from 0.5 days to 0.45, because 1,000 patients a quarter staying 0.4 days longer adds 400 bed-days and moves the average to 4.15 days. Five hundredths of a day is the whole commercial cost.

Discussion questions

  1. If sprint evenings prove only 1.4 times as risky once rider selection is accounted for, which parts of Prerna's October decision should be reversed, and which should stand regardless?
  2. Parijat earned roughly ₹46.04 lakh from the bed-days that excess readmissions consumed. Who should answer for a harm that appears in the accounts as income, and what instrument would make that real?
  3. Rozana's recovery cost ₹8.49 lakh of quarterly revenue and 8,200 daily active users to stop 18,700 people checking a sleep score at 3 a.m. Make the strongest case that this trade was wrong, and say what evidence would settle it.

13. Going deeper

Outputs vs outcomes vs impact
The layer distinction this topic stands on; it unlocks guardrail design.
What a product manager does
Why Prerna's win was an agenda, not a veto.
PM myths vs reality
Dismantles the “mini-CEO” story that equates responsibility with authority.
Origins of product management
Why the role inherited accountability without formal power.
PM vs PMM vs TPM vs project manager vs founder
Who else could have owned Padav's segment cut.
PM archetypes
Why a growth PM and a platform PM read Figure 1 differently.
How the PM job changes by company stage
One duty, three failure mechanisms, one instrument each.
case40v1-pm.ethics.intro:
Qadam Credit Services: Agla Qadam

An Indian-context case on the product manager's responsibility for outcomes

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday 11 October 2026, Qudsia Qureshi was still at her dining table in Bengaluru with four printouts in front of her. As vice-president of product at Qadam Credit Services, she had to say in the morning what the company would do with a feature called Agla Qadam.

Live to thirty-five per cent of borrowers since 1 June 2026, it was by every measure the growth team tracked the best thing Qadam had built in two years. The decision due on Monday 12 October was whether to finish the national rollout before the festive quarter, ship a quieter version, or take it off the repayment screen.

What had changed was a memo, six days old, from a data scientist in Austin whom Qudsia had hired herself, and interview notes from eleven districts of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Between them they suggested that for a meaningful share of its users the feature was a way of getting deeper into debt, and that the company had been reading its own numbers in a way that hid this.

She had written one line at the top of a blank page and had not got past it: What has this product done to them, not for them? She knew it was the right question; she did not know what it obliged her to do, and she knew what the answer cost. Diwali fell on 8 November, twenty-eight days away; the board met on Thursday 22 October.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Qadam was founded in 2021 by Xerxes Gazdar, nine years an underwriter at a large Indian non-banking finance company, and Xitij Gaonkar, an engineer from a Pune payments firm. UPI and the NPCI rails reached the smallest shopkeeper in the country; almost nothing built on them lent him working capital at a defensible price.

The app, launched in 2022, lent self-employed borrowers — tailors, vegetable vendors, kirana owners — ₹5,000 to ₹40,000, repaid weekly by UPI autopay and underwritten on Account Aggregator transaction history. All-in cost to the borrower averaged 34.4 per cent a year; the local alternative was a moneylender at four to six per cent a month, which is 48 to 72 per cent a year before compounding. The founding story was that Qadam had taken forty points off the price of credit.

The decision that constrains everything today was taken in November 2024. Qadam was eighteen months from its own NBFC licence when Gazdar withdrew the application and signed an exclusive five-year origination agreement with Girvi Finance Systems, a Mumbai NBFC with cheap capital. Girvi would hold every loan; Qadam would source, underwrite, service and collect for 7.0 per cent of principal disbursed. In exchange Qadam accepted a default loss guarantee over five per cent of the portfolio it originated — the ceiling the Reserve Bank of India permits — so that its own cash absorbs the first slice of credit loss; and a covenant requiring ₹550 crore of disbursal a quarter, a miss stepping the fee down to 5.0 per cent for four quarters and giving Girvi a ninety-day exit right.

Revenue is therefore a function of how much the company lends, not of how well the loans perform, while the first five per cent of losses is its own. Exhibit 1 gives the September-quarter position.
