3. The industry

Small-ticket digital lending in India in 2026 is crowded, regulated and profitable. KreditBee, Navi, Paytm Postpaid, LazyPay and the lending arms of Bajaj Finserv compete for part of Qadam's borrower, as do credit lines on UPI itself and the instruments Jio Financial Services and Reliance Retail put in front of the same shopkeepers. Nobody has a durable underwriting advantage; what they have is distribution and the cost of money.

Regulation sits close. The RBI's digital lending guidelines require a Key Fact Statement stating the annual percentage rate before the agreement is executed, money moving only between borrower and regulated lender, and a grievance officer named in the app. The default loss guarantee circular caps a partner's first-loss exposure at five per cent of the portfolio, exactly where Qadam sits, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the consent under which bank statements are fetched. Nothing says when an offer may be shown.

The exposure is not only Indian. Since April 2026 Qadam has licensed its underwriting and collections stack to a Mexican consumer lender for ₹18 crore a year, managed by Xavier Quenim. Mexico's banking regulator has opened a thematic review of design practices in consumer credit apps, and Quenim's client has twice asked for written confirmation that nothing in the stack reads as a dark pattern.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

Agla Qadam — "the next step" — was designed between February and May 2026 by Qais Qidwai's growth team in Gurugram, on a genuine field insight: borrowers who finished a loan cleanly often needed capital again within weeks, but had to re-apply, re-consent and wait, and many went to the moneylender. On the penultimate instalment, the app now showed a pre-approved amount, large and in rupees, with one accept button.

Three further build choices were each defensible alone. The offer carried a ten-minute countdown, because an open-ended offer had tested badly and Girvi's policy required limits re-checked. The APR and total repayable sat behind a "view terms" tap, because the first screen was already dense in seven languages. And the amount shown was full eligibility, because a lower number had drawn complaints that Qadam was stingy.

Within three weeks it was obvious the feature worked: acceptance ran at 27.5 per cent of borrowers who saw the screen, and by the close of the September quarter it had produced ₹89.32 crore of disbursal. Qidwai had the national rollout scheduled for mid-October, before Diwali.

Figure 1. Sequence of events. Marker spacing is indicative and not to scale; the dates are exact.

Qidwai's case rested on Exhibit 2, circulated on 14 September: read quickly, it says the more loans a borrower has taken, the less likely the loan is to go bad.

Between them sits the pilot. From 1 August to 30 September 2026, sixty-one days, Qadam ran three arms of 60,000 borrowers each from the thirty-five per cent already on the feature. Arm C kept Agla Qadam as built. Arm G guard-railed it: no countdown, APR and total repayable on the first screen, a seventy-two-hour gap after final repayment, two consecutive top-ups at most, and an affordability check re-pulling bank data before setting the amount. Arm P removed the offer from the repayment screen, leaving top-ups only to a borrower who went looking.

5. The people

Figure 2. Who sits where. Dashed box: functions reporting outside the product line.

Xerxes Gazdar, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. He signed the Girvi agreement and is negotiating a ₹480 crore Series C with Qila Growth Network at a ₹3,900 crore pre-money valuation, conditional on an annualised run-rate of at least ₹2,400 crore in the December quarter. He has told Qudsia the decision is hers. He has not told her the run-rate condition is non-negotiable, or that the board has seen a slide carrying the national-rollout number.

Qais Qidwai, head of growth, Gurugram. He built Agla Qadam and owns the disbursal target the covenant depends on. His position: Exhibit 2 shows repeat borrowing is safer, every competitor offers at repayment, and Arm P is an abstention, not a product. His variable pay is set on quarterly disbursal. He is not saying he saw the countdown's effect on the APR-view rate in July and did not raise it, because nobody had asked for that metric.

Gracy Xalxo, principal data scientist, Austin. She will not go further than her memo: Qadam does not know what the feature does to borrowers, having never measured borrowing elsewhere, and both Exhibit 2 and the last row of Exhibit 4 are used past their evidence. She wants a 180-day holdout first. Her contract ends in March, and she has not said she would rather not have her name on the rollout memo.

Xenia Quadros, design director, Amsterdam. She did not design the countdown; it was added after her handover. She has written that the first screen meets the letter of the Key Fact Statement rule and fails its purpose, and offers Arm G's layout as a four-day fix. She also argued in 2024 for showing full eligibility, and has not mentioned that it is the strongest single driver of average ticket.

Quratulain Qazi, general counsel and grievance officer, Mumbai. Formally Qadam is compliant: the Key Fact Statement is rendered before execution, the officer named, money moving only between borrower and Girvi. Informally, a nineteen per cent APR-view rate is "the kind of number a thematic review finds" — which she has not put in writing. She also handles the Mexico contract and knows what a dark-pattern finding would do to ₹18 crore of licensing revenue.

Qamrun Qaiser, head of field operations and collections, Lucknow. She commissioned Exhibit 6 because her agents kept meeting borrowers who could not say what they owed in total. Her staff are paid a recovery incentive and twenty-eight have been counselled this year for calling outside permitted hours. She wants the top-up capped at two consecutive rollovers, and has not said that a cap would cut her team's recovery rate on its easiest segment, or that her incentive scheme is part of what Exhibit 6 measures.

Xitij Gaonkar, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune. Indifferent between designs, acute about sequencing: Arm G's affordability check needs fresh Account Aggregator consent, adding a screen, a DPDP-compliant notice and an estimated eleven per cent drop-off before any amount is shown. He can ship Arm G by 23 October or Arm C by 15 October, not both. He has not said his team has carried the rollout as committed since August.

Xavier Quenim, head of international, Mexico City. He wants whichever version survives a regulator reading it in Spanish; his bonus rides on a second licensing client he expects in January. He has not told the India team that his existing client has already copied the countdown.

6. Exhibits on the money and the field

Finance modelled the December quarter under each option, holding non-top-up disbursal flat at the September quarter's ₹356.80 crore and assuming 6,40,000 borrowers reach a repayment moment at national coverage. Exhibit 5 is what Gazdar will put to the board.

Top-up delinquency estimates are Exhibit 4's final row; other loans are held at the FY26 rate of 7.2 per cent. The fee step-down to 5.0 per cent follows automatically from a covenant breach and applies to the whole book, not only to top-ups. Annualised shortfalls are four times the quarterly figure and assume no behavioural change. Source: Qadam finance, 9 October 2026.

Read as finance intends it, guard-railing costs ₹43.35 crore a year against FY26 profit before tax of ₹16.08 crore, and pull-only ₹45.88 crore. Both push the annualised run-rate below the Series C floor of ₹2,400 crore: ₹2,448 crore under Option 1, ₹1,971.20 crore under Option 2, ₹1,708.80 crore under Option 3.

Xalxo appended one line the board pack omits. If Girvi waived the step-down and the fee stayed at 7.0 per cent, Option 2's net contribution would be ₹1,689.12 lakh against Option 1's ₹1,787.32 lakh: a shortfall of ₹98.20 lakh a quarter, or ₹3.93 crore a year. On the same basis Option 3 would cost ₹11.70 crore a year. Of the ₹43.35 crore the board will be shown for Option 2, ₹39.42 crore is the November 2024 contract, not the screen.

Exhibit 6 is Qaiser's survey: 214 borrowers with three or more top-ups, interviewed in Hindi across eleven districts between 1 and 12 September 2026.

Exhibit 6. Field interviews, 1 to 12 September 2026, 214 borrowers with three or more top-ups
ReportedBorrowersShare of 214

Could not state the interest rate on the latest top-up12859.8%

Categories overlap and respondents could report more than one, so the column does not sum to 214 or to 100 per cent. The sample is not random: it is drawn from the route lists of collections agents in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, and the interviewers were employed by the same function, which may bias answers in either direction. The window is twelve days and does not coincide with the sixty-one-day pilot window in Exhibit 4, so the two cannot be compared rate for rate. Source: Qadam field operations, Lucknow.

It is the only evidence in the pack that asks a borrower anything, and the weakest sample on the table. Its two most important findings point opposite ways: 45.3 per cent said the newest loan was mostly repaying the last; 56.5 per cent said the top-ups had grown their business. Thirty-five of the 214 said both.

7. Voices

"Every number in Exhibit 2 is correct. It is also the wrong number, because it cannot see the people who stopped existing in the data. If you want to know what we do to a borrower, follow the borrower."

Gracy Xalxo, memo of 6 October 2026

"Follow the borrower where? Half of them borrow somewhere we cannot see, at four to six per cent a month, and your conclusion sends them back there in the festive quarter. I would like the ethics of that written down too."

Qais Qidwai, reply on the product channel, 6 October 2026

"The screen takes nineteen seconds at the median; the agreement flow where the APR lives takes four minutes. We built a product where the fast path is the expensive one. I am not saying it is illegal. I am saying I would not show my mother that screen."

Xenia Quadros, design review, 7 October 2026

"Girvi has no appetite to waive the step-down; the covenant is what the credit committee approved. If disbursal falls nineteen per cent we will be asked why we gave an exclusive to a partner that can turn its own volume off."

Quresh Gandhe, chief risk officer, Girvi Finance Systems, call of 9 October 2026

"My agent in Sitapur told me what the lady said. First: Qadam saved me in 2024. Then: now every Friday I am paying Qadam from Qadam. Both are true for her."

Qamrun Qaiser, to Qudsia Qureshi, 8 October 2026

"I will not tell you what to do and then take the credit. But the term sheet has a run-rate condition, and 1,971 is not 2,400. Decide knowing that."

Xerxes Gazdar, 10 October 2026

8. The options as Qudsia sees them

Option 1: complete the national rollout on 15 October, as built. It clears the covenant and the Series C condition and delivers ₹1,787.32 lakh of net contribution in the quarter. It also ships, knowingly, a screen on which eighty-one per cent of accepting borrowers never see the price — after Exhibits 3 and 6 have been circulated. The compliance exposure is unquantified; the Mexico question is unanswered.

Option 2: ship the guard-railed version by 23 October. APR on the first screen, no countdown, two consecutive rollovers at most, affordability checked. It costs ₹43.35 crore a year as the board will see it, of which ₹39.42 crore is the fee step-down rather than the design. It breaches the covenant, gives Girvi a ninety-day exit right, misses the Series C floor and lands eight days later than Option 1, with the Diwali push already bought. Acceptance falls 38.2 per cent against Arm C — including borrowers the top-up was genuinely helping.

Option 3: take the offer off the repayment screen. The cleanest answer to Qudsia's question and the most expensive: ₹45.88 crore a year, a 30.2 per cent fall in run-rate, and acceptance of 8.0 per cent — the feature ceasing to exist for the 92 per cent who do not go looking.

Qudsia had written these out twice and both times sensed the page was wrong before the options were. All three are settings of one screen. None touches the recovery incentive behind the 27.6 per cent in Exhibit 6, or the guarantee that makes Qadam's cash depend on borrowers it is paid to enlarge, or the fact that nobody has asked a borrower what else they owe. Arm G bundles four changes and the pilot cannot say which did the work. And nothing separates the 56.5 per cent whose business grew from the 45.3 per cent paying Qadam from Qadam, because nobody has tried to tell them apart.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Gaonkar can ship Arm C on 15 October or Arm G on 23 October; nothing ships after 29 October, and the festive freeze runs to 12 November. Qidwai's ₹6.40 crore campaign budget is committed to a Diwali push that assumes the as-built screen. The Girvi covenant is ₹550 crore in the December quarter and the step-down is automatic. The Qila Growth Network term sheet lapses on 15 December; runway at the FY26 burn is eleven months. Quratulain Qazi will sign off on all three options and has asked in writing to see whichever screen is chosen before any borrower does. Quddus Gidwani, on the board for the existing investors, has the pilot data and has not said how he reads it.

And the thing that is not a constraint but will not leave her alone: whatever Qadam decides, 6,40,000 people will reach a repayment moment in the December quarter, and what they see there is what Qadam chose to show them.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Separate what Agla Qadam does for borrowers from what it does to them. Which exhibits speak to the first, which to the second, and which exhibit does Qadam not have?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 come from the same loan book and point in opposite directions. Reconstruct how each was produced. Which can carry the weight its author puts on it, and what would settle the question?
  3. Arm G changes four things at once. If you could test only two of them before 23 October, which two, and what would you give up by not testing the others?
  4. Exhibit 5 shows a ₹43.35 crore annual cost for Option 2, of which ₹39.42 crore arises from the November 2024 fee step-down. Does that change what the decision is? Who inside Qadam can act on that distinction, and when was the last moment anyone could have?
  5. Half the borrowers in Exhibit 6 also borrow from a moneylender at four to six per cent a month. Build the strongest case that Option 3 harms borrowers more than Option 1 does. What evidence would refuse that case, and does Qadam have it?
  6. It is Monday morning, 12 October 2026. What do you do, what do you stop, and what do you measure? Draft the three sentences you would say to the board on 22 October, including the one stating plainly what Qadam has already done to some of its borrowers, and who was accountable for it.

11. Sunday, 11.45 pm

Qudsia turned Exhibit 6 face down and read Qaiser's line again from memory. Now every Friday I am paying Qadam from Qadam. Against it she set the number she could not argue away: 121 of the 214, who said the thing had worked. She had owned this product since January and had asked for Exhibit 3 only in October. The memo had not come to her, and she had not gone looking.

Outside, somebody's generator started. She wrote a second line under the first: If I ship Arm C on Wednesday and I am wrong, who finds out, and when? Then she sat looking at both, and she still did not know what she would say at nine.
exp20v2-pm.ethics.intro:
The PM's responsibility for outcomes

Own what the product does to people, not only for them.

1. A dashboard that was pleased with itself

On Monday 14 September 2026, Lavanya Joglekar sat in a meeting room at Laghu Rin Labs, a Pune lender making small instant loans through a phone app. She was the product manager for "Top-Up", a feature that offered a pre-approved loan of ₹8,000 to any customer whose previous loan had closed. It had launched six weeks earlier, on Monday 3 August. The growth dashboard was entirely green: take-up was 18 per cent, disbursals were ahead of plan, and Mohit Ranade, the chief executive, had told the board that Top-Up would deliver ₹2,500 lakh of disbursals in each ninety-day cycle.

Nalini Garg, the data analyst on Lavanya's team, had asked for ten minutes. She had sorted borrowers by a pattern the dashboard did not show: customers who closed a loan and took the next one within three days, three times in a row. Roughly a quarter of all borrowers fitted it. Nirmala Sethi, who led customer support, added that calls beginning "I can't clear this without borrowing again" had risen through August. Nobody had designed Top-Up to produce that.

The decision was due by Friday 18 September, before the festival season. If Lavanya changed nothing, the numbers would look excellent and the harm would surface later as defaults, complaints and perhaps a regulator's question. If she acted, she would cut a feature that worked by the only measure set. This page follows her choice to build one idea: responsibility extends beyond what the product does for users to what it does to them.

2. The idea

A product manager is accountable for the changes in people's lives that the product causes, including those nobody intended, to the extent that a reasonably diligent team could have foreseen or detected them. An output is something the team ships or the product produces, such as a loan disbursed. An outcome is a change in someone's behaviour or circumstances that results. Impact is the longer-run effect on the business and the people concerned. Josh Seiden's Outcomes Over Output (2019) popularised the first distinction for product teams. The extension to unintended outcomes is older: the sociologist Robert K. Merton's 1936 paper "The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action" argued that deliberate action produces effects its authors never wanted. In the 1990s Batya Friedman and colleagues developed "value sensitive design", which asks designers to identify everyone a technology touches.

The problem the idea solves is a gap in accountability. A team measured on adoption and revenue has no reason to look elsewhere, so unowned harms persist until they become expensive. The sentence Lavanya could repeat in the room without sounding glib was this: "We are accountable for what the product does to people, not only for what people do with it."

Figure 1 shows why the idea is demanding. Responsibility is largely instrumentation: you cannot be accountable for something nobody is looking at.

3. How it works, step by step

Lavanya's team reconstructed the sequence in the week after the review, including the steps usually left implicit.

Step one: write the intended outcome as a change in a person. "Increase disbursals" describes the firm. "A customer with a salary delay of a week covers rent and repays from the next pay-cheque" describes a person. The second sentence is testable, because it implies the customer should not need another loan soon after repaying.

Step two: list who else is affected: the borrower, the household, collections staff and the firm's balance sheet, written down before launch.

Step three: choose a harm proxy. Harm itself, such as stress, is not observable in a database; a proxy is an observable stand-in. Nalini's proxy was the "treadmill borrower": a customer who takes three loans in ninety days, each within three days of closing the previous one. It is imperfect but countable.

Step four: set a guardrail, a number that must not worsen beyond a stated limit while the primary metric is pushed. Step five: assign an owner and a date. Step six, most often omitted: agree the trade rule before seeing the result, so the team cannot reason backwards from a number it likes.

4. A worked example, line by line

Nalini built a model over a single ninety-day cycle for 1,20,000 customers shown the Top-Up offer. Every loan is ₹8,000 and carries a fee of 4 per cent, which is ₹320 per loan. Table 1 compares the current design (A) with a redesign (B) that Lavanya's team drafted: the next offer appears only seven days after a loan closes, and no customer can take more than two Top-Ups in ninety days. B's behaviour figures come from a two-week test arm, so they are estimates, not observations.

Table 1. One ninety-day cycle, 1,20,000 customers shown the offer (money in ₹ lakh)
LineA: currentB: redesign
Customers shown the offer1,20,0001,20,000
Take-up rate18%15%
Borrowers21,60018,000
Treadmill borrowers5,4001,800
Other borrowers16,20016,200
Loans per treadmill borrower32
Loans made (16,200 + treadmill loans)32,40019,800
Disbursal (loans × ₹8,000)2,592.001,584.00
Fee revenue (loans × ₹320)103.6863.36

Treadmill borrowers are 25 per cent of A's borrowers (5,400 of 21,600) and 10 per cent of B's (1,800 of 18,000). Treadmill loans are 16,200 in A and 3,600 in B. In B, where the cap is two loans, a treadmill borrower is one who uses both.

Read the table from the top. A's 21,600 borrowers are 18 per cent of 1,20,000. Of them 5,400 are treadmill borrowers taking three loans each, so A makes 16,200 loans to the others and 16,200 to the treadmill group: 32,400 in all. At ₹8,000 each that is ₹2,592 lakh disbursed, above the ₹2,500 lakh promised. Fee revenue is 32,400 × ₹320 = ₹103.68 lakh, of which ₹51.84 lakh comes from the quarter of borrowers on the treadmill. B disburses ₹1,584 lakh, 38.9 per cent less than A, missing the target by ₹916 lakh. Its revenue is ₹63.36 lakh, of which the treadmill group contributes ₹11.52 lakh, or 18.2 per cent.

Revenue is not profit. Table 2 subtracts credit losses. Assume the other borrowers default on their outstanding ₹8,000 at 1.5 per cent, which is 243 customers and ₹19.44 lakh in both designs. The unknown is the default rate among treadmill borrowers. The team had seen too little repayment history to be sure, so Nalini ran two values.

Table 2. Net contribution after credit losses (₹ lakh), by treadmill default rate
ScenarioTreadmill defaultsAll defaultsCredit lossFee revenueNet
A at 12%64889171.28103.6832.40
B at 12%21645936.7263.3626.64
A at 20%1,0801,323105.84103.68-2.16
B at 20%36060348.2463.3615.12

Treadmill defaults = treadmill borrowers × rate (A: 5,400; B: 1,800). Credit loss = all defaults × ₹8,000. Net = fee revenue minus credit loss.

At a 12 per cent treadmill default rate, A nets ₹32.40 lakh and B ₹26.64 lakh: A wins by ₹5.76 lakh, and a purely financial reading favours leaving Top-Up alone. Change one input to 20 per cent and the ranking flips. A loses ₹2.16 lakh while B earns ₹15.12 lakh, a gap of ₹17.28 lakh. A's break-even is where the treadmill loss equals the contribution from everyone else: ₹103.68 lakh less ₹19.44 lakh leaves ₹84.24 lakh, and each percentage point of treadmill default costs ₹4.32 lakh, so A breaks even at 19.5 per cent. B breaks even only at 30.5 per cent. The choice turns on a quantity nobody had measured, and A is far more exposed to it. A product manager who owns outcomes owns that uncertainty too.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Foreseeable is not the same as intended

The test is foreseeability, not intent. Nobody at Laghu Rin wanted customers on a treadmill, but a feature that offers money the moment a loan closes makes repeat borrowing predictable.

Output, outcome and impact are different layers

The ₹2,592 lakh is an output. A customer clearing rent is an outcome. A household's savings two years on is impact. Teams report an output as though it proved an impact.

A proxy is not the harm

The treadmill pattern could also describe a trader who restocks weekly and repays comfortably. A proxy flags candidates for inspection; it does not convict. Nalini's next step was to read fifty accounts.

The counterfactual matters

Some treadmill borrowers would otherwise have used a local moneylender at far worse terms. Whether Top-Up harms depends on what customers would have done without it, and that comparison must be estimated honestly.

Responsibility is not paternalism

Owning outcomes does not mean overriding customers' choices. Cooling-off periods and clear disclosure respect autonomy while reducing foreseeable harm. The Reserve Bank of India's digital-lending rules push lenders towards transparency, but compliance is a floor, not a definition of responsibility.

What the idea cannot tell you

It cannot say how much revenue a given harm is worth. Table 2 shows which design earns more; it does not say whether ₹5.76 lakh justifies exposing 3,600 additional customers to the treadmill. That is a judgement about values, and the idea ensures it is made knowingly.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products; small and large firms

In a consumer product the user and the affected person are the same, and harm is often behavioural: time lost, money spent, habits formed, visible in usage data. In a B2B product buyer and end user diverge. A workforce-monitoring tool may satisfy the HR head who buys it while burdening employees who never chose it, so the stakeholder list must reach beyond the contract signatory. In a marketplace an outcome for one side can be a harm for another: a delivery platform that squeezes partner earnings to hold consumer prices has chosen between its sides, whether or not it says so.

Company size changes the mechanism, not the duty. In a thirty-person firm the product manager can read accounts personally, but survival pressure makes harm feel like a luxury. In a large firm, risk and compliance functions exist, and the danger is assuming someone else owns it. Mateus Ferreira, a risk partner in Lisbon who advised Laghu Rin, told Lavanya that a control function can reject a design but cannot notice a pattern only the product team's data reveals.

7. Common mistakes

Treating compliance as the finish line. Symptom: the launch review ends at legal sign-off. Misunderstanding: what is permitted equals what is acceptable. Diagnostic: ask "Which post-launch number would make us pull this, and who reads it?"

Instrumenting only the intended branch. Symptom: ten adoption metrics and none about regret. Misunderstanding: the metrics reflect the whole product. Diagnostic: finish "The worst thing a customer could say about this is..." and check a metric exists for it.

Deciding the trade rule after the result. Symptom: a threshold that quietly moves each week. Misunderstanding: flexibility is wisdom. Diagnostic: find the written guardrail with its date.

8. What good looks like

Suppose Laghu Rin had done this before 3 August. The brief names the borrower's outcome as bridging a short gap, lists the four stakeholders, and sets the treadmill proxy with a guardrail of no more than 10 per cent of borrowers, read every Monday by Nalini with Lavanya accountable. It records that if the guardrail trips, the offer is slowed rather than switched off. Six weeks in, the dashboard shows 25 per cent, the team knows what to do, and the meeting is about execution, not discovery. Good looks unremarkable: the harm is small because someone was looking.

9. What Lavanya decided

She did not have the 20 per cent default figure, and did not pretend to. On Friday 18 September she recommended design B, with a written guardrail of no more than 10 per cent of borrowers on the treadmill, read every Monday. She told Mohit Ranade that B would miss the ₹2,500 lakh promise by ₹916 lakh, and that A's net advantage at a 12 per cent default rate was only ₹5.76 lakh, against a loss at 20 per cent. A's edge was small, uncertain and borne by customers least able to afford it; B's cost was a missed target the board could understand. Mohit asked for one change: show both designs' figures to the board on Thursday 5 November, so the choice was visible.

What to learn next. Outputs, outcomes and impact are the foundation this topic builds on. Then study guardrail metrics and experiment design, which make the responsibility measurable.

Two questions to sit with. First, if Nalini's fifty-account review showed that most treadmill borrowers were small traders restocking profitably, which of your conclusions would change, and which would not? Second, your own product has a metric on a wall somewhere that is green. Which group of users would you have to examine to find out whether that green is hiding something?
case20v1-pm.ethics.intro:
Ekatva Learning Works: The Streak Decision

A product case on the PM's responsibility for outcomes

1. Opening

On the evening of Friday 9 October 2026, Ojaswini Bhatt sat in a glass meeting room on the fourth floor of Ekatva Learning Works' Pune office, with two printed pages in front of her and a decision due on Monday. Ojaswini was the product manager for Ekatva Maths, the company's flagship app for children in Classes 3 to 8. On Monday 12 October the engineering team would freeze code for the Diwali release, and the freeze would lock in whichever of three engagement designs she chose. The festive campaign was to begin on 19 October. Diwali itself fell on 8 November.

The question was not whether the new design worked. The test had shown that it did. The question was what it did to the children who used it, and what the company was willing to give up to avoid that.

2. Company background

Ekatva Learning Works was founded in 2019 by two former engineers from a Pune services firm. It sells a subscription to a gamified maths and reasoning app, aimed at families in tier-2 and tier-3 cities where coaching centres are thin and the cost of a private tutor is high. The plan is simple: ₹3,600 a year, billed through UPI autopay on the NPCI rails and processed by Razorpay. At the end of September 2026 the app had 2,40,000 paying families, which made annual recurring revenue about ₹86.4 crore.

The market is crowded. PhysicsWallah and Vedantu dominate the older-student segment and have moved downward into middle school. Ekatva's pitch is that it is gentler and cheaper than the large coaching platforms, and its brand, "maths without fear", says so on the Play Store page. Growth had slowed, however. Annual renewal sat at 58 per cent, and the board had told the founders that a number nearer 65 per cent was needed to raise the next round.

3. The situation

In July, the growth team added two mechanics to the app. The first was a "streak": a counter of consecutive days on which the child completed a lesson, which reset to zero if a day was missed. The second was a parent alert: when a child's streak was at risk, the parent received a push notification that read, for example, "Aanya is about to lose her 23-day streak. Other children in her class are ahead." Ojaswini had inherited both mechanics when she took over the product in August.

From 1 September to 28 September, 28 days in all, Ekatva ran a controlled test on 60,000 families, split into three arms of 20,000. The control arm kept the existing app. Arm A made the mechanics sharper: a streak that could be saved only by a late-evening "rescue lesson", and up to three parent alerts a day. Arm B, the calm design, removed the loss-based streak, replaced it with a weekly progress summary for parents, capped notifications at one a day, blocked alerts after 8 pm, and added a parent control to set the child's daily time. Exhibit 1 gives the results.

Exhibit 1. Four-week test, 1 to 28 September 2026 (20,000 families per arm)
MeasureControlArm A (sharper streak)Arm B (calm design)
Families active in week 412,400 (62.0%)14,600 (73.0%)13,000 (65.0%)
Families with a session after 10 pm in week 42,600 (13.0%)5,000 (25.0%)2,200 (11.0%)
Tickets citing an upset child, over 28 days7022040
Tickets per 1,000 families3.511.02.0

Percentages are of the 20,000 families in each arm. "Upset child" tickets are support contacts where a parent mentioned crying, fear or refusal to sleep. Source: Ekatva product analytics and support desk.

Arm A held 73.0 per cent of families active against 62.0 per cent for control, an 11-point gain. It also doubled the share of families with late-night sessions, from 13.0 to 25.0 per cent, and more than tripled complaints from 3.5 to 11.0 per 1,000 families. Arm B was the quieter result: 65.0 per cent active, 3 points above control, with late-night use and complaints both below control.

The team's view of it differed by location. In Kraków, the contract data scientist Euan Gallagher pointed out that the test ran only four weeks, and that renewal, the number the board cared about, had not been observed at all. In Nairobi, Eunice Wanjiru, who led customer success for Ekatva's small African pilot, reported that the pilot's parents had asked for exactly the time controls Arm B contained. In Bengaluru and Pune, the engineers were indifferent to either design but wanted a decision before the freeze.

Figure 1. Key dates. Marker spacing is indicative, not to scale.

4. The people

Eshwar Kulkarni, head of growth, Pune. He built the streak and the parent alerts, and he owns the renewal target. He argues that every competitor uses these hooks and that Ekatva cannot be the only company to disarm itself in the festive quarter.

Oviraj Khanna, co-founder and CEO, Pune. He wants the 65 per cent renewal number for the board, but he built the brand on "maths without fear" and has said so in public.

Ekta Malhotra, the company's counsel, Mumbai. She has flagged that the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 restricts tracking and behavioural monitoring of children and requires verifiable parental consent. She has not concluded that the alerts breach it, but wants the design reviewed before any expansion.

Euan Gallagher and Eunice Wanjiru, in Kraków and Nairobi, as described above. A child psychologist the team consulted in Edinburgh declined to be named but described loss-framed streaks as a known source of anxiety in younger children.

5. Exhibits on the economics

Finance modelled annual renewal for each design. Control renewal is the observed 58 per cent; the rates for A and B are finance's estimates from the test, since no test family had yet reached its renewal date. Exhibit 2 applies each rate to the 2,40,000 paying families at ₹3,600 a year.

Exhibit 2. Estimated renewal revenue by design (2,40,000 families, ₹3,600 each)
DesignRenewal rateFamilies renewingRevenue (₹ lakh)Gain over control (₹ lakh)
Control58%1,39,2005,011.200.00
Arm A everywhere66%1,58,4005,702.40691.20
Arm B everywhere61%1,46,4005,270.40259.20

Revenue = families renewing x ₹3,600, shown in ₹ lakh. Rates for A and B are estimates, not observations.

Arm A is worth ₹691.20 lakh over control, and Arm B ₹259.20 lakh. The gap between them is ₹432.00 lakh. Arm A reaches a 66 per cent renewal rate, above the board's 65 per cent bar, while Arm B at 61 per cent does not.

A third possibility used the app's age split. Of the 2,40,000 families, 1,56,000 have a child under 11 and 84,000 have a child aged 11 or more. Exhibit 3 shows what applying B to the younger group and A to the older group would yield, assuming the same renewal rates hold within each group.

Exhibit 3. Split design: B for under-11s, A for ages 11 and above

Under 11B1,56,00061%95,1603,425.76

Blended rate = 1,50,600 / 2,40,000. Total revenue exceeds control by ₹410.40 lakh.

6. The options

Option 1: Ship Arm A to everyone. This delivers the largest gain, ₹691.20 lakh over control, and clears the board's target. The cost falls on children: late-night use doubles and distress complaints more than triple, and the company would be shipping that effect knowingly, with legal review unfinished.

Option 2: Ship Arm B to everyone. This gives up ₹432.00 lakh against Option 1 and misses the 65 per cent target, but it improves on control for revenue, for late-night use and for complaints, and it is consistent with the brand.

Option 3: The split. Younger children get B, older children get A. It earns ₹410.40 lakh over control and keeps the most sensitive group safe, but it still exposes 84,000 children to a design that doubled late-night use, and rests on an assumption the test did not check.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What did Ekatva's product do for families, and what did it do to them? Which exhibit separates the two?
  2. Euan Gallagher says the evidence is four weeks old. Which conclusions in Exhibits 1 to 3 does that weaken, and which does it leave intact?
  3. If the board's 65 per cent target conflicts with the children's outcomes, whose job is it to say so, and to whom?
  4. Which option would you take on Monday, and what would you measure after Diwali to find out whether you were wrong?

8. A note for the learner

Product ethics, at its plainest, starts from this idea: a PM owns the outcomes of the product, including the ones nobody intended. Outputs are what the team ships, outcomes are what changes for the user, and Arm A is a clean example of an output that moved the company's metric while worsening the user's. The distress tickets were not a bug report. They were the product telling the team what it did to children.

A well-reasoned answer starts with the user data before the revenue data, notes that the revenue figures are estimates while the harm signals are observations, and names the cost of the choice plainly.

One defensible path is Option 2, with conditions. Ship Arm B to everyone on Monday. Tell the board that the 61 per cent estimate is below target and that the shortfall against A is ₹432.00 lakh, roughly the price of not pressuring children. Ask for a further eight weeks to test improvements inside B, for example a family goal and a teacher-style celebration of effort, that might close the gap without loss-based hooks. Commission the legal review before any alert reaches a parent again. Track, after Diwali, actual renewals against the estimates in Exhibit 2.

The split is tempting but weaker. It treats an 11-year-old's sleep and anxiety as an acceptable price, and its numbers rest on an assumption the test never examined. Option 1 would be defensible only if the harm were small, and the data say otherwise.
exp20v2-pm.triad:
The product triad

1. A Tuesday in July

On Tuesday 14 July 2026, Esha Naidu, the product manager responsible for new-user growth at Gullak Savings Labs, a Pune-based app that lets salaried Indians save small sums into liquid mutual funds, opened a document titled "Q3 priorities" and found it contained nothing except a list of twelve features, each pasted in by a different senior person. Gullak had acquired 2,50,000 new sign-ups in the previous quarter. Of these, 60,000 had made a first deposit, which is the event that matters, because a user who never deposits earns the company nothing. The board's target for the coming quarter was 70,000 first depositors, a gap of 10,000. Commitments were due Friday 31 July.

Esha's instinct was to rank the twelve items herself. Her chief executive, Fatima Dalvi, had other ideas. "Do not bring me a list you have ranked alone," she said. "Bring me the one you, Gargi and Gopal would each defend in front of me." Gargi Ranade led design; Gopal Vernekar led engineering. Esha had worked beside both for a year without ever setting down what each owned that she did not.

Engineering capacity at Gullak was finite; whatever was chosen on 31 July would consume the quarter, and a feature that merely looked sensible in a planning document would cost the company a sceptical board's goodwill.

2. The idea

The product triad is the working arrangement in which a product manager, a designer and an engineering lead share ownership of a product's outcomes, instead of passing work to one another like a relay baton. Each is accountable for a different kind of risk. The product manager owns value and viability: will customers want this, and can the business sustain it? The designer owns usability: can people actually work out how to use it? The engineering lead owns feasibility: can it be built with the time, skill and technology available, and kept running afterwards? Marty Cagan, a Silicon Valley product leader, set these out as the four risks of product work: value, usability, feasibility and viability.

The arrangement was invented to solve a particular failure. In the older sequential model, a product manager wrote a requirements document, a designer made screens to match it, and engineers built what the screens showed. Each handover discarded information: engineers found constraints too late to change the design, and designers found the customer problem misunderstood only when users failed in testing. Teams that put all three in one conversation from day one found these things out in a week, not a quarter.

The sentence Esha could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "Between us we own three questions, whether it is worth doing, whether people can use it and whether we can build it, and none of us may answer another's question alone."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have four steps, and the third is the one most often left implicit. First, the three agree on the outcome: a measurable change in customer behaviour, not a list of features. Esha's team chose "more sign-ups completing a first deposit". An outcome differs from an output, which is a thing shipped. Second, they inspect the customer problem together, so that the designer hears what the product manager hears in user interviews and the engineer sees the same funnel data. The funnel was the sequence sign-up, identity verification (KYC, the "know your customer" check that Indian regulators require before an investment account opens), then first deposit.

Third, each role generates options out of its own expertise and then tests the others' assumptions. This is the implicit step. When Gargi proposed shortening the KYC flow, the engineer's contribution was not a nod but a question about the verification vendor's rules; when Gopal said a new rule engine was possible, Gargi's contribution was to ask who would understand it. The roles are three sources of objection, arriving early when objection is cheap. Fourth, they commit to one option together and each states the evidence they would accept that it failed. No handover occurs, because everyone was present at the decision.

The product manager has no authority over the other two. Gargi and Gopal report into their own functions, and Esha's influence rests on the clarity of her reasoning; the power to command would suppress the very objections the triad exists to produce.

4. A worked example

Esha, Gargi and Gopal narrowed the twelve items to one candidate: a redesigned KYC flow that pre-fills details from the user's Aadhaar-linked digital locker, with the user confirming rather than typing. Gargi's usability tests suggested KYC completion would rise from 60 per cent of sign-ups to 66 per cent. Gopal estimated six engineer-weeks. The calculation below follows the funnel one step at a time. Each row uses the row above, and the 40 per cent deposit rate among verified users is held constant.

Exhibit 2. Quarterly funnel under three scenarios (sign-ups: 2,50,000)

Contribution means revenue less direct servicing cost per depositor over twelve months; ₹400 is the figure Gullak's finance team uses. ₹400 × 6,000 = ₹24,00,000 = ₹24 lakh; ₹400 × 3,000 = ₹12,00,000 = ₹12 lakh. Depositor counts are exact; no rounding is applied.

Cost is the second half of the calculation, and it belongs to all three roles, not only engineering. The table prices time at the rates Gullak uses internally.

Exhibit 3. Cost of the KYC redesign

Total cost ₹6,20,000 = ₹6.2 lakh (3,60,000 + 1,50,000 + 1,10,000).

On the design estimate, ₹24 lakh of year-one contribution against ₹6.2 lakh of cost gives a ratio of about 3.9 (24 ÷ 6.2 = 3.87). Now change one input. Gopal reports that the verification vendor limits how much of the pre-filled data it will accept, so the lift is more likely 3 percentage points than 6: KYC completion of 63 per cent, not 66. Every other figure is unchanged. The funnel produces 63,000 depositors, 3,000 added, ₹12 lakh of contribution, and a ratio of about 1.9 (12 ÷ 6.2 = 1.94). The project is still positive, but it now closes 30 per cent of the gap, not 60 per cent. One input, supplied by the engineer and not the product manager, halved the benefit.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

The triad is not a hierarchy with a product manager at the top

People often describe the product manager as "the CEO of the product". The phrase is flattering and misleading: it implies authority the role does not have. The product manager is accountable for the decision being sound, which is different from making it.

Ownership of a risk is not ownership of a topic

The designer may hold views on pricing and the engineer may doubt the customer problem. What each owns is the final word on a question of their expertise, not a monopoly on speaking.

A triad is not a committee

A committee seeks consensus on everything. The triad seeks agreement on the outcome and the evidence, then lets each role decide within its own domain. Where they disagree irreconcilably, the product manager typically breaks the tie on value, the designer on usability and the engineer on feasibility.

It is confused with the cross-functional team

A cross-functional team includes everyone needed to ship: testers, analysts, data engineers. The triad is the smaller core of three whose judgement shapes what is built. Conflating them produces thirty-person "triads" that decide nothing.

Other partners matter and the triad does not remove them

Legal, compliance, data science and finance hold real constraints; the rules of Gullak's investment partner shaped the KYC flow as much as any of the three. The triad is the minimum, not the whole set.

It cannot tell you whether the problem is the right one

Three well-coordinated people can still work diligently on a problem nobody has. The triad improves the quality of decisions after a problem is chosen; it does not choose it. That depends on evidence from customers.

Seniority distorts it

When one member is a founder or a long-serving executive, the others stop objecting. Before relying on a triad, ask whether each person says "no" on the record, and whether any option was ever dropped because of a junior colleague's objection.

6. How it looks in different settings

In consumer products the designer's role is often the heaviest, since small friction in a flow costs a large share of millions of users; the Gullak example sits here. In B2B products, the buyer, the user and the administrator are different people, so the product manager's value question widens and the engineer's feasibility question includes integration with the customer's own systems, which the team cannot control. In marketplaces, where buyers and sellers must both be satisfied, the triad often needs two sets of usability work and the engineer carries a particular burden of trust and safety mechanisms, because a design that favours one side may collapse the other.

Scale changes it too. In a company of twenty, the triad may be the founder, one designer and a lead engineer. In a company of two thousand there are many triads, and the new difficulty is overlap: two teams can ask the same engineer for the same quarter. The discipline shifts from forming a triad to deciding what each is accountable for.

7. Common mistakes

The relay. From outside, the designer receives a finished specification and the engineer receives finished screens. The misunderstanding is that collaboration means communication after decisions. The cheapest diagnostic: ask the engineer when they first saw the problem. If the answer is "when the ticket arrived", the triad is nominal.

The product manager as filter. Customer research reaches the designer and the engineer only as the product manager's summary. The misunderstanding is that the role owns customer contact. Diagnostic: ask the designer about the last customer conversation they attended.

Estimates treated as promises. The engineer says "six weeks" and the number is entered into a plan as a commitment. The misunderstanding is that feasibility is a number, not a range with conditions. As Exhibit 2 showed, an engineer's knowledge of a vendor constraint can change the case entirely. Diagnostic: ask what assumption would double the estimate.

The design review as sign-off. The designer is consulted at the end, to polish. Diagnostic: count the options the designer proposed, not the options they approved.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of Esha's decision shows four things. All three would have watched the same five or six recorded sessions of users stalling in the KYC step. The Exhibit 2 funnel would have been built in the room, with the engineer supplying the vendor limit before the design estimate became a forecast. The written proposal would contain the cautious case beside the optimistic one, and a statement of what result in the first fortnight after launch would cause them to stop. And each role would be able to explain the others' reasoning: Esha could describe why the vendor limit mattered, and Gopal could say why confirming beats typing for users.

9. Closing: what Esha decided

On 28 July, the three met for ninety minutes. Esha did not bring the ranked list. She brought the funnel and asked Gopal to attack the 66 per cent. He did, and the cautious case of 63 per cent became the planning figure. At ₹12 lakh of contribution against ₹6.2 lakh of cost, the redesign was still worth doing, but Gargi pointed out that it closed only 3,000 of the 10,000 gap. They agreed to ship it first, as the cheapest step, and to pair it with a second experiment on the first-deposit screen, where 60 per cent of verified users still did not deposit. Esha told Fatima that one change would not reach 70,000, and that she would sooner say so on 31 July than in October. Fatima accepted the plan, because three people had put their names to the reasoning.

Next, study empowered teams versus feature teams: the triad says who must be in the room, and the next idea asks whether that room is given problems to solve or features to deliver.

Two questions to sit with. First, which of the three questions, worth doing, usable, buildable, does your own team answer least well, and who currently answers it by default? Second, when did a colleague last change your mind with an objection you did not want to hear, and what does your answer say about whether your team has a triad or only the vocabulary of one?
exp40v2-pm.triad:
The product triad

Product management, design and engineering as co-owners of an outcome: what each owns, what the arrangement costs, when it is the wrong shape, and where practitioners disagree.

1. Two decisions, eleven days apart

On Monday 5 October 2026, Nilanjan Phatak had eleven days to commit a release scope and no honest way to fit it into the capacity he had. Phatak is product manager for the claims desktop at Pukaar Support Systems, a Bengaluru firm whose software serves the claims agents of fourteen Indian general insurers. Of Pukaar's ₹46 crore of annual recurring revenue, ₹7.2 crore came from Nabh General Insurance in Mumbai, 15.7 per cent of the book, up for renewal on 31 March 2027.

Padmanabh Jalota, who runs claims operations at Nabh, had asked for automation of first notification of loss, the intake call in which an agent records a new claim. Nishant Palkar, Pukaar's sales lead, had written it into the renewal narrative; Parth Chitale, the engineering lead, had sized it at 46 engineer-weeks; Oindrila Sen, the design lead, had not seen one recording of a Nabh intake call. Scope locked on Friday 16 October, for release on Tuesday 12 January 2027.

Eleven days earlier, on Thursday 24 September 2026, Nivedita Padhye had the opposite problem: evidence without a mandate. Padhye is product manager for Pavan Nirmal, a connected room air purifier built in Coimbatore by Pavan Air Works and sold at ₹8,990 with a filter subscription at ₹349 a month. Pavan had sold 1,40,000 units and held 86,000 subscriptions, an attach rate of 61 per cent; the cassette was replaced every 90 days.

Oviya Narayanan, Pavan's engineering lead, had instrumented the particulate sensor across 2,400 volunteer households and found that in the median Indian home the cassette held specification for about 150 days, not 90; Pramod Ovalekar, who owns the hardware, confirmed the media from Pankh Filtration Industries in Hosur had always carried that margin. Pranali Nagarkar, the design lead, had the unwelcome question: what does the app tell a customer who has been paying monthly for filters she did not need? Nobody had authority over anyone else, and Niranjan Pusalkar wanted a recommendation.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree about it

The product triad, or trio, is the arrangement in which a product manager, a product designer and an engineering lead hold joint ownership of an outcome, with decision rights divided by the kind of risk each is best placed to retire rather than by the stage of work each performs. Marty Cagan's division names four. Value: will anyone want this enough to change behaviour? Viability: can the business sustain it at its price, cost and compliance posture? Usability: can a real person, under pressure, work out what to do? Feasibility: can it be built and kept running? The product manager owns value and viability, the designer usability, the engineer feasibility, and all three own the outcome — which is why none may answer another's question alone.

It was invented against one failure. In the sequential model a product manager wrote requirements, a designer dressed them and engineers built the drawings; each handover discarded what mattered most, so the engineer met the vendor constraint after the flow was designed and the designer learned the problem had been misread when users failed in testing.

The history is older than the vocabulary. Neil McElroy's 1931 brand-man memo at Procter & Gamble created single-person accountability for a commercial result; Toyota's shusa, the chief engineer Clark and Fujimoto called the "heavyweight product manager" in 1991, went the other way — one integrator with authority over the whole vehicle. Microsoft's three-in-a-box omitted design and Scrum named one product owner and no designer; Jeff Gothelf's Lean UX (2013) restored the designer as co-owner, and Amazon's single-threaded leader is the shusa in modern dress.

Five positions are live and they do not reconcile. The co-equal trio school signs "no one of the three may decide alone what gets built" and refuses "the trio must reach consensus on everything". The heavyweight integrator school signs "one named person must be accountable for the whole and able to overrule any specialist" and refuses "rights should be partitioned by risk type". The design-led school signs "where the experience is the product, design holds the final word on the whole". The engineering-led school refuses "every team needs a dedicated designer". Scrum orthodoxy signs "the backlog needs one accountable owner" and cannot sign "design is a co-owner of outcomes", having no such role.

3. Mechanics in depth, with the arithmetic

Expert practice has five steps, and the third and fifth get skipped. Agree the outcome, not the output: Phatak worked back from a feature request to the share of intake calls completed without a post-call correction. Look at the same evidence together: Sen had never watched an intake call, Chitale had never seen the correction data. Generate options, then attack each other's assumptions. Name each risk with a probability. Write down the evidence that would make you abandon the plan, before the build.

The fourth step admits a quantitative treatment. For each risk let p be the team's own probability that its assumption is wrong and Clate the cost of discovering it after the January release; expected rework avoided is p × Clate, and the premium is the cost of testing it early, paid either way. Every late-cost figure below is derived rather than asserted.

Exhibit 1. Cost of building the Nabh first-notification-of-loss scope
RoleWeeks₹ lakh per week₹ lakh
Engineering461.1050.60

Total54—58.00

Fully loaded internal rates: 46 × 1.10 = 50.60, 6 × 0.90 = 5.40 and 2 × 1.00 = 2.00, which sum to 54 weeks and ₹58.00 lakh.

₹58.00 lakh is the write-off if the value assumption fails outright. Reworking the auto-filled form after launch was costed at 22 engineer-weeks (₹24.20 lakh), 7 design-weeks (₹6.30 lakh) and half a product-management week (₹0.50 lakh): ₹31.00 lakh. A policy master unable to answer inside the 900 milliseconds an agent on a live call tolerates forces a caching layer — 32 engineer-weeks (₹35.20 lakh), 4 design-weeks (₹3.60 lakh) and ₹5.20 lakh of infrastructure, or ₹44.00 lakh. The viability failure is arithmetic: the contract prices a notification at ₹14, measured cost was ₹23, and Nabh's year-one volume is about 1,80,000, so ₹9 × 1,80,000 = ₹16.20 lakh of loss plus ₹9.80 lakh to retrofit a cheaper model — ₹26.00 lakh.

Exhibit 2. The four risks on the Nabh scope, priced (₹ lakh)

Expected rework avoided = probability × post-release cost: 0.30 × 58.00 = 17.40; 0.35 × 31.00 = 10.85; 0.40 × 44.00 = 17.60; 0.20 × 26.00 = 5.20. The three money columns sum exactly to 6.30, 159.00 and 51.05.

The two-week discovery that retires all four costs ₹6.30 lakh and avoids ₹51.05 lakh of expected rework: a little over eight to one (51.05 ÷ 6.30 = 8.1). Halve every probability and it falls to ₹25.53 lakh against the same ₹6.30 lakh — still four to one, a net expected gain of ₹19.23 lakh. The case rests not on the probabilities being right but on late discovery being an order of magnitude dearer than early.

The fifth step turns a triad from a meeting into a mechanism. Chitale's abandonment condition was a measured 900 millisecond response in Nabh's staging environment, not an assurance from its integration team; Sen's was five of eight agents completing the form without scrolling back; Phatak's was Jalota confirming in writing that his quality team would accept the automated transcript. Exhibit 4 sets the two sequences side by side: the relay does not do less work, it finds the same four things six to eight weeks later, at the pale-bar prices.

4. When the arrangement applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. More than one class of risk must be material. Pukaar passes: no single risk in Exhibit 2 exceeds ₹17.60 lakh of expected rework, so no one role could have saved the project alone. Pavan's dominant uncertainty is sensor drift, which is Narayanan's, but the decision that follows is Padhye's. Late discovery must be dearer than early. Pukaar's ratio is 8.1 to 1; Pavan's is worse than any ratio, because 38,000 of its units cannot be updated at all. Decision rights must sit inside the team, where Pukaar partly fails. The three must reach the same conversation within a working day. Olgierd Zawadzki, Pavan's firmware contractor in Kraków, is three and a half hours behind Indian time, which leaves usable overlap; a twelve-hour gap would not.

The idea is actively misleading when the value question has already been answered elsewhere and cannot be reopened. Palkar had written the first-notification scope into a renewal narrative Jalota had read, and a discovery sprint whose conclusion sits in a signed order form teaches the team that the ritual is empty. The expert move is to say aloud that the team is executing a sold commitment, and to negotiate for the right to decide next time.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

In multi-product companies triads multiply and collide: Pukaar runs three teams of 11, 12 and 11 engineers, 34 in all, against three designers — one designer per 11.3 engineers, and the seam is the calendar rather than the structure chart. On platform teams the designer may have no interface to design, usability risk having moved into documentation and error messages. In regulated products compliance is a fourth risk with a veto: Pukaar's quarter already held 22 engineer-weeks of IRDAI-mandated logging. In hardware tooling lead times are external, so feasibility becomes a date.

Exhibit 5. The Pavan Nirmal installed base, 24 September 2026
CohortUnits soldCan receive over-the-air firmwareActive subscriptionsAttach rate
v1, shipped before March 202538,000No21,00055%
v2, shipped from March 20251,02,000Yes65,00064%
Total1,40,000—86,00061%

Attach rate = subscriptions ÷ units: 21,000 ÷ 38,000 = 55.3%; 65,000 ÷ 1,02,000 = 63.7%; 86,000 ÷ 1,40,000 = 61.4%, shown rounded. Units sum to 1,40,000 and subscriptions to 86,000 exactly; over-the-air updates reach 1,02,000 of 1,40,000 units, 73 per cent.

Any change to the filter schedule therefore lands on 73 per cent of the fleet and leaves 21,000 paying v1 subscribers on the old behaviour: neither a feasibility problem Narayanan can solve nor a usability problem Nagarkar can design away, but a two-prices-in-one-fleet problem, and Padhye's because it is a viability question.

AI-native products entangle two risks the model treats as separate: whether a model reaches an accuracy bar is unknowable until tried, so feasibility becomes probabilistic, and because value depends on that accuracy the value question cannot be settled first. Mature teams make the evaluation set the shared artefact — the designer specifying what a tolerable failure looks like, the engineer what the model can reach, the product manager the accuracy at which the economics work.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Risks, not functions. The partition is of risk, not subject matter, and the tell is an engineer who says "that's a product question" when asked whether the problem is worth solving. The obvious reading, everyone in their own lane, inverts the mechanism.

The three speak in different time units. Engineering cost lands inside a quarter, value arrives as an annuity, usability debt accrues silently. Watch for a case setting the ₹75.50 lakh of build Phatak chose against the ₹187.2 lakh of annual recurring revenue it was expected to earn without saying which recurs.

Feasibility is a distribution, not a date. Chitale's 46 weeks is a median with a tail, and the tell is a single-point estimate; the expert's question is "what assumption would double this?" Treating an estimate as a promise teaches engineers to inflate and product managers to discount.

Usability risk is not screen risk. By the time screens exist, most usability has been settled by the data model and the sequence of system calls, and the tell is a designer invited after the schema review. No agent can be shown a confidently auto-filled form if the policy master answers in 2.4 seconds.

Authority would destroy what it is meant to improve. The product manager's influence is the quality of her argument, because formal authority over the other two suppresses the objections the arrangement exists to produce. The tell is a quarter in which nobody said no on the record.

Rates from different windows are not comparable. Pavan's 3.4 per cent monthly churn is a twelve-month figure; the 4.6 per cent Narayanan quoted for a silent change came from a two-month episode in 2024. Side by side they imply a comparison the data cannot support.

Fractional designers are not fractional. A designer at 20 per cent across five teams does not deliver a fifth of a designer; she delivers reviews, because attention does not divide linearly. The same holds for risks with no seat at all — compliance, supply, data quality — silently assigned to whoever is most optimistic.

The triad improves answers; it cannot choose the question. Three well-coordinated people can work beautifully on a problem no customer has, and the tell is excellent collaboration rituals beside flat outcome metrics.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

The four risks are the same everywhere; what varies is their relative size and who can best retire them. In consumer products usability risk is largest in absolute terms, because small friction multiplied by millions is the whole business. In B2B and enterprise the buyer, the user and the administrator are three people, so value risk splits — will the buyer pay, will the user adopt — and feasibility extends into systems the team does not control, as Nabh's policy master shows. In platform and marketplace products viability dominates; in hardware shipped atoms turn feasibility into scheduling; in AI products feasibility and value stop being separable.

Stage changes the shape more than type does. At twenty people the triad is often the founder, one designer and a lead engineer, and its weakness is that the founder's value judgement cannot be contradicted. At Pukaar's size the binding constraint is design supply at 1 to 11.3, so the discipline is allocation rather than formation; at two thousand, two teams need the same engineer in one quarter and the work becomes defining what each triad owns.

8. Three worked examples

One: the audit-trail export (succeeded). Pukaar's third candidate was a compliance-grade audit export, 22 engineer-weeks. At Exhibit 1's rates — ₹24.20 lakh of engineering, 2 design-weeks at ₹0.90 lakh and one product-management week at ₹1.00 lakh — the total is ₹27.00 lakh. Three prospects represented ₹1.9 crore, ₹1.6 crore and ₹1.3 crore of recurring revenue, ₹4.8 crore in all. Palkar put the win probability at 15 per cent without the export and 45 per cent with it, applied uniformly: expected revenue rises from ₹4.8 crore × 0.15 = ₹72 lakh to ₹4.8 crore × 0.45 = ₹216 lakh, a gain of ₹144 lakh against ₹27.00 lakh. The uniform probability is the weak joint.

Two: the filter-health card (succeeded). In 2025 Nagarkar found nine of twelve test users reading Pavan's filter indicator as a fault light. The redesigned card cut filter-related support contacts from 4,900 a month to 2,100 — a fall of 2,800, or 57 per cent — worth 2,800 × ₹92 a contact = ₹2.58 lakh a month, ₹30.91 lakh a year. Narayanan supplied the confidence interval that let the card say "about 40 days left" rather than a false precision.

Three: Pukaar Insight (failed). In FY25 Pukaar built an analytics module with a triad that existed on a slide: a designer at 20 per cent across four teams, an engineering lead whose contract ended before launch, and a product manager running discovery alone.

Exhibit 6. Pukaar Insight: what was spent and what was recovered (₹ lakh)
Line₹ lakh
Engineering, 96 weeks at ₹1.10 lakh per week105.60
Design, 8 weeks at ₹0.90 lakh per week7.20
Product management, 6 weeks at ₹1.00 lakh per week6.00

Brackets denote a recovery: 34 engineer-weeks at ₹1.10 lakh = ₹37.40 lakh. 105.60 + 7.20 + 6.00 − 37.40 = 81.40.

Three of fourteen customers enabled the module and 212 of 2,900 claims agents used it weekly, 7.3 per cent. The failure was structural rather than one of effort: a 20 per cent designer produces reviews, not options, and a contractor lead has no stake after his term. The recovery was to stop the module, salvage the query engine for the audit export, and require a named designer at half time or more on every team.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

The relay dressed as a triad.
Sign: the engineer first meets the problem as a ticket. Diagnostic: when did you first see this problem, and in what form? Cost of catching it late: Exhibit 6's ₹81.40 lakh.
The product manager as sole channel to customers.
Sign: research arrives as a summary deck. Diagnostic: ask the designer to describe the last customer conversation she attended rather than read about.
Estimates entered as commitments.
Sign: single numbers with no range. Diagnostic: what assumption would double this? Cost: the ₹44.00 lakh feasibility line in Exhibit 2.
The unowned fourth risk.
Sign: compliance or supply named in no plan. Diagnostic: whose name is against this risk, and what would they say to stop a release?
A triad with no decision rights.
Sign: routine decisions escalate. At Pukaar nine decisions in the June quarter waited a median of six working days for an executive slot; four were sequential, so 24 of the quarter's 62 working days went on waiting — 39 per cent. Diagnostic: name the last decision the three of you made that nobody above you revisited.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Co-equal trio or single accountable owner? The integrator school rests on Clark and Fujimoto's finding that vehicle programmes with heavyweight chief engineers were faster and more coherent than matrix-run ones, and on Amazon's record with single-threaded leaders: partitioned rights produce averaged products and slow escalation. The trio school answers that four risks require expertise no single head holds, and that one owner merely relocates the handover inside one calendar. The integrator position fails if named integrators show worse usability and feasibility surprises; the trio position fails if trios decide slower without better outcomes.

Three or four, and does continuous discovery scale? A growing camp holds that data science in analytics-heavy products, and the machine-learning lead in AI products, are co-owners rather than contributors; the orthodox reply is that three is already hard and the model lead's judgement belongs inside feasibility. Teresa Torres holds that the trio must talk to customers weekly; sceptics answer that for Pukaar's fourteen gatekept accounts weekly contact is neither available nor representative.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the triad can recite four risks. Someone who has internalised it can state which risk is largest this week and whose name is on it, without preparation; arrives at feasibility conversations with the economic consequence already worked out, so a constraint changes a decision and not only a plan; and writes the abandonment condition down before the build.

12. What each of them decided

On Friday 16 October 2026, Phatak committed the triage queue and the audit export — 34 plus 22 engineer-weeks, 56 of the 78 available in the quarter — and declined the bespoke first-notification scope for January. The triage queue saves Nabh's own operation measurably: 1,100 agents × 24 claims a day × 300 operating days × 40 seconds = 88,000 agent-hours a year, which at ₹260 an hour is ₹2.29 crore of Nabh's cost, of which Pukaar had contracted to capture ₹43.2 lakh a year, about 19 per cent. Its build cost — 34 engineer-weeks at ₹1.10 lakh, 9 design-weeks at ₹0.90 lakh and 3 product-management weeks at ₹1.00 lakh — is ₹48.50 lakh, which pays back on Nabh alone in roughly 13 months. The remaining 22 engineer-weeks held the first-notification work, ₹6.30 lakh of it the discovery of Exhibit 2, with an April release offered to Jalota conditional on the four abandonment conditions.

Exhibit 7. Pavan Air Works: subscription economics per subscriber per month (₹)
ScenarioPriceCost to serveContributionAssumed monthly churnExpected lifetime contribution
Today: 90-day filter shipments34980.00269.003.4%7,912
A: 150-day shipments, price held, no announcement34958.40290.604.6%6,317
B: 150-day shipments, price cut to ₹249, explained24958.40190.602.2%8,664

Cost to serve today: filter ₹118 ÷ 3 months = ₹39.33, logistics ₹44 ÷ 3 = ₹14.67, support and payment fees ₹26.00 — ₹80.00 exactly. On a 150-day cycle: ₹23.60 + ₹8.80 + ₹26.00 = ₹58.40. Expected lifetime contribution = contribution ÷ monthly churn: 269.00 ÷ 0.034 = ₹7,912; 290.60 ÷ 0.046 = ₹6,317; 190.60 ÷ 0.022 = ₹8,664.

Padhye declined to decide on 24 September, which was right and unpopular: the ranking in Exhibit 7 turns entirely on churn assumptions nobody had measured. Option A survives only if a silent change holds monthly churn below 290.60 ÷ 7,912 = 3.67 per cent, a quarter of a point above today's 3.4; option B beats the status quo only if churn falls below 190.60 ÷ 7,912 = 2.41 per cent. So the triad converted a decision into a measurement: from 12 October, 6,000 randomly chosen v2 subscribers were offered the repriced plan with Nagarkar's filter-health explanation for three months. At 3.4 per cent monthly churn, 6,000 × 0.966³ leaves 5,409 subscribers and 591 cancellations; at 2.2 per cent, 6,000 × 0.978³ leaves 5,613 and 387 — a gap of 204. The 21,000 v1 subscribers were excluded, and what Pavan owes them was recorded as unresolved. Taken fleet-wide at ₹190.60 across 86,000 subscribers, annual contribution would fall from ₹27.76 crore to ₹19.67 crore, down ₹8.09 crore.

Discussion questions

  1. Phatak declined a scope his largest customer had asked for, eleven days before a commitment date and six months before a ₹7.2 crore renewal. On the evidence of Exhibits 1 and 2, was he discharging the value-and-viability ownership the triad gives him, or exceeding it?
  2. Exhibit 7's ranking depends on three churn numbers, two of them guesses and one measured over a non-comparable window. Whose risk is that — Padhye's viability risk, or Narayanan's feasibility risk in the sensor measurement that started the discussion?
  3. Pukaar Insight failed with a 20 per cent designer and a contractor engineering lead, and the fix was a staffing rule rather than a process change. Is that the right diagnosis, or did the rule make the next failure more expensive to start?

13. Going deeper

What a product manager does — the triad only makes sense once the product manager's own contribution is specified. Empowered teams versus feature teams — the triad says who must be in the room; this says whether that room is handed problems or features, which is what Phatak was negotiating. PM myths versus reality — "CEO of the product" is the commonest corruption of the arrangement. Origins of product management — McElroy, the shusa and three-in-a-box explain why the schools of section 2 disagree. PM versus PMM, TPM, project manager and founder — the roles most often mistaken for triad members. PM archetypes — which risk a product manager is strongest at retiring. How the PM job changes by company stage — section 7's differences, worked through. The end-to-end product lifecycle — where each risk peaks.
case40v1-pm.triad:
Wachan Energy Network: The Promise in the App

A teaching case set in Hyderabad, October 2026

1. Sunday night, Gachibowli

The rain that was to end the monsoon arrived over Hyderabad on Sunday 18 October 2026, and Shubhada Kolte watched it from the Wachan Energy Network office in Gachibowli. On her screen were two documents she could not reconcile. One was a slide for Thursday 29 October's board product review, eleven days away: the new reservation feature had cut the time a rider waited for a charged battery by nearly a quarter. The other was Mayumi Takeda's memo from Osaka, dated 2 October: waiting time at Wachan's Hyderabad stations had risen since the feature shipped, logs attached.

Both were honest. Each used a different instrument, pointed at a different population, over a window that did not match the other's. Underneath them lay the question the quarter beginning 1 November depended on: whether riders could not find a charged pack, could not trust that they would, or whether nobody was accountable for the difference.

Kalyan Yarlagadda, the founder, had sent one line at six: Keep it simple on Thursday. One plan, one number. Shubhada had three plans and four numbers, and Pune wanted a decision by Monday morning.

2. How Wachan came to be built this way

Wachan Energy Network was founded in March 2021 by Kalyan Yarlagadda after eleven years in two-wheeler distribution. Wachan owns the packs, the cabinets and the charging; a rider swaps a depleted pack for a charged one in under two minutes. By September 2026 it ran 412 stations in four cities and 10,016 packs, and did 2,30,640 swaps for ₹2.35 crore of net revenue, a run rate of about ₹28.15 crore. It had raised ₹244 crore across two rounds and sunk ₹39.14 crore into stations and ₹58.09 crore into packs: ₹97.23 crore of hard assets.

One 2022 decision shapes everything available to Shubhada today. For the second-generation pack, the founding engineers chose a proprietary form factor with a closed connector and their own cell-level telemetry board, built around modules from Hanbit Cell Modules in Seoul. The reasoning is still defensible: the board reads every cell group's state of health, so packs retire before they fail in a rider's hands. The consequence: Wachan can neither buy nor admit another maker's pack, and cannot change charging schedules without shipping safety-critical firmware. That firmware moves on a certified train leaving every six weeks — next on 23 October, 4 December and 15 January — because every build clears the safety review adopted for AIS-156 testing. The app ships whenever Pune likes.

So the company has two clocks: what product can promise quickly lives in the app, and what keeps the promise lives behind the six-week clock, in Osaka.

3. The industry around it

India's battery-swapping market in 2026 is crowded at the bottom and unsettled at the top. Battery Smart and Sun Mobility have built large networks in the north and west; Ola Electric and Ather sell fixed-battery scooters, removing riders from swapping; Mahindra Last Mile Mobility's three-wheelers dominate the passenger-auto segment Wachan serves. The demand behind it all is quick commerce: riders contracted to Zepto, Swiggy, Blinkit and Flipkart's logistics arm, for whom eight minutes at a cabinet is a lost delivery.

Policy is both tailwind and threat. PM E-DRIVE incentives have pulled capital in, while NITI Aayog's battery-swapping policy work and the Bureau of Indian Standards' interoperability drafts point to a future in which any pack fits any cabinet — for Wachan's pack, an existential question, not a compliance chore. Rider location, which the reservation feature consumes freely, falls within the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the consent flow has not been revisited since 2024.

Wachan also has one foot outside India. In April 2026 Pennine Last Mile, a Manchester operator of electric cargo bikes and vans, signed a letter of intent to licence Wachan's station software for 60 stations in north-west England: £1.8 million over three years, about ₹19.8 crore at ₹110 to the pound, with a £400,000 milestone — ₹4.4 crore — on go-live. Go-live is 31 March 2027, conditional on sterling billing, UK data residency and a GDPR posture Wachan lacks. It is the only revenue on the horizon with a signature attached.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Exhibit 1 is the network as finance reports it. Hyderabad is the oldest, densest market and carries 46 per cent of swaps; Lucknow, opened in January 2026, is still thin. The figure Shubhada had stared at all month is Hyderabad's utilisation: 24.0 swaps per station-day against a design assumption of 18.
