The last ten weeks begin with a complaint that was not about availability at all. Through the first half of 2026, Afreen Siddiqui's support team in Lucknow kept logging one kind of call: a rider had ridden four kilometres to a cabinet, found every slot occupied by a pack still charging, and lost an order. The packs existed, in the wrong state at the wrong minute. Shubhada's reading, supported by Sanika Vedpathak's arrival model in Vancouver, was that the shortage was not of packs but of certainty. From that came Reserve-a-Pack: tap a cabinet on the map, the app holds a charged pack for fifteen minutes, ride to it. Copenhagen designed the flow in July, Pune built it, and the cabinet side needed only a slot-lock firmware change. It launched in Hyderabad alone on 10 August 2026, the logic deliberately simple: fifteen minutes, always, for everyone.

Fifty-three days after launch, on 2 October, with the September month closed, Mayumi's memo arrived. By then Sanika had circulated Exhibit 3, the basis of the board slide, which read once is encouraging: of 18,000 monthly active riders in Hyderabad in September, 2,268 completed a swap on a reserved pack, 12.6 per cent end to end. Read twice it is less comfortable. Only 3,780 of the 5,040 reservations started were confirmed by a cabinet; 1,260 times there was no spare charged pack to hold. What the held packs cost, nobody asked until October. The 1,512 missed holds removed 22,680 pack-minutes — 378 pack-hours — from Hyderabad circulation in September. At ₹10.21 of contribution a swap (Exhibit 7), and assuming a held pack would otherwise serve 0.8 to 1.0 swaps an hour, the loss is ₹3,100 to ₹3,900 for the month: roughly a quarter to a little under a third of one Hyderabad station's monthly rent and power infrastructure, ₹13,104. On that arithmetic the problem is a rounding error. Bhanwar Shekhawat's objection is that the arithmetic is the wrong shape: two-thirds of the missed holds, 1,008 of them, fall in the evening peak between seven and ten, withdrawing 252 pack-hours from the cabinets where riders already queue.

5. The people

Shubhada Kolte, vice-president of product, Hyderabad, owns the roadmap, the reservation metric and the board slide, and wants a visible win. She has told nobody that she chose the fifteen-minute hold herself, because a variable hold needed firmware she could not get before Diwali.

Kalyan Yarlagadda, founder and chief executive, Hyderabad, wants one plan, one number, and a Series C conversation opening in January with a utilisation story. He is privately unsure the proprietary pack was the right bet, and will not have that opened before the board.

Ritesh Chinchwade, engineering director for platform and app, Pune, nine engineers, delivers what is specified and is measured on that. He does not say, in front of Mayumi, that his team defined "confirmed" in a way that flatters the feature.

Mayumi Takeda, principal embedded engineer for pack and cabinet firmware, Osaka, four engineers, wrote the memo and alone can change charging schedules; her incentive is an unbroken safety record. She has not mentioned the charge-scheduling change she has tested in simulation, because proposing it concedes that availability is partly hers.

Signe Holmgaard, design director, Copenhagen, is four and a half hours behind Hyderabad and absent after four. She argues the flow answers a question design was handed rather than asked: by the time she saw the brief, the hold was fifteen minutes. She is close to leaving and has not said so.

Sanika Vedpathak, data science lead, Vancouver, built both the arrival model that justified the feature and the funnel that measures it, and needs the model to be seen to work. She has not said that her model assumed 85 per cent of holds would be honoured, against the 60 per cent observed.

Afreen Siddiqui, rider experience lead, Lucknow, is closest to what riders say and furthest from the roadmap; her incentive is ticket volume, which leaves her indifferent between fixing a cause and suppressing a symptom.

Bhanwar Shekhawat, head of network operations, Jaipur, owns all 412 stations and pack rebalancing, and is paid on uptime and swaps per station-day. He wants the feature off in the evening peak, or 1,200 more packs, and does not mention that his Hyderabad rebalancing routes come from a spreadsheet last revised in March.

Zain Peerbhoy, partnerships, Manchester, holds the Pennine relationship and the only signed revenue, and needs sterling billing, data residency and an availability story by 31 March 2027. Pennine's operations director has twice asked him for cabinet-log figures rather than the app's; he has not told Hyderabad.

Exhibit 6's claim is easy to agree with and hard to act on: three surfaces on three clocks jointly manufacture availability, while planning allocates to each separately.

6. The economics of a swap

Exhibit 7 is the per-swap picture finance maintains, and why every argument here becomes one about packs.

Against ₹18 crore of cash at 30 September, the month's outflow of ₹2.51 crore leaves 7.2 months of runway, into May 2027.

7. In their own words

"The controller has no opinion about which rider deserves a pack; it locks the slot it is told to lock. If product tells it to lock 3,780 slots and 1,512 of those riders do not come, the controller has done its job and the network has not."

Mayumi Takeda, memo of 2 October 2026

"My number is not a worse version of Mayumi's. Hers includes every fleet driver who never opens the app; mine cannot. If anyone puts both on one slide with an arrow between them, we deserve what follows."

Sanika Vedpathak, product-analytics channel, 5 October

"Switch it off from seven to ten. I am not asking for a study. At Kukatpally I watched four drivers wait while two slots sat locked for riders who never came. One asked me whether Wachan keeps packs for its own people."

Bhanwar Shekhawat, operations review, 2 September

"We shipped a promise on a surface that cannot keep promises. Fifteen minutes was not a design decision and not an engineering decision. It was a calendar decision."

Signe Holmgaard, design review, 24 September

"Riders do not file a ticket saying 'your reservation policy is miscalibrated'. They say the app lied. Twelve hundred said it last month, and we cannot tell you how many were refused and how many were late, because we coded both alike."

Afreen Siddiqui, email to Shubhada, 1 October

8. The options as Shubhada sees them

Exhibit 8 is the arithmetic she has worked against since the board's 28 September request. The quarter from 1 November to 30 January is thirteen weeks: nine app and platform engineers give 117 person-weeks and four firmware engineers 52, 169 in all, of which reliability and on-call take 24 and 16, leaving 93 app weeks and 36 firmware weeks. The six asks want 94 and 52.

Exhibit 8. Capacity and asks, 1 November 2026 to 30 January 2027 (person-weeks)

Source: estimates from Ritesh Chinchwade and Mayumi Takeda, 9 October 2026, at a stated confidence of "within thirty per cent". Firmware weeks are not interchangeable with app weeks and cannot be hired inside the quarter: 52 asked against 36 available is 1.44 times capacity. Design capacity, two people, is not shown.

Shubhada has derived three options, aware that all three are of the same type.

Option A: make the promise better. Reserve-a-Pack v2 — a hold window varying with the rider's distance, the cabinet's queue and the hour, with a penalty for repeated no-shows. Thirty-six person-weeks, fourteen of them firmware, which fits the 4 December train if the specification freezes by mid-November. It defends the board slide and attacks the 1,512 missed holds, but assumes the feature is worth saving, and spends 39 per cent of scarce firmware weeks on the surface Mayumi thinks matters least.

Option B: make availability real. Drop the reservation work; spend firmware on pack health scoring and the charge-scheduling change Mayumi has in simulation, so cabinets hold more charged packs when riders want them. Twenty-two person-weeks, twelve of them firmware. It attacks Exhibit 4's telemetry row and Exhibit 5's second bucket, shows riders nothing by January, and leaves the peak-hour locks in place unless the feature is switched off too.

Option C: serve the signed revenue. Pennine, 24 person-weeks, plus the fleet dashboard quick-commerce partners keep asking for, 26 weeks, deferring the rest to February. It books ₹4.4 crore and opens a market where swapping is not yet contested — and means nobody works for a quarter on what Pennine's operations director keeps asking about.

Bhanwar has a fourth, unwritten because it is not a product decision: buy 1,200 packs from Hanbit, ₹6.96 crore, 38.7 per cent of the company's cash, lead time sixteen weeks, and stop arguing. Signe has a fifth, unwritten because Shubhada cannot cost it: that product, design and engineering first agree what "available" means, who measures it and which of them may say no — and that until that is settled, every option above returns in February.

9. The deadline and what cannot move

The board product review is on Thursday 29 October. The quarter begins on 1 November, seven days before Diwali on 8 November, when quick-commerce volumes run 30 to 40 per cent above a normal week. Anything touching the pack must be specified by mid-November for the 4 December train; the next train, 15 January, is too late this quarter. The Hanbit order must be placed by 15 November for packs to land by 7 March. Pennine's go-live is 31 March 2027, with the ₹4.4 crore milestone. Cash is ₹18 crore; the outflow of ₹2.51 crore a month gives 7.2 months. Firmware engineers cannot be hired inside the quarter, and Mayumi will not sign a build she has not tested for four weeks. The DPDP consent work has no owner; Signe's notice period is three months.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 3, 4 and 5, state in one sentence what Reserve-a-Pack did to rider experience in September, then argue the opposite.
  2. Exhibits 3 and 4 use different instruments, populations and windows. What single measurement would discriminate between them, and who would own it?
  3. Sanika's model assumed 85 per cent of holds honoured; 60 per cent were. Whose assumption was that, and when should it have been contested?
  4. The fifteen-minute hold was chosen because a variable hold needed firmware nobody could get. Is that a product decision, a design decision, an engineering decision or a planning artefact — and who should have made it?
  5. Exhibit 8 shows 52 firmware weeks asked against 36 available while app capacity is nearly balanced. What does that asymmetry imply about how Wachan decides what to build, and about the 2022 pack decision behind it?
  6. It is Monday 19 October; the board meets on the 29th and the 4 December train closes in mid-November. What do you do that morning, in what order, and what goes on Kalyan's one slide? If the board asks which number will move by January, what do you say?

Sunday night, continued

At a quarter past eleven Shubhada closed the memo and opened the board deck. The slide still said minus twenty-three per cent. In the attendants' WhatsApp group, someone in Kukatpally had posted a photograph of four riders waiting under a cabinet awning, two slots lit amber for packs held for riders who never arrived; Bhanwar had forwarded it at 10:48 pm. She looked at it a while, then typed one line in a blank document — What do we mean by available? — aware that the answer would commit four engineers in Osaka and nine in Pune for thirteen weeks, and not knowing whether the question was the beginning of a plan or an elegant way of not having one.
case20v1-pm.triad:
Jaagrit Fees Systems: Who Owns the Outcome?

A teaching case on the product triad

1. Opening

On Monday 12 October 2026, Sanjana Rathinam arrived at the Jaagrit Fees Systems office in Pune with a calendar entry she had been dreading. On Friday 23 October the company's quarterly planning committee would meet in Mumbai, and Sanjana, the group product manager, had to present one plan for the last quarter of the year. The plan would set what six engineers, one designer and one product manager did between 2 November and the end of January.

The timing mattered. The second-term fee cycle would open in the first week of November, days before Diwali on 8 November, when families are stretched by travel, gifts and school fees together. Two plans were circulating. One was a list of features that principals had asked for. The other was a question Sanjana had asked for a month without a good answer: why did three out of four parents who received a fee reminder still not pay through the app?

2. Company background

Jaagrit Fees Systems was founded in 2019 in Pune by Mahesh Chinnappa, a former finance manager at a chain of private schools. The product began as a way for a school office to send fee reminders and collect payments by UPI instead of cheques and cash at a counter. By October 2026 it served 640 schools, mostly CBSE-affiliated, in Pune, Nashik, Indore, Nagpur and Coimbatore, with an average of 900 students each, or 5,76,000 student accounts in total.

The schools pay Jaagrit a subscription of ₹75 per student per year, which gives annual revenue of ₹4.32 crore (5,76,000 students at ₹75). That is ₹67,500 per school on average. Payments run through Razorpay and the UPI network run by NPCI, under the RBI's rules on payment intermediaries. Competition comes from school-management platforms such as Teachmint, which bundle attendance and fees, and from consumer apps such as PhonePe, where a parent can pay a fee without installing anything from the school.

Growth had come largely from the sales team. Sandesh Parulekar, the head of sales, based in Mumbai, closed schools by promising what each principal asked for. Last year 32 schools did not renew, or 5 per cent of the 640 now on the books. Using the average, that is about ₹21.6 lakh of annual revenue gone (32 schools at ₹67,500). The exit calls were polite and vague.

3. The situation

Sanjana inherited a product team that worked in sequence. Sandesh brought requests to her, she wrote a requirements document, the designer produced screens, and engineering built what the screens showed. Rohit Gadre, the engineering lead in Pune, described it plainly: "We hear about a problem when it is already a ticket with a deadline."

Exhibit 1 shows what happened to the reminders sent for the first-term cycle in July. Of 5,76,000 reminders, 60 per cent were opened, and 60 per cent of those parents reached the payment screen. Of those, 70 per cent finished paying. The overall result was 1,45,152 completed payments, or 25.2 per cent of accounts. The rest paid cash at the school office, which the app was meant to end. The largest loss is at the first step, where 2,30,400 reminders were never opened; the smallest, 62,208 parents, is at the payment screen, closest to the money.

4. The people

Mahesh Chinnappa, the chief executive in Pune, wants renewals to improve and fears the company is losing its way. He is open to a different method but wants results before the year ends.

Sandesh Parulekar, head of sales in Mumbai, wants every request answered. He regards time spent on interviews as time not spent on the pipeline.

Rohit Gadre, engineering lead in Pune, wants to build things that are clear and finite. He is tired of payment-link bugs he knows how to fix and has never been given room to fix.

Lieke Bosman, design lead in Amsterdam, wants to be involved when the problem is defined, not after. Njeri Gathogo in Nairobi wants fewer tickets and has the clearest picture of what parents say.

6. The options

Option A: Build the backlog. Engineering would spend all 60 available person-weeks on Exhibit 4 in order of schools asking, dropping the library module (6 person-weeks, so 66 less 6 leaves 60). Five of six items would ship. The upside is that Sandesh can say yes to most schools and the work is concrete. The cost is that no one has tested whether these items change renewals, and the funnel stays untouched.

Option B: Run the triad on one outcome. Sanjana, Lieke and Rohit would jointly own a single outcome: raise the share of accounts paying through the app from 25.2 per cent to 35 per cent by the end of January. For four weeks, two engineers, the designer and Sanjana would sit in parent calls, school offices and Njeri's tickets, using 8 person-weeks of engineering time. The remaining 52 person-weeks would go to the bets the three agreed on, perhaps including items from Exhibit 4. The upside is that the work follows evidence. The cost is that for a month the company ships little, and Sandesh must tell schools their requests are being weighed.

Option C: Keep the relay and add speed. Sanjana would write a payment specification in three weeks, Lieke would design for three, and engineering would start in week seven. Six engineers building for six weeks give 36 person-weeks; with 12 on maintenance, 24 would sit idle or drift to other work (72 less 12 less 36). The upside is that nothing changes in how people work. The cost is that the relay stays, the engineers' knowledge of the payment bugs arrives late, and the cycle opens before anything ships.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Who is Jaagrit's customer: the school that pays the subscription, the parent who pays the fee, or both? How does Exhibit 2 change your answer?
  2. What does each member of the triad bring that Sanjana alone could not?
  3. Using Exhibits 1 and 4, which request, if any, connects to the outcome Mahesh cares about? What would you want to know before believing it?
  4. Which option would you take to the committee on 23 October, and what would you say to Sandesh on the way out?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. The triad treats the product manager, designer and engineer as co-owners of an outcome. The PM brings the customer and the business: is this worth doing? The designer brings the parent's experience: can a tired person do this on a phone? The engineer brings what is possible, and at what cost. Teams that start from a backlog ask only what to build; a triad asks first what problem a customer has.

What a good answer looks like. A good answer separates the buyer (the school) from the user (the parent), notes that Exhibit 2 puts 65 per cent of tickets (1,920 plus 1,200 of 4,800) in two fixable categories, and recognises that Exhibit 4 does not fit the capacity anyway. It also admits the cost of Option B: a month of fewer visible releases.

One defensible path. Option B, time-boxed. Make payment completion the shared outcome, and commit the four weeks of discovery with a hard end date of 27 November. Let Rohit fix the expired-link and failed-UPI faults at once, because they are 40 per cent of tickets and need no research. Ask Lieke to redesign the student-code step. Give Sandesh a clear message for schools: requests are logged against the outcome and answered in January. Keep parent chat (8 person-weeks) in view as the item most plausibly linked to the outcome, and decide on it with evidence. If discovery shows the funnel is not driving non-renewal, say so and move to the backlog with better reasons. Options A and C leave Exhibit 1 where it is.
case20v1-pm.waterfall.agile:
Bhavya Billing Systems: One Roadmap, Two Kinds of Work

A teaching case on choosing a development approach

1. Opening

On the morning of Tuesday 17 November 2026, a week after Diwali, Chitra Anantharaman sat in a glass-walled meeting room on the third floor of her company's office in Baner, Pune, with a one-page planning sheet and a deadline. By Friday 20 November she had to tell the board and her fifteen engineers how the next twenty-four weeks of product work would be run. Planning would begin on Tuesday 1 December.

The sheet held two items. The first was a compliance upgrade that had to be live by 1 April 2027. The second was a collections feature that nobody could yet describe with confidence. Chitra, Vice President of Product at Bhavya Billing Systems, suspected that these two items should not be managed in the same way. The board, however, had asked for a single roadmap with a single date.

2. Company background

Bhavya Billing Systems sells cloud invoicing and GST filing software to small manufacturers and distributors, mostly firms with annual turnover between ₹2 crore and ₹40 crore. It was founded in Pune in 2017. It has 14,200 paying customers, each paying an average of ₹18,000 a year, which gives annual revenue of ₹25.56 crore (14,200 x 18,000 = ₹25,56,00,000).

The company competes with Tally, which many customers already use for bookkeeping, with Zoho Books, Vyapar and ClearTax, and with the invoicing modules that Razorpay bundles with its accounts. Bhavya's argument is depth for the Indian distributor: e-way bills, multiple godowns and tax-rate changes that arrive in the invoice screen the day the GST Council notifies them.

Two government-linked facts shape the year. Businesses are connected to the Invoice Registration Portal run under the GST Network, and Bhavya's compliance counsel expects the e-invoicing turnover threshold to fall again, bringing a new band of small businesses into scope from 1 April 2027. Bhavya has 3,100 customers in that band. At ₹18,000 each they represent ₹5.58 crore a year, or 21.8 per cent of revenue. Invoices still sit unpaid for weeks.

3. The situation

Chitra's team has two candidate workstreams. The first, call it Workstream A, is the e-invoicing upgrade. The technical specification is published, the integration route through GST suvidha providers is documented, and the company has built a similar connector before. Engineering estimates sixteen weeks with nine engineers.

The second, Workstream B, is a collections assistant: automated reminders sent to a distributor's buyers over WhatsApp, with a dashboard showing who owes what. It came from a sales hunch and a pattern: 11,000 customers issue credit invoices and many complain about late payment. What a distributor would actually pay for is unclear. Engineering estimates twenty-four weeks with six engineers, but admits it is a guess: WhatsApp Business templates need platform approval and nobody knows how buyers will react.

The company has been burned before. Exhibit 1 shows three recent projects. The 2023 tax-rate module was planned in detail and delivered almost on time, and customers adopted it. The 2025 auto-reminders first version was also planned in detail, ran 70 per cent late, and was used by only 12 per cent of eligible customers. The 2025 dispatch tracker was run in two-week cycles inside an eight-week box, shipped on time and was adopted by half its eligible base.

Exhibit 2 sets out the two workstreams. Each engineer-week is costed at ₹60,000, a loaded figure covering salary, tools and overhead. Workstream A and Workstream B each come to 144 engineer-weeks and ₹86.4 lakh, so the full programme is 288 engineer-weeks and ₹172.8 lakh. The board's alternative, one integrated plan, would use all fifteen engineers for twenty-four weeks: 360 engineer-weeks, or ₹216 lakh (360 x 60,000 = ₹2,16,00,000), because the slower item sets the pace.

Exhibit 3 summarises thirty customer conversations that Caleb Mutua's team ran in October. Twelve customers (40 per cent) wanted WhatsApp reminders to their buyers, nine (30 per cent) wanted a way to flag a disputed invoice, six (20 per cent) wanted part-payment tracking, and three (10 per cent) wanted none of it.

The people closest to the work see it differently, from different places.

4. The people

Bharat Kulkarni, head of engineering, Bengaluru. He leads the fifteen engineers across Bengaluru and Pune. He wants a frozen scope, and does not want agile to become an excuse for never finishing.

Bala Krishnamurthy, head of sales, Chennai. He sells to distributors across the south and wants the reminders feature announced before the January sales conference. He has told three large accounts it is coming.

Britta Janssen, product designer, Amsterdam. She works three to four hours behind Pune, and she wants two weeks with real distributors before a screen is built. She has watched buyers ignore messages that sounded like a bank.

Caleb Mutua, customer-success lead, Nairobi. He runs the support desk remotely and hears every complaint first. He worries that the compliance deadline is being treated as one more feature when a missed date means customers cannot legally invoice.

5. The options

Option 1: One integrated plan. Specify both workstreams in full, freeze the scope, and release together. This gives the board and Bala a date. The cost is ₹216 lakh, and because B governs the pace, the combined release would land about 18 May, some 47 days after the compliance threshold. It would also fix a design for B that nobody can yet justify.

Option 2: Agile for everything. Run two-week sprints across all fifteen engineers with no committed scope or date, and let the backlog order itself by what customers say. This respects the uncertainty in B and could help Britta's discovery work. The cost is that A has no committed end date, even though the date is imposed from outside, and the 3,100 customers worth ₹5.58 crore have no assurance.

Option 3: Split by how well the work is known. Plan Workstream A with a fixed scope, milestones and a certification window, using nine engineers for sixteen weeks (₹86.4 lakh). Treat Workstream B as a lean experiment: four six-week tranches of six engineers, each costing 36 engineer-weeks or ₹21.6 lakh, with a decision gate after each. Total for B is capped at ₹86.4 lakh. The cost is two ways of working in one team, and a sales story for Bala that is a pilot, not a promise.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, what separated the tax-rate module from the first reminders version? What does the pattern suggest about when detailed up-front planning works?
  2. For each workstream in Exhibit 2, how known are the requirements and the technology? Which approach does that point to, and why?
  3. What does Exhibit 3 tell Chitra about the reminders hypothesis, and what would she want to learn in the first six weeks before spending more?
  4. Rank the three options against the deadline, cost, and risk of building something customers do not use. What would you tell Bharat, Bala and the board?

7. A note for the learner

This case asks you to choose an approach by how known the requirements and technology are, not by fashion. Waterfall and agile are different ways of walking the same lifecycle. Where the destination is known and the cost of a late or wrong release is high, as with a statutory deadline, plan the route. Where the destination is itself a hypothesis, plan the next experiment and keep the commitment small. Lean adds measuring what customers do, not what they say.

A defensible answer is Option 3. Workstream A has a published specification, a proven connector and an immovable date; it is the textbook case for a plan with milestones, and Caleb's concern is answered by a date that arrives nine days early. Workstream B looks like the 2025 reminders project, which was planned in detail, ran 70 per cent late and reached 12 per cent adoption. Exhibit 3 shows that the 12 customers who want reminders are only 40 per cent of a small sample, so the first tranche should test one narrow thing: for the 12 reminder-seeking distributors, does a WhatsApp reminder bring payment sooner?

The money supports the split. Four tranches of ₹21.6 lakh equal ₹86.4 lakh, the same ceiling as the plan, but Chitra can stop after any gate and keep the unspent balance. If B were stopped after tranche one, she would have spent ₹21.6 lakh and saved ₹64.8 lakh. Option 1 spends ₹216 lakh and misses the deadline; Option 2 saves nothing and risks the 21.8 per cent of revenue tied to compliance.

Chitra should tell Bala to describe reminders as a pilot with named distributors, and tell Bharat that his frozen scope is exactly what Workstream A gets. The gate criteria must be agreed before the first tranche starts, or they will bend to hope.
exp40v2-pm.waterfall.agile:
Waterfall, Agile and Lean

Choosing an approach by how known the requirements are — and by what the smallest increment costs.

1. Two decisions, eight days apart

On 3 February 2026 Sudeshna Vanmali, head of product at Tolmol Credit Exchange in Mumbai, had ₹1,380 lakh to sequence and six banks to satisfy. Tolmol runs a supply-chain finance platform: buyers post approved invoices, suppliers ask for early payment, lenders fund the discount. The 2026 programme would replace the lender connection built for one bank in 2021, rework the credit-decision engine, rebuild supplier onboarding and pass a certification the banks' auditors read.

Tapan Mhatre, the chief technology officer, wanted one specification and one cut-over moving all six banks together, since six migrations meant six rounds of bank-side testing. Rukmini Asrani, the chief risk officer, wanted compliance frozen on paper before a line was written, because a certification finding after go-live would reach the banks' boards. Satyajit Ranadive, who would run it, noted that nobody had watched a supplier complete the new journey, and that Radek Zawadzki's team in Kraków had never worked against two of the interfaces. "We are asked to pick one method," Sudeshna said, "for four problems that do not resemble each other."

Eight days later in Pune, Shubhangi Devarkonda faced the mirror image. Tatsat Health Network sells a ₹299-a-month diabetes-coaching subscription; its coach is a language model that reads glucose logs. Rishabh Mundkur's squad had just finished six two-week cycles on onboarding, and Tarini Ghaisas had numbers showing it worked. The next module was harder: the coach would prompt a clinician review when a pattern looked dangerous, and Dr Sharada Kavalekar, the clinical adviser, said that was not something to learn from users in fortnightly instalments. The consumer company was being pushed toward a plan, the enterprise company toward iteration.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A development approach is a policy on two questions: how much is decided before work starts, and what must happen before a decision is revised. Plan-driven approaches decide much in advance and treat revision as an exception for change control; iterative approaches decide a little, build, expose and revise. Lean is not a third point on that line but a discipline about the size of the units moving through either.

The history is better than the slogans. Winston Royce's 1970 paper drew the familiar cascade and then argued it invited failure, because testing came last; the diagram outlived the warning, and United States defence procurement standardised the sequence in DOD-STD-2167 in 1985. Barry Boehm's spiral model of 1986 made risk, not phase, drive sequence. Iteration was old — Craig Larman and Victor Basili trace it to NASA's Project Mercury — long before the Agile Manifesto at Snowbird, Utah, in 2001. Lean came from elsewhere: Taiichi Ohno's system at Toyota, named in the West by James Womack in 1990 and given quantitative form by Donald Reinertsen in 2009.

Four schools argue. The plan-driven school, strongest in avionics, signs that when a late error costs more than the analysis that would prevent it, the analysis comes first; it will not sign that requirements can be fully known in advance. The agile school signs that working software in a user's hands is the only reliable measure of progress, and refuses to sign that scope, date and budget can all three be fixed without one being a fiction. The lean-flow school signs something sharper: batch size, queue length and cost of delay are the controlling variables, and the waterfall-versus-agile argument is a proxy for one about batch size. It will not sign that iteration is intrinsically valuable, since an iteration producing no information is waste wearing a sprint label. The discovery school of Steve Blank, Eric Ries and Teresa Torres signs that the riskiest assumption be tested with the cheapest artefact that can test it, usually not software.

This page argues closest to the third. What decides these cases is not how uncertain each piece is, but the cost of the smallest increment that can carry a decision — the least you must spend before the world can tell you something. Where that is small, iterate; where it is large, lower it. Only when it cannot be lowered is planning everything up front correct rather than merely comfortable.

3. Mechanics: pricing the decision

Expert practice refuses the programme as the unit. Sudeshna broke the ₹1,380 lakh into four workstreams plus ₹110 lakh of programme management, and asked three questions of each: what would undoing it cost if the specification proved wrong and we learned at go-live; how likely is that; and where does the information that would settle it live. The third does most of the work: Rukmini's certification requirements sat in published circulars, buyable by reading, while the onboarding journey's sat in supplier behaviour no document held.

The ₹240 lakh of expected regret is a little under a fifth of the ₹1,270 lakh build. Less obviously, the ranking by regret is not the ranking by uncertainty: supplier onboarding is the most uncertain workstream and carries the least regret of the three large ones, because it is cheap to redo.

Expected regret is half the calculation, and the half most teams do. The other half is the cost of delay. Each integrated bank was worth ₹26 lakh of annual platform fee, or ₹0.50 lakh per bank per week, so holding all six until one cut-over declines revenue as well as adding risk. The same arithmetic fixes cadence. The onboarding journey holds twenty-four features over forty-eight weeks; each release costs ₹1.2 lakh, and each finished-but-unreleased feature costs ₹0.4 lakh a week. 4. When it applies, as tests

Claim one: iterate when the information you need exists only in behaviour you have not observed. Tolmol's onboarding journey passes, since no supplier had used it; Tatsat's clinician-review module fails, because what makes a pattern worth escalating lives in clinical guidance. Claim two: plan up front when undoing costs more than the analysis that prevents it. Tolmol's certification passes, at ₹220 lakh against perhaps ₹18 lakh of review; Tatsat's onboarding copy fails, since rewriting a screen costs a day. Claim three: iterate only when an increment small enough to teach you something can be delivered. Tatsat passes trivially; the lender rail passes only after design work, since one bank can go live alone only if the rail is versioned. Claim four: match the approach to the unit. Both pass; both organisations resisted it.

It is actively misleading in three situations. When the binding constraint is a third party's calendar — a regulator's filing window, a bank's change freeze — iteration speed buys nothing. When the cost of a wrong release falls on someone who did not consent, the expected-regret calculation is not the firm's to make. And when a team invokes uncertainty to avoid research, shipping becomes an expensive way to read a document.

5. Hard edge cases and seams

In multi-product companies a shared component forces its slowest consumer's cadence on everybody; a versioned interface with a deprecation window lets five banks move while one lags behind. In two-sided businesses the sides rarely tolerate the same approach: Tolmol's suppliers can be shown an unfinished journey, while its lenders sign annual change-controlled agreements. Iterate on the low-switching-cost side; hold the other steady.

In regulated work mature practice is agile delivery inside a documented sequential wrapper. A firm building software of a medical kind under India's Medical Devices Rules, or a lending feature tested against the Reserve Bank of India's IT governance expectations, still iterates weekly; design history and traceability are produced continuously rather than reconstructed before the audit. The teams that suffer write it afterwards.

In hardware plus software the freeze date is the whole story. Rachana Instruments Works, which builds haematology analysers, freezes its optics bench on a dated gate, after which a change costs ₹64 lakh and eleven weeks; its firmware ships every three weeks. Mature firms decouple rather than argue: hardware revision and software release train carry separate version numbers. In AI-native products behaviour is a distribution, not a function, so the unit of up-front work becomes the evaluation set: Dr Kavalekar's three hundred labelled traces are a plan-driven artefact describing outputs instead of mechanisms.

At the seams, practice diverges from description. Annual budgets are committed in one sequential act, procurement signs fixed-scope contracts because that is what it can audit, and the real resequencing happens in a quarterly re-plan nobody calls a change request. The roadmap shown to customers is waterfall; the backlog is agile.

6. Expert versus competent practitioner

Asking where the information lives

The competent practitioner marks a component uncertain and reaches for iteration; the expert asks who already knows. Standards, circulars and the firm's support tickets are cheaper than a release. The tell is a plan whose first week holds reading rather than a sprint zero; the obvious reading confuses the unknown with the undiscoverable without shipping.

Engineering reversibility rather than debating it

Competent teams argue about whether a decision is reversible; experts spend money making it so, with feature flags, versioned interfaces, old and new engines on one stream of traffic. The tell is a budget line with no user-visible output: it buys lower regret, moving points downward in Exhibit 2.

Carrying the cost-of-delay term

Most teams can estimate rework and cannot say what a week of delay costs. Tolmol could: ₹0.50 lakh per bank per week. Once it exists, a six-week delay taken to reduce risk has a price comparable with the risk bought off.

Knowing that front-loading is not waterfall

Stefan Thomke and Takahiro Fujimoto's work on front-loading problem solving describes spending early on cheap simulation so expensive discovery does not come late. That is a lean move, not a plan-driven one, which is why a spike thrown away can be the best fortnight in a programme. The reading that discarded work is waste is backwards: the output was information.

Refusing to confuse commercial shape with epistemic shape

A fixed-price contract does not make requirements known. The tell is a specification written by a vendor's pre-sales team in three weeks and signed by a buyer who has never watched the workflow: the contract transfers risk without removing it.

Naming irreversible decisions instead of scoring components

Within any workstream most changes are cheap and a few are ruinous. Tolmol's onboarding journey is cheap to change except for the supplier identifier scheme, which propagates into every lender's records. The expert names the three or four decisions to make carefully and treats the rest as free.

Stating what a before-and-after comparison assumes

Tatsat's ₹10.52 lakh of monthly uplift below holds the previous quarter's rates constant, crediting one squad with everything else that moved, including marketing mix and post-Diwali seasonality. It is a counterfactual, not an experiment, and the expert says so.

Hearing the governance argument inside the method argument

When a stakeholder insists on a fixed specification, the dispute is often about authority over scope rather than epistemology. The diagnostic is who loses a sign-off if the approach changes: Tapan's preference was partly engineering, partly a wish not to negotiate with six change boards.

7. Where the differences are real

The arithmetic of expected regret and cost of delay is identical across product types; what differs is the cost of the smallest increment that can carry a decision, and how many parties must consent to it. In consumer products that cost is near zero and consent is nobody's, so iteration dominates and the scarce resource is a rule for reading the data. In B2B and enterprise products the increment is cheap to build and expensive to deliver, since delivery means a customer's testing and change window; the usual remedy — fix the outcome and the budget, float the feature list — restores iteration to a process that forbids it. In marketplaces no increment reaches one side without unbalancing the other.

In hardware the increment is dominated by tooling, so the expert makes the irreversible part small. In AI products the increment is cheap and the verification expensive, inverting the shape: a prompt change takes an hour, and showing it did not degrade behaviour on three hundred labelled cases takes a week. The overstated difference is culture: a regulated firm does not plan more out of caution.

Stage changes less than is claimed, with one exception. A pre-revenue company has almost no irreversibility and should iterate on nearly everything; a scaling company acquires its first expensive undo decisions — a data model with ten million rows, a contract with a bank — and notices a year late. Incumbents are slow because every increment needs consent from parties who gain nothing. The exception: a large company can buy reversibility and a startup cannot, so the startup must iterate while the incumbent may choose.

8. Three worked examples

Tolmol's lender rail: staging a decision that looked indivisible

Tapan's single cut-over would put all six banks live in week 48 of a programme starting 2 March 2026, which is 1 February 2027. Staging puts the shared rail and the first bank live in week 20, on 20 July 2026, then one bank every five weeks to week 45, which is 11 January 2027. Counting bank-weeks earned by week 52, staging yields 32 + 27 + 22 + 17 + 12 + 7 = 117 against the cut-over's 6 × 4 = 24, a gain of 93 bank-weeks at ₹0.50 lakh each. An error found after bank one costs ₹140 lakh rather than ₹400 lakh, so expected regret falls from ₹80 lakh to ₹28 lakh, and against both, six cut-overs replace one.

Tatsat's onboarding: six cycles, and what they were worth

Between 6 October and 29 December 2025, Rishabh's squad of six ran six two-week cycles at ₹7.5 lakh each, ₹45 lakh in all, on one question: why so few installs reached a first log.

Installs grew 7.8 per cent while activation rose from 24.0 per cent to 31.2 per cent, a gain of 7.2 points or 30 per cent in relative terms, and revenue from new subscribers rose 46 per cent. Against the third column the uplift is ₹10.52 lakh a month, or ₹126.26 lakh over a year against ₹45 lakh of cycle cost. Tarini was careful: that column assumes the rates would have held, and six cycles were not the only change.

Rasad Procurement Services: the failure and the recovery

On 9 April 2024 Rasad Procurement Services approved a ₹2,150 lakh programme to replace a twelve-year-old purchasing suite across six hundred buying units in one cut-over eighteen months later, on 9 October 2025. Its requirement document ran to 1,900 pages.

Rasad spend to 20 November 2025₹ lakh

Total spent, nothing in production2,980

Exhibit 7. Against an approved ₹2,150 lakh; the integration phase had been estimated at ₹280 lakh.

Nothing was live on the date. The cause was not the plan's existence but its deferral of every integration to the end: the first time a real purchase order travelled from a buying unit through approvals to a payment instruction was in week 74 of 78, and it failed in four places at once. Six weeks later, on 20 November 2025, the programme was re-cut into seven modules with independent go-lives. Over the following eight months a further ₹520 lakh took 240 of the 600 units live on three modules, bringing spend to ₹3,500 lakh, 62.8 per cent above the approved figure. The recovery kept the original document, so it was never true that nobody knew what was wanted, and the first module live was the one whose integration had failed first in testing. Its whole contribution was to resequence, hardest unknown first.

9. Failure modes and early warnings

The frozen specification that thaws. Early sign: the change-request log grows faster than the burndown. Diagnostic: what share of this month's hours went outside approved scope? Caught late, change traffic becomes the project, as at Rasad, where a phase estimated at ₹280 lakh cost ₹820 lakh.

Integration deferred to the end. Early sign: by the midpoint, no real record has travelled the whole path. Diagnostic: name the date on which one did. Caught late, integration runs to three times its estimate with no slack left, which is how a programme reaches its date with nothing in production.

Iteration with no decision rule, and the invisible queue behind it. Early sign: reviews produce learnings, nothing has been killed in six months, and cycle time rises while items completed per cycle stay flat. Diagnostic: what did you last stop because of evidence, and how many items are started but not released? Tolmol's squad had 42 against a throughput of six a week, which by Little's Law is a cycle time of seven weeks. Caught late, a year's capacity has gone at iteration's price without its product.

Staging without decoupling. Early sign: each staged release requires all six banks to retest. Diagnostic: can one consumer upgrade while others do not? Caught late, the team pays six cut-over costs and earns none of the ₹46.5 lakh.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does the cost of change still rise steeply with time? Boehm's data from the 1970s and 1980s showed defects costing orders of magnitude more to fix late. Kent Beck argued in 1999 that automated tests, continuous integration and small releases flatten the curve, and the Accelerate research of Forsgren, Humble and Kim supports him. For Beck to be wrong, the flattening would have to fail for schema, protocol and cross-boundary changes; for Boehm to be wrong, his data would have to be an artefact of its era's tooling.

Can scope, date and budget all be fixed? The agile position is that one must float or someone is lying. Enterprise procurement answers that fixed-price contracts are signed and delivered daily, the float hidden in a scope padded at bid time — in which case fixed-price delivery is iteration with a concealed buffer.

Is estimation useful? Bent Flyvbjerg holds that estimates are systematically optimistic and should give way to reference-class forecasting against comparable projects; the throughput school forecasts from a team's measured history; the no-estimates position holds that estimating buys less than slicing work smaller. They part company on whether a number should reach a board.

Can an AI-native product be specified? One camp says evaluation sets replace specifications and the only honest approach is to iterate against measured behaviour. The other says a system whose outputs affect health or credit needs documented evaluation before deployment — and that the evaluation set is a specification in cases.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this picks an approach and defends it as a philosophy. Someone who has internalised it decomposes before deciding, and runs three cadences inside one programme. They state in rupees both the cost of undoing each significant decision and the cost of a week's delay. They spend on reversibility early, which looks like overhead and is insurance priced correctly. They write down their belief about what they do not know, with a number and a date to revisit it. And when a method argument turns heated they ask who loses a sign-off.

12. What they decided

On 24 February 2026 Sudeshna took four answers to Tolmol's board rather than one. The lender rail would stage bank by bank, buying the ₹66.5 lakh of Exhibit 4 and accepting ₹32 lakh of extra cut-over cost, with ₹40 lakh of the rail's ₹540 lakh earmarked to version the interface. Certification would be frozen before work began, because its information lived in documents and cost ₹220 lakh to undo. The credit engine would run in shadow for eight weeks, converting a ₹150 lakh undo into a comparison. Supplier onboarding would release every three weeks, from Exhibit 3's flat optimum. Rukmini's condition was that Exhibit 1's probabilities be re-estimated once bank one was live.

Shubhangi did the opposite of her company's instincts. Tatsat would stop iterating on the clinician-review module before it started: the labelled traces would be agreed first, and no version would reach a subscriber until it matched the panel on an agreed share. The information lived in clinical guidance rather than subscriber behaviour; the cost of a missed escalation fell on someone who had not consented; and the smallest increment that could teach her anything was not a release but an evaluation.

For discussion.

  1. Exhibit 1 supports freezing certification. Does it also justify freezing the lender rail's interface specification, at ₹400 lakh to undo? What distinguishes the two?
  2. Exhibit 6's third column assumes the previous quarter's rates would have held. Name two rival explanations for the ₹10.52 lakh.
  3. Rasad's recovery changed only the sequence. Was that a planning failure or a sequencing failure, and what would you have asked in April 2024?

13. Going deeper

  • The end-to-end product lifecycle — the path all three walk.
  • The software development lifecycle — these phases, in working parts.
  • What a product manager does — Exhibit 1's decisions are the job.
  • PM myths versus reality — most concern who controls scope.
  • Origins of product management — part brand, part programme management, which is why the debates sound like both.
  • PM, PMM, TPM, project manager, founder — risk retirement is often the TPM's craft.
  • PM archetypes — each sits elsewhere on this map.
  • How the PM job changes by stage — reversibility is a privilege of scale.
exp20v2-pm.waterfall.agile:
Waterfall, Agile and Lean

When should a team plan everything up front, and when should it iterate?

1. A budget, a board and two plans

On the morning of 12 January 2026, Isha Parthasarathy, head of product at Jalmitra Metering Systems in Bengaluru, carried two project plans into a board meeting. Jalmitra makes ultrasonic water meters and sells them to housing societies, which use the readings to bill residents for tanker and borewell water. The company had approved ₹420 lakh to build its next product: a meter with a cellular radio, paired with a billing application for the societies' managing committees. Of that sum, ₹180 lakh was set aside for hardware and ₹240 lakh for software.

The first plan, drawn up by Hriday Nambiar, who ran hardware and manufacturing, was a single fourteen-month sequence: requirements, design, build, test, launch in March 2027. The second, which Isha had sketched with Ioana Marinescu, the firmware lead in the company's small Cluj engineering office, proposed shipping software in four monthly-scale increments and learning from each. Jagdish Venkatesan, the chief financial officer, put the question plainly. "I can approve a fixed plan or a flexible one. Tell me which of these I am buying, and what it costs me if I am wrong."

The stakes were concrete. Jalmitra had pre-sold pilot units to 38 societies, and a wrong guess about the billing application would cost their patience. A wrong guess about the meter casing would cost a steel injection mould, which could not be altered cheaply. Isha suspected the two halves of the product deserved different answers.

2. The idea

A development approach is a rule for how much of a project is planned before work starts, and how much is allowed to change once it has. Three families dominate the vocabulary.

Waterfall completes phases in strict order: gather all requirements, design, build, test, release. Each phase ends in a sign-off, and work does not flow backwards. The name is usually traced to a 1970 paper by Winston Royce, who drew the sequence and then argued that it was risky as it stood, since testing came last and surprises there were ruinous. Waterfall suits projects where changing course late is very expensive, such as bridges and factory tooling.

Agile delivers working increments in short cycles and lets what is learned from each reshape the next. It was named in February 2001, when seventeen practitioners met at a ski lodge in Utah and wrote the Agile Manifesto, which prizes working software, customer collaboration and responding to change over comprehensive documentation and following a plan. It was invented to solve a specific problem: in software, requirements were frequently wrong or incomplete when written, and a plan that assumed otherwise carried that error all the way to launch.

Lean is older and broader. It descends from the Toyota Production System, shaped from the 1950s by Taiichi Ohno, and was named in the West by James Womack and colleagues around 1990. Its concern is waste: any work that does not deliver value to a customer, including work waiting in a queue. Eric Ries carried the instinct into new products in 2011 as the lean startup, where progress means validated learning.

The sentence Isha could repeat in the meeting: "Plan up front in proportion to how expensive a mistake is to undo, and iterate in proportion to how likely we are to make one."

3. How it actually works

The choice rests on two inputs: how well the requirements are known, and how well the technology is known. Requirements here means what users need the product to do; technology means whether the team knows how to build it with confidence. Each can be high or low, giving four situations.

Reading the grid, step by step: first, for each component, ask what a user has actually told you, as against what you assume. Second, ask whether anyone on the team has built this sort of thing before. Third, ask what it costs to change the component after it is built. Practitioners usually leave this implicit, yet it decides the matter, because it sets the price of being wrong.

For Jalmitra, the casing sat in the top-right cell: the dimensions of the pipe fitting were fixed by plumbing standards, and the mould would cost ₹90 lakh. The billing application sat top-left: committees had described their needs in meetings, but nobody had watched one reconcile a month of tanker water against forty flats. The radio firmware sat lower right: requirements clear, but Ioana's team had never made a battery-powered meter hold a cellular connection for six years.

Lean entered the picture in the factory and in the software queue alike. Hriday's assembly would be organised to move meters through in small batches with limited work in progress; Isha's team would cap the number of features being built at once. Lean is a discipline applied inside either of the first two.

4. A worked example

Isha built a small model of the software budget. The ₹240 lakh buys twelve features at ₹20 lakh each. She did not know how many would prove wrong, meaning that users, on first meeting the feature, would reject or substantially change it. Call that number n.

Her assumptions were as follows. Under the Waterfall plan, all twelve features reach users together at launch. A wrong feature is then rebuilt in full (₹20 lakh) and unwinding what was built on top of it adds half again (₹10 lakh), so each wrong feature costs ₹30 lakh to fix. Under the Agile plan, the twelve features ship in four blocks of three. A wrong feature is discovered after its own block, when little depends on it, so unwinding adds only 10 per cent (₹2 lakh), and each costs ₹22 lakh. Each of the four blocks carries ₹4 lakh of release and feedback overhead, ₹16 lakh in all.

Wrong features (n)Waterfall: 240 + 30nAgile: 240 + 16 + 22nAgile minus Waterfall
