Software cost, ₹ lakh, exact values (no rounding). Base build of 12 features at ₹20 lakh is ₹240 lakh. Negative differences mean Agile is cheaper.

With no wrong features, Agile costs ₹16 lakh more, which is purely its overhead: iteration is a fee paid for insurance. Each wrong feature then costs Waterfall ₹8 lakh more than Agile (₹30 lakh against ₹22 lakh), so the insurance repays itself when the number of wrong features multiplied by ₹8 lakh reaches ₹16 lakh, which is two features. At two the plans cost the same, ₹300 lakh. At Isha's gloomy estimate of five wrong features, about 42 per cent of twelve, Agile saves ₹24 lakh.

The second pass changes one input. Suppose that discovery interviews with the 38 pilot societies reduced the expected number of wrong features from five to one. The table now reverses the verdict: Waterfall at ₹270 lakh beats Agile at ₹278 lakh by ₹8 lakh. The uncertainty it insures against shrank below the point where the premium is worth paying. The decision therefore turns on one judgement, whether more than one feature in six (two of twelve) will be wrong, and the model's value lies in forcing that judgement into the open.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

The choice is made per component, not per company.

Jalmitra's casing, radio and billing application had different knowledge levels and different prices of change, and so deserved different approaches within one programme. Hybrids are what Exhibit 1 predicts.

Waterfall is not the same as bad planning.

Planning up front is rational when requirements are stable and late change is costly. What fails is the pretence that unknowns can be specified away.

Agile is not the same as no plan.

Short cycles still need a goal, a budget and a definition of finished. Agile moves some planning from a single large act at the start into a repeated small act at each cycle.

Lean is not "cheap".

Waste, in the lean sense, includes work waiting, work redone and features nobody uses. Cutting headcount leaves all of these intact.

The cost-of-change curve is a model, not a law.

The claim that a defect costs ten or a hundred times more to fix late traces to studies from the 1970s and 1980s, and later practice (automated tests, frequent releases) flattened the curve for software. It did not flatten it for steel moulds. Hence Isha's two premiums, 50 per cent and 10 per cent, are assumptions to be argued over, not constants to be looked up.

Iteration without a customer is only repetition.

Four increments shown only to colleagues leave the n in the model exactly where it was.

The model cannot tell you n.

It converts a belief about wrong features into a cost; it does not produce the belief. It also leaves out time. Every month of delay in a Waterfall launch is revenue not earned, and every month of iteration is a month a competitor may use.

Ask before relying on it.

What is our evidence, as opposed to our confidence, that requirements are known? What does changing this component cost in rupees and in weeks? Who decides when a cycle's output is good enough? If nobody can answer, no approach label will rescue the plan.

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products, requirements are usually the larger unknown and release is cheap, so short cycles and experiments dominate. In B2B products such as Jalmitra's, a few customers hold large contracts and may demand fixed scope and dates, which pulls toward Waterfall-style commitments even where the software is uncertain. The usual remedy is to fix outcome and budget while keeping the feature list flexible. In marketplaces, the product is two sides interacting, and no plan can predict their behaviour, so teams ship small and watch the balance of buyers and sellers.

Stage matters as well. An early-stage company has little to protect and can iterate freely. A large company has regulators, vendors and dependent teams, and must coordinate iteration across all of them. Jalmitra sat between: its meters needed formal certification, while its software could change weekly.

7. Common mistakes

Starting from the backlog. The symptom: a long ranked list of features exists before anyone has described the customer's problem. The misunderstanding: that delivering the list is progress. The cheapest diagnostic: ask the team to state, in one sentence, which user problem each of the top five items removes.

Waterfall in Agile clothing. The symptom: sprints, stand-ups and boards, yet nothing reaches a user for six months. The misunderstanding: that ceremonies create feedback. The diagnostic: the date a real customer last used the product and told the team something.

Iterating on the irreversible. The symptom: a second mould, or a second hardware revision, bought because "we are agile". The misunderstanding: that all change costs the same. The diagnostic: write the price of changing each component next to it.

8. What good looks like

A team handling this decision well would have written the component grid before the budget meeting. It would state, for each component, the evidence on requirements, the experience on technology and the price of late change. It would fix hardware scope behind formal gates, spike the highest technical risk early, and ship software in small releases to named customers. Above all it would write down its belief about n.

9. Closing

Isha told the board that Jalmitra was buying neither plan. The casing and assembly line, ₹180 lakh in all, would follow a gated sequence: ₹90 lakh for tooling, ₹30 lakh for certification and ₹60 lakh for a pilot batch. The billing application would be built in four increments, with Ioana's team running a two-week technical spike on the radio before anything else was committed. Her reasoning was the model's: the committees had never been observed using such an application, so she judged that more than two of twelve features were likely to be wrong, which made the ₹16 lakh of overhead worth paying. Jagdish approved the ₹420 lakh with one condition, that the belief about n be revisited after the first block.

To go further, study the software development lifecycle, which breaks the phases named here into their working parts, and keep the end-to-end product lifecycle in mind as the single path that every approach walks differently.

Two questions to sit with. First, which component of a product you know well has the highest cost of late change, and does its team plan accordingly? Second, if you had to put a number on how many of your next twelve features users would reject, what would it be, and what evidence would move it?
case40v1-pm.waterfall.agile:
Jatayu Aerial Works: The Plan the Board Asked For

Nashik, February 2027 — choosing how to build when only half the work is knowable

1. Sunday night, Trimbak Road

On the evening of Sunday 7 February 2027 the first floor of Jatayu Aerial Works, on Trimbak Road in Nashik, held one person and four whiteboards. Jyotika Lanjewar, Vice President of Product, had told everyone else to stay away. On the longest board were three programme names, a budget and a date. On the shortest, in blue marker: Who exactly is the customer for the thing we are about to build?

At ten the next morning she had forty minutes with the board to present one development plan for 2027. The board had met on Friday 15 January, twenty-four days earlier, and approved ₹9.60 crore of programme spend. Two words went into the minutes: one plan, with dates. Three parallel experiments, Jiten Lulla the Chief Financial Officer had said, were a way of spending a year, not a plan.

She did not think the three items were the same kind of work. One was governed by a regulator that would not negotiate. One rested on a hypothesis her own field data had undermined. The third was not on the board's agenda, and a number she found on Saturday suggested it mattered most.

2. How the company got here

Jatayu was founded in Nashik in 2019 by two agricultural engineers who had been flying hired multirotors over grape trellises. What they built was a spraying service, not a drone business: farmers, producer organisations and dealers bought acres sprayed, and Jatayu organised the machines, pilots and chemistry.

The decision that shapes February 2027 was taken in September 2023. Pressed by its lead investor, Kalanidhi Growth Fund, the board chose to design and certify Jatayu's own 10-litre airframe rather than buy certified machines and build out the service layer. The argument was a moat.

Fourteen months and ₹11.40 crore later, in November 2024, the certificate came through; Exhibit 2 shows where the money went. The machine works and operators like it. The moat never appeared. By December 2026 more than a dozen agricultural drone models held Indian type certificates, Garuda Aerospace, Marut Drones and IoTechWorld Avigation were selling into the same districts, IFFCO was spraying through its cooperative network, and the price of a comparable machine had fallen from ₹11.20 lakh in 2023 to ₹6.40 lakh, a drop of 42.9 per cent.

The decision did create a constraint. A type certificate is issued against one configuration. Change the tank volume, the frame geometry or the pump and it must be amended through testing at a Quality Council of India authorised entity before a machine may legally spray. The hardware roadmap is a regulated sequence.

3. The industry around them

Indian agricultural drone services rest on three unstable supports. Subsidy is one: the Sub-Mission on Agricultural Mechanisation and the Namo Drone Didi scheme put machines into a district faster than demand grows, so the per-acre price drifts down. Agronomy is the second: Nashik grape growers, whose export consignments are screened for residue under APEDA's programme, pay for dose accuracy, while in Vidarbha cotton the same grower looks only at cost per acre. Regulation is the third: the Drone Rules of 2021, type certification, remote pilot certificates and, for plot-level farmer data, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023.

The exposure is not only Indian. Flight-control boards come from a contract manufacturer in Taipei that quotes sixteen weeks and will not quote until the design is frozen. In November 2026 Kelani Estates Partners, a tea and rubber plantation group in Colombo, signed a letter of intent conditional on machines Jatayu does not yet make.

4. The situation in detail

Financial year 2026 is summarised in Exhibit 1. Jatayu sprayed 6,20,000 acres through 310 machines held by 268 independent operator partners: exactly 2,000 acres per machine. Revenue was ₹34.11 crore, operator payouts ₹20.75 crore, contribution ₹13.36 crore. The organisation in Exhibit 3 costs ₹102.60 lakh a month, or ₹1,231.20 lakh a year, leaving ₹1.05 crore. Sales took ₹5.60 crore and administration ₹3.29 crore, so the year closed with a loss before tax of ₹7.84 crore. Cash on 31 December 2026 was ₹28.40 crore: about 43 months at that burn rate.

Three things believed in mid-2026 are no longer safe to believe. First, that growers would pay for prescription spraying. Between June and August 2026 Jagmohan Lakra's team ran 120 conversations about a variable-rate service — a multispectral map, a dose prescription per zone, a spray run that follows it — at a premium of ₹190 an acre. Seventy-eight of the 120 said they would pay, which is 65.0 per cent. That figure went into the board pack.

Second, that the kharif pilot would confirm it. Kshitija Lonare's agronomists gave free prescription maps to 41 of those 78 from July 2026. Seven of the 41 changed their spray plan, which is 17.1 per cent. When the premium was quoted to all 41 in the rabi follow-up, December 2026 to January 2027, three paid, which is 7.3 per cent. The panels of Exhibit 5 do not describe the same world, and nobody agrees which misleads.

Third, that the 16-litre machine was a demand problem rather than a timing problem. Kelani Estates wants a larger tank for tall canopies; Lahar Agri Inputs Trading, a dealer group in the Uttar Pradesh terai, says the same machine would open sugarcane. Exhibit 6 adds the two claims to ₹13.30 crore a year. Lakshmanan Kuppuswamy's estimate is twelve months from a 1 March 2027 start, which means March 2028. The Kelani season opens 1 October 2027, five months before the machines could legally fly.

On Saturday 6 February, in the operator ledger, Jyotika found a fourth number. Of the 268 operator partners, 61 left during financial year 2026, which is 22.8 per cent. Replacing one costs about ₹46,000, so churn carried ₹28.06 lakh of direct cost. Jonali Kalita's desk had reported the reasons for eighteen months: collisions inside the ten-day spray window, delayed payouts, no insurance for a crashed machine. None of it was on the January slide.

5. The people

Kunal Jaywant, Head of Engineering, Bengaluru. Nineteen software engineers. He wants whatever is chosen frozen by 1 March; his team spent 2026 being redirected and he lost four. Unsaid: he thinks the prescription layer is a research project in feature clothing, but Jagmohan's revenue case is the board's only growth story.

Lakshmanan Kuppuswamy, Head of Airframe, Coimbatore. Eleven engineers, all of whom the 16-litre programme would consume. The only person here who has been through a type certification, and he will not compress twelve months. Unsaid: three of them are queue at the testing entity, which he cannot forecast.

Kshitija Lonare, Head of Agronomy, Nashik. She reads Exhibit 5 as growers valuing the prescription but refusing to pay, because the dealer's agronomist advises free with the chemical. Unsaid: her maps reached eleven of the 41 late.

Jagmohan Lakra, Head of Sales, Indore. Carries a 2027 number and has already described the prescription service to two dealer groups. He says the pilot measured willingness to pay for a half-built product. Unsaid: the Lahar terai figure came from a lunch.

Joana Lencastre, product designer, Lisbon. Four and a half hours behind Nashik, and has never seen a grape trellis. She wants six weeks with operators first: the real interface is the operator's day, not the farmer's phone. Unsaid: she sketched a scheduling flow in January.

Katarzyna Jaworska, data scientist, Kraków. Built the multispectral pipeline and is the prescription layer's strongest advocate: its prescriptions came from one season of imagery over few crops, so a weak result says little about the method. Unsaid: the model needs farmer records whose DPDP consent basis nobody has costed.

Jonali Kalita, Customer Success Lead, Guwahati. Three people, and the only part of the company that speaks to operators weekly. She has asked for scheduling and payout tooling since mid-2025. Unsaid: she has stopped escalating and is looking elsewhere.

Jiten Lulla, Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai. He set the ₹9.60 crore cap and wants one committed plan for Kalanidhi Growth Fund before the Series C conversation late in 2027. Unsaid: the fund has told him a plan missing a stated date is worse than one with fewer dates.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Give me a frozen specification on 1 March and I will give you a date. Give me a hypothesis and I will give you a team that has quit by August.”

Kunal Jaywant, engineering review, 28 January 2027

“Three paid out of forty-one. Jagmohan may be right that we tested it badly. But we did not test willingness to pay for a prescription. We tested whether a grower pays ₹190 an acre while the dealer's agronomist advises for nothing.”

Kshitija Lonare, email to Jyotika, 2 February 2027

“A pilot run by scientists is not a product. You sent a map as a PDF after the window had opened. I have two dealer groups who will sign in April if it exists in April.”

Jagmohan Lakra, same thread, 2 February 2027

“I cannot shorten the certification. Freeze the design in week six instead of fourteen and Taipei starts the board revision earlier: we may recover six weeks. I will not promise seven months. Last time somebody promised a certification date we wrote off two sets of moulds.”

Lakshmanan Kuppuswamy, chat thread, 4 February 2027

“Both candidate products are for the farmer. Nobody here has spent a day with the person who flies the machine, decides whose field is sprayed first, and waits eleven days to be paid. Sixty-one left last year.”

Joana Lencastre, design review, 5 February 2027

8. The options as Jyotika currently sees them

Option 1: hardware first, planned end to end. Commit Programme B at ₹569.40 lakh over twelve months, specify it fully, freeze the design, run it as the regulated sequence it is. Add Programme C at ₹158.40 lakh with the capacity left over, for ₹727.80 lakh inside the ₹960.00 lakh budget, and defer the prescription layer. The weakness is Exhibit 6: the money attached to the machine is one unsigned letter and one lunch, it arrives five months after the Colombo season opens, and 108 units must be bought by operators leaving at 22.8 per cent a year.

Option 2: the prescription layer, in short cycles. Commit Programme A at ₹436.05 lakh over nine months but run it as four cycles with a gate after each, keep Programme C alongside for ₹594.45 lakh in total, and treat the ₹190 premium as a hypothesis to be settled by kharif 2027. At the 65.0 per cent attach rate of Exhibit 5A, 4,03,000 of last year's 6,20,000 acres carry the premium, worth ₹765.70 lakh a year, and A pays back inside seven months. At the 7.3 per cent rate of 5B the same arithmetic gives about 45,370 acres and ₹86.20 lakh a year, a payback of roughly five years.

Option 3: both, reduced. A and B together cost ₹1,005.45 lakh, ₹45.45 lakh over the cap, and need 14 of the 19 software engineers before C is considered. Cutting both to fit means a certification with no margin for the queue Lakshmanan cannot forecast, and a prescription layer too thin to test anything. All three come to ₹1,163.85 lakh, ₹203.85 lakh over, and need 21 software engineers against 19.

Late in the evening Jyotika drew a box around the blue-marker sentence. Each option assumes the unit of decision is a programme, chosen now and funded for its whole length. None asks whether the three are the same kind of question, or whether the farmer is the customer. Joana's line had stayed with her: the operator is the one who leaves.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Money: ₹960.00 lakh of approved 2027 programme spend against ₹1,163.85 lakh if all three run; cash ₹28.40 crore, loss before tax ₹7.84 crore. People: 44, of whom 19 write software and 2 design, with A and C competing for both while all 11 Coimbatore engineers go to B. Regulation: no configuration change may fly before the type certificate is amended, and twelve months includes three of unforecastable queue. Contracts: the Kelani letter of intent lapses if machines are not operating by 1 October 2027; the Kadamba contract, 62,000 acres and ₹161.20 lakh of contribution, goes to re-tender on 31 May 2027. Supply: Taipei needs a frozen design, then sixteen weeks. Data: nobody has scoped the consent basis for plot-level farmer records under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Place the three programmes in Exhibit 4 by how well the requirements and the technology are known. What does each placement imply about how it should be run?
  2. Exhibits 5A and 5B describe the same growers and disagree by nearly nine times. What must you believe for each to be the better guide, and what evidence before kharif 2027 would move you most?
  3. Exhibit 1 shows Nashik earning ₹260 of contribution an acre against ₹170 in Madhya Pradesh. What does the Kadamba footnote do to that comparison?
  4. Exhibit 6 attaches ₹1,330.00 lakh a year to a machine that cannot be certified before March 2028 and needs 108 units costing ₹928.80 lakh that operators must finance. How much belongs in a plan, and how would you defend it to Jiten Lulla?
  5. The 22.8 per cent operator churn sat in Jonali Kalita's queue for eighteen months and on nobody's slide. What does that say about how this company decides what to build?
  6. It is ten o'clock on Monday 8 February 2027. What goes on the one page, which dates does Jyotika commit to and which does she refuse, and what does she say to Jiten Lulla and Kunal Jaywant when each objects?

Sunday, later

By nine the blue-marker sentence was still the only thing on the short whiteboard. Jyotika had drafted the one page three times. The first committed to Programme B and a 1 October 2027 date she did not believe. The second committed to nothing and would not survive the first question. The third had two columns, dates we can give and dates we cannot yet give, and she could not decide whether that was honesty or a resignation letter with a budget.

Her phone showed a message from Jonali Kalita, sent at 20:41: two more operators had left that week, both in the terai. Jyotika read it twice, turned off the light, and did not pick up the marker again.
exp20v2-pm.failure:
Why Products Fail

Foundations · The PM Role & Foundations

1. The decision on the table

On 9 April 2026, Sarita Vengurlekar, head of product at Shitalaya Cold Chain Systems in Pune, walked into a board meeting carrying a request she had not written and a doubt she had not voiced. The request, drafted by the engineering team, was for a further ₹1.6 crore (160 lakh) to build version two of ThandaTrack, a temperature sensor and mobile application for the milk chilling centres that cooperative dairies run in villages. Shitalaya had already spent ₹2.4 crore (240 lakh) over fourteen months, from February 2025, on version one.

The product was, by any engineering standard, good. Each sensor logged a bulk milk cooler’s temperature every five minutes, and the application alerted staff when milk crossed 4 degrees Celsius, beyond which a batch is likely to be rejected at the dairy plant. Tejaswini Sawant, the lead engineer, had met every item on a backlog of 212 requested features. The difficulty was the sales ledger. Of 120 cooperatives approached since launch, 9 were still paying. Vikas Tamhane, the lead investor, put it plainly: “If it is this good and nobody wants it, which one of those is wrong?”

If version two shipped and the pattern held, the company would have spent ₹4 crore (400 lakh) on a product whose paying base could be counted on two hands. If she opposed the request and was wrong, she would have halted a product a few features from taking off. This page follows her reasoning on the first question any product manager must answer: why do products fail, and which failure is most likely to be mine?

2. The idea

A product fails when it does not earn enough value from its users to repay the cost of building and running it. Failure is a persistent gap between what the customer gives (money, time, switching effort) and what the maker spends, not a missing feature or an ugly screen.

The vocabulary was assembled in pieces. In the 2000s, Steve Blank, a Silicon Valley entrepreneur turned teacher, argued under the name customer development that startups die from missing customers more often than from missing technology. Eric Ries popularised the approach in 2011 as the Lean Startup. CB Insights, a research firm, read 101 start-up post-mortems and found that 42 per cent of founders named “no market need” as a cause of failure, the most common answer. Respondents could name several causes, so the shares overlap and cannot be added together.

The sentence Sarita could repeat in the meeting without sounding glib was this: “Most products fail because we built something nobody needed badly enough to pay for, and everything else is usually a symptom.” Note badly enough: need has a magnitude, which most teams skip.

3. How failure actually works

It helps to see failure as four questions that must be answered yes, in order. A later yes is worthless if an earlier answer is no.

Gate one, need, asks whether a defined group of people has a problem that is frequent, painful and currently costing them something. Gate two, value, asks whether this product beats what they already do, including doing nothing. Gate three, usability, asks whether they can operate it. Gate four, economics, asks whether the price exceeds the cost of delivering and supporting it.

ThandaTrack’s team had worked backwards. They began with a sensor they knew how to build, wrote a backlog, and treated the backlog as evidence of demand. A backlog records what existing users mention, not what non-users need; practitioners rarely say so. Of the 212 requests, 190 came from the 9 paying centres and the 18 pilot users, a population already selected for tolerance. The 102 cooperatives that never became paying pilots were not in the backlog at all, because they had said nothing.

When Sarita asked the sales team why those centres declined, the recurring answer was that the secretary of the cooperative already had a manual routine. A helper checked the cooler at 5 a.m. and 5 p.m., and a rejected batch cost a few thousand rupees. The problem was real but small and tolerated. That is gate one failing quietly; no feature could repair it.

4. A worked example

Sarita rebuilt the sales funnel from the contact log; each rate is the share of the row above that passed.

The chain compounds: 120 × 0.40 = 48; 48 × 0.375 = 18; 18 × 0.50 = 9. Each later figure uses the count before it, so 9 renewals is 7.5 per cent of the original 120 (0.40 × 0.375 × 0.50 = 0.075). ThandaTrack was priced at ₹36,000 a year per centre, which is ₹3,000 a month. Eighteen pilots paid ₹6.48 lakh in the first year (18 × ₹36,000), and nine renewals now pay ₹3.24 lakh a year.

The second question was whether the economics could ever repay the build. Serving one centre cost ₹14,000 a year (hardware depreciation, data, field support), so each contributed ₹22,000 (₹36,000 less ₹14,000). Pass 2 changes a single input, the price, to ₹60,000, holding everything else fixed.

Raising the price by two thirds cuts the required base by more than half, because the margin, not the price, drives the sum. Yet even in pass 2, Shitalaya would need roughly twelve times its present 9 centres (105 / 9 = 11.7), and no one has shown they would buy at ₹60,000. Arithmetic cannot rescue a product whose gate one is unproven. It only says how large the unproven thing must be. In pass 1 the required penetration, 9.1 per cent of the territory, already exceeds the 7.5 per cent of approached cooperatives that stayed, and the approached ones were the friendliest.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Cause and symptom are different things

Running out of cash is the most visible death certificate and the least useful diagnosis: revenue did not arrive because of one of the four gates, and a bridge loan treats only the symptom.

Need has a magnitude, not just a presence

Almost every problem exists for somebody. The test is whether it is painful enough to change a habit and pay for the change; a few thousand rupees of spoilage is a problem, not necessarily a budget line.

Users and buyers are often different people

The chilling-centre helper who would receive the alert was not the secretary who signs the payment. Vinayak Sonawane, chairman of one cooperative that declined, said that alerts at night would simply mean more calls to a man he already paid little. A product that delights the user but burdens the payer, or the reverse, fails at the hand-off.

“Competitor” includes the status quo

ThandaTrack’s strongest rival was a helper with a thermometer, not another sensor company. Listing only vendors misses the incumbent that costs nothing.

Polite interest is not evidence

Many of the 48 cooperatives that saw a demonstration called it “very useful”. Compliments cost nothing; commitments such as money, a letter of intent or an introduction to the payer do.

Survivorship bias contaminates the lessons

Post-mortems such as the 101 above come from founders willing to write one, who tend to prefer causes outside their control. Read the 42 per cent as a signal, not a measurement.

Timing is separate from need

A product can answer a real need too early, before the infrastructure exists, or too late, after a rival has become the default. A customer interview rarely reveals either.

What the idea cannot tell you

The four gates tell you where to look, not what to build. They cannot generate the insight for a new product or guarantee success; they only stop you paying for untested assumptions.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

In consumer products, gate one is usually satisfied by sheer breadth of unmet wants; the failures cluster at gate three and gate four, where habit and the cost of acquiring each user decide survival.

In B2B products, as ThandaTrack shows, the buyer, user and payer diverge, sales cycles are long, and a pilot is not a purchase. The cleanest early evidence is a paid pilot with a named budget holder, and the cleanest warning is a pilot that nobody renews.

In marketplaces, which connect two groups such as farmers and buyers, the need must exist on both sides at once, and the failure mode is a thin side.

Size changes the failure too. An early-stage company fails by running out of runway before learning; a large one by not noticing, because a profitable core can fund a failing product for years. Sarita’s board, though early-stage, behaved like a large firm’s: the sunk ₹2.4 crore felt like a reason to continue.

7. Common mistakes

Mistaking the backlog for the market

Symptom: the team is busy, releases ship on time, and sales do not move. Misunderstanding: requests from existing users are treated as demand from non-users. Cheapest diagnostic: count what share of the backlog came from people who do not yet pay; here it was 190 of 212 from existing users, so 22 items, about 10.4 per cent, came from anyone else.

Counting compliments as demand

Symptom: strong demonstration scores and weak conversion. Misunderstanding: enthusiasm is treated as commitment. Cheapest diagnostic: ask for a prepayment or a letter of intent, and see how many of the 48 who watched will sign.

Optimising a funnel that has no source

Symptom: frequent redesigns of onboarding while renewals stay flat at 50 per cent. Misunderstanding: the problem is assumed to be in gate three. Cheapest diagnostic: interview the 9 that did not renew and ask what they do now instead.

Letting sunk cost vote

Symptom: the case for more money begins with how much has been spent. Misunderstanding: past spending is treated as an asset. Cheapest diagnostic: ask whether the team would approve the same ₹1.6 crore as a first investment today.

8. What good looks like

A good version of this decision begins eight months earlier, before any sensor was built. Suyash Thorat, then a junior analyst, spends six weeks in chilling centres at 5 a.m.. The team writes down what would have to be true for the product to matter, for instance that centres lose at least ₹1 lakh a year to rejected batches, and what would count as proof, such as 9 of 30 cooperatives (30 per cent) prepaying a quarter’s fee. They then run the service by hand, with staff sending text messages from a spreadsheet, for a total cost of ₹6 lakh. That is one fortieth of the ₹2.4 crore actually spent (240 / 6 = 40).

If the thresholds are missed, the team has lost ₹6 lakh and a few weeks, and moves on. If they are met, the build proceeds on evidence, and the backlog is drawn from the 30 and not only from the 9. The failure conditions were written down while nobody was invested in the answer.

9. What Sarita decided

She did not ask the board to reject version two outright, because she lacked evidence that it would fail. She asked it to decline the ₹1.6 crore tranche and to approve instead an eight-week test costing ₹6 lakh, starting immediately. Eight weeks from 9 April ends on 4 June 2026, when the results would be put before the board. Her reasoning was that the tranche cost nearly twenty-seven times the test (160 / 6 = 26.7), and that the test would answer what fourteen months had not: whether the people who feel the problem, and those who pay, would commit money. She wrote the pass mark on the whiteboard before the test began, 9 of 30 prepaying, and asked Vikas to sign beside it.

Next comes what makes a good product idea: failure analysis says what to avoid; that page asks what to look for. Two questions to sit with. First, which gate in your own current project has the least evidence behind it, and what would you have to see to change your mind? Second, if the money already spent on your product were zero, would you still approve the next tranche?
exp40v2-pm.failure:
Why Products Fail

Foundations · The PM Role & Foundations · near-expert reading

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On 24 September 2026 in Nagpur, Ishwari Kanetkar read a funding request she meant to oppose. Jayesh Karnik, head of engineering, had asked the board of Khadaan Safety Industries for ₹7.2 crore to build the second generation of Khabardaar, a collision-avoidance system for vehicles in opencast mines and quarries. Khadaan had spent ₹11.6 crore on engineering in the twenty-six months from July 2024 to August 2026. The product worked, met the standards the Directorate General of Mines Safety expects, and in six instrumented months at one site cut motion-triggered alerts from 328 a month to 211.

The order book was the difficulty. Khadaan had approached 86 sites; 31 trialled; 17 issued a purchase order; 6 renewed the subscription. Kedar Inamdar, the founder, read that as a sales problem and Karnik as a feature problem. Kanetkar suspected worse: that the product was priced above the value it delivered to whoever signed.

A week later, on 1 October, Jahnavi Kamath faced the mirror image in Bengaluru. Khilaadi Sports Network had launched its app for amateur cricket and football teams nineteen months earlier, on 1 March 2025, and nobody doubted teams wanted it: 24,60,000 installs. Kabir Joshipura, the chief executive, had raised ₹14.8 crore and spent ₹11.3 crore, ₹4.6 crore of it on installs — 40.7 per cent of all spending. In September the product earned ₹4.85 lakh and cost ₹71.20 lakh to run, so the remaining ₹3.5 crore would last a little over five months.

Both were finished and good, and both were failing. The standard answer — no market need — is false for one and misleading for the other. It names not a cause but the commonest reported symptom of an arithmetical condition, and the expert’s first move is to find which term the evidence is weakest on.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree about it

A product fails when the contribution it can capture, across every buyer it can reach and retain, is smaller than the cost of building, selling and running it, within the time the firm can finance. Contribution, not revenue, because a product can be bought enthusiastically and lose money per unit. Retain, because one purchase is not a customer. Selling, because in business markets it often exceeds building.

The history relocates blame. Until the 1980s failure was blamed on execution; Don Norman moved some to design. In the 2000s Steve Blank argued that start-ups die from absent customers rather than absent technology, and Eric Ries systematised this in 2011 as the Lean Startup. CB Insights, reading start-up post-mortems, found “no market need” the most-cited cause; in a later tranche of roughly a hundred it put running out of cash or failing to raise first, at around 38 per cent, with no market need behind at around 35 per cent. Founders named several causes each, so the shares overlap and must not be added.

That relocation is contested. The customer-development school signs that demand risk dominates and is testable before building, but not that demand can be found by asking: interviews establish a problem, not willingness to pay. The jobs-to-be-done school of Clayton Christensen and Bob Moesta signs that the unit of analysis is the progress a customer seeks, not that segments or stated preferences reveal it. Marty Cagan’s four-risks school spreads failure across value, usability, feasibility and viability, declining the ranking of demand first. The market-timing school — Bill Gross placed timing ahead of team and idea — signs that the dominant variable is exogenous, not that research would catch it. The base-rate school signs that failure is irreducible: Ron Kohavi reported roughly a third of Microsoft’s evaluated ideas improving their target metric, a third doing nothing and a third doing harm, so its remedy is cheaper experiments. The organisational school holds that above a few hundred people the modal cause is internal.

They do not reconcile, because they describe different populations: the base-rate school is right about features inside a working product, where the counterfactual is measured, the customer-development school about new products in new markets, where it is not.

3. Mechanics: the five terms, and where the evidence is

The practitioner’s treatment is multiplicative.

N × p × q × r × Λ > C

N is the buyers the firm can reach; p the share for whom the problem sits above their action threshold; q the share of those for whom the product beats the incumbent alternative net of switching cost; r the share converted and kept at a bearable cost of sale; Λ the lifetime contribution per retained buyer; C the build plus fixed cost. Because they multiply, a factor-of-two optimism in three of them is an eightfold error; and because different functions estimate them — N by market research, Λ by the price list, p and q by nobody — the error is never evenly spread. Rank the terms by sensitivity times ignorance and spend the evidence budget there; most business cases do the reverse.

Khadaan’s June 2024 case put N at 268 opencast mines and quarries in India with fifteen or more heavy vehicles, p at 0.70, q at 0.60, r at 0.50, and Λ at ₹26.67 lakh assuming four fifths of buyers renewed. Twenty-six months replaced three: 17 of 86 approached issued an order, or 19.8 per cent, and 6 of 17 renewed, or 35.3 per cent. The step left implicit, and absent from the formula as written, is the cost of sale: ₹214 lakh of field sales and trials to win 17 sites, or ₹12.59 lakh per site won against a lifetime contribution of ₹21.04 lakh. That ratio is 1.67, where a durable business product wants three.

4. When the standard answer applies, and when it misleads

Claim one: test demand first when build cost greatly exceeds the cost of a decisive demand test. For Khadaan the test was cheap: four radio units at two sites, alerts logged by hand for ten weeks, and one conversation about what that was worth, for about ₹34 lakh — a thirty-fourth of the ₹11.6 crore eventually spent. For Khilaadi it fails: demand was never in doubt, and a demand test would return a reassuring, useless answer. Where the doubt is value capture rather than value, a demand test is a way of being busy.

Claim two: “no market need” is right only when the problem costs the customer less than their threshold for action. Khadaan’s buyers put a lost-time haul-road incident, with stoppage, at about ₹18 lakh, and reported roughly 1.4 a year per site: ₹25.2 lakh of annual exposure against a ₹5.04 lakh subscription, 20.0 per cent of it. The need is well above threshold.

Claim three: a product is viable only if the buyer’s return exceeds their hurdle, computed on the share of the problem it actually removes. Here Khadaan died. Five-year exposure per site is ₹126 lakh; ownership is ₹38.85 lakh of hardware plus five subscriptions of ₹5.04 lakh, so ₹64.05 lakh. Khabardaar’s own evidence showed near-misses falling from 41 a month to 27, down 34.1 per cent, so take 34 per cent of exposure as removed: ₹42.84 lakh. The buyer spends ₹64.05 lakh to avoid ₹42.84 lakh, a return of 0.67, and no feature changes that. Jameel Kidwai, safety head at one of the eleven sites that did not renew, had done the sum: “It is a good machine. It is not a good purchase.”

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Hardware plus software. The ₹229.90 lakh of unsold units is not a loss and never appears in Exhibit 1, but it is cash that cannot be redeployed, and it biases later decisions towards the existing design. Hardware firms commit the bill of materials too early: the specification freezes at tooling, so q and Λ are fixed years before measurement.

Regulated markets. A mandate creates a budget but also a job engineers rarely imagine: the buyer is hiring defensible evidence of compliance, not less hazard. Khabardaar reduced the hazard and logged it in a format nobody could file.

Two-sided products. Khilaadi listed 1,410 turf and ground owners, of whom 282, or 20.0 per cent, took a booking in September 2026: 36,162 active players over 282 grounds, or 128 each. Supply was the constraint, and every rupee of the ₹4.6 crore install budget went to the abundant side. The sides sat in different teams: Kshama Ingle’s growth team was measured on installs and hit its number; Ipsita Jena in Bhubaneswar, who signed grounds, had four people and no marketing line. Nobody failed at their job and the product failed anyway.

AI-native products. Ishaara Voice Labs in Hyderabad sells a Marathi and Telugu voice agent answering service queries for tractor dealers. On 10,000 queries a month it resolves 91 per cent unaided and escalates 900. At ₹4.80 of inference and telephony per query it costs ₹48,000; the 900 escalations cost the dealer ₹64 each, or ₹57,600 — ₹1,05,600 in all, ₹10.56 a query against ₹19.00 for an all-human desk, a saving of ₹8.44 or 44.4 per cent. Ishaara prices at ₹6, earning ₹60,000 against ₹48,000 of cost, a 20.0 per cent margin. Its metrics are computed on the 91 per cent; the dealer lives with the 9 per cent, whose cost sits beyond the boundary. AI-native products fail with good dashboards.

What mature companies actually do. Stated policy is a stage-gate review with a kill at each gate; observed behaviour is starvation. The product moves under another vice-president, the team shrinks by attrition, and nobody can say when it ended. That reflects the political cost of a kill, not hypocrisy.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Failure is a rate, not an event. Competent teams ask whether the product is failing; experts ask how fast they learn against how fast they spend. The tell is a team that cannot say what would make them stop — not optimism, but a condition nobody wrote down.

“No market need” is often value-capture failure in disguise. The reported cause comes from founders writing afterwards, biased towards exogenous causes. The tell is the Khadaan pattern: engagement in a small cohort, warm references, renewal near a third. Real absence of need produces indifference, not enthusiasm then non-renewal.

A failing product and a failing business model are different objects. Khilaadi’s product succeeded: 35 per cent of joiners played a recorded fixture, and a fifth of those still played a year later. Charging the player failed. The tell is healthy retention beside revenue that does not scale with it, and the mistake is to answer with product work.

The incumbent alternative is a portfolio of workarounds, not a rival. Khabardaar competed against a spotter with a whistle, a radio protocol and a rule about right of way, all free at the margin. The tell is a customer who cannot name a vendor but describes a routine in detail; analyses listing only vendors overestimate q.

Second-order effects turn working features negative. Khabardaar produced about 4,100 alerts a month per site, of which 3,772, or 92 per cent, came from stationary machines inside the eight-metre zone — about 7.5 per fitted vehicle per working day. Operators muted the cab unit: the feature worked and the product worsened. The tell is usage falling while trigger rate rises.

Sunk cost enters through the specification, not the budget. Everyone knows not to let past spending justify future spending; almost everyone lets it define the options. Karnik’s document, titled “Khabardaar 2.0”, opened with a feature list, settling the real question silently. The tell is an agenda on which every option is an increment.

Kill decisions are cheap only if the organisation can metabolise them. A team that killed a product and was promoted kills the next one early; a team that watched a kill end careers keeps products alive by calling them pivots. The tell is a run of pivots with no fall in headcount — not cowardice, but a firm that has not made honesty survivable.

A threshold written after the data is not a threshold. Pre-registration is the cheapest discipline in product work and the most abandoned. The tell is a pass mark that moves: “ten of sixty-four would have been good, but three is respectable for a new category.”

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

The terms are universal; which is weakest is not.

Product typeWeakest termCharacteristic tell
ConsumerΛ and rAbundant need, negligible capture; acquisition exceeds lifetime value
B2B, small and mid-marketr, through cost of saleSold one at a time at a cost no margin carries
Enterpriseq, net of switching costPilots that delight users, never reaching a budget holder
Platform and marketplacethe thinner side’s pInvestment flows to the side easier to count
Hardware and physical goodsΛ, fixed at toolingBill of materials committed before value is measured
AI-nativeΛ, through the error tailStrong aggregate accuracy; residual borne by the customer

Enterprise and small-business products are lumped together as B2B and should not be. Khadaan sells mid-market: buyers are site-level, the contract is ₹38.85 lakh of hardware, and the ₹12.59 lakh cost of sale is fatal because the contract is too small to carry it. An enterprise seller with a ₹6 crore contract absorbs that cost and fails instead at q.

Stage changes the clock, not the mechanism. A seed-stage company fails by exhausting runway before learning anything decisive: Khilaadi, with five months left. A scale-up fails by scaling a motion whose unit economics were never established: Khadaan, where every win enlarges the loss. A large company fails by not noticing. Where the difference is not real, say so: the arithmetic does not change, nor the order of testing.

8. Three worked examples

Khilaadi: proving the ceiling rather than the price

In August 2026 Ingle ran a price ladder across 4,800 active players, 1,200 per cell.

The ladder found no better price; it proved there was none. ₹4.6 crore of marketing over the 36,162 players active in September is ₹1,272 each. Amateur cricketers play in a league for three or four.

Khabardaar: what ₹34 lakh in 2024 would have bought

In mid-2024, before tooling, four radio-only units at two sites for ten weeks would have produced both the near-miss reduction of about a third and the eight-metre nuisance problem. 34 per cent of the ₹126 lakh exposure is ₹42.84 lakh, so one question — can we deliver this under ₹21.42 lakh of five-year ownership cost? — would have reached the table in September 2024. The answer was no at the designed bill of materials, which needs a 66.6 per cent cut. That is not a version two; it is a different product.

Jatan Instruments: when disciplined discovery produced the wrong kill

Jatan Instruments Group of Coimbatore spent ₹41 lakh in 2022 on a low-cost school hearing screener. Its discovery was exemplary: of 64 schools interviewed across two states, 7, or 10.9 per cent, had a budget line for screening, and 3, or 4.7 per cent, would prepay. The pass mark, written in March 2022 and signed by the board, was 10 of 64 prepaying, or 15.6 per cent. Jatan missed it and killed the product in November 2022, correctly by its own rules.

In July 2024 a state school-health programme put hearing screening on a funded procurement list. Kinaara Devices Group, holding a dormant prototype, won 2,900 units at ₹52,000 over fourteen months: ₹15.08 crore of revenue at about 38 per cent gross margin, roughly ₹5.73 crore of gross profit. Jatan re-entered as a component supplier, shipping 4,100 acoustic modules at ₹9,400 in 2025-26 — ₹3.85 crore at 31 per cent, or ₹1.19 crore of gross profit. The false kill cost it about ₹4.54 crore.

The failure was not of rigour but of the quantity measured: the pass mark tested present budget, p conditional on today’s funding, and treated it as p. Nothing distinguished “they do not need this” from “they cannot buy this yet”, which have opposite implications.

9. Failure modes, warning signs and the cost of lateness

Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost if late
Backlog mistaken for marketReleases ship; pipeline does not moveWhat share of the backlog came from non-payers?A release cycle a quarter
Value asserted, never pricedNo customer has seen a return calculationWhat does the buyer spend today, and what share do we remove?Khadaan: 26 months, ₹11.6 crore
Engagement read as willingness to payRetention flattens; revenue does not followRevenue ceiling per active user?Khilaadi: 19 months, ₹11.3 crore
Pass mark written after the dataThe threshold is restated in reviewWhere is the dated document, and who signed it?False kills and continuations

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether failure is predictable. The discovery position holds that most new-product failures were detectable for a few per cent of the eventual spend, resting on cases like Khabardaar, where ₹34 lakh would have exposed an ₹11.6 crore error. It would be wrong if the decisive information were unavailable before building — if buyers could not value a hazard reduction they had never experienced. The irreducible-failure position holds that outcomes are dominated by variance discovery cannot touch: when firms measure carefully most well-reasoned ideas still fail, and the best hit rates belong to those running the most tests. It would be wrong if hit rates rose with better prior reasoning rather than volume.

The second concerns where to look. The timing position holds that p is exogenous, moving with infrastructure, regulation and price curves, so the characteristic error is earliness mistaken for wrongness. Jatan is its evidence: a correct answer in 2022, a wrong one in 2024, no defect between. It would be wrong if late entrants to newly funded markets systematically lost to incumbents who had waited. The organisational position holds that above a few hundred people the modal cause is internal, and Khilaadi’s split teams are its evidence. It would be wrong if products inside large firms failed at the rate of independent products in the same market.

The third and sharpest is whether “no market need” should remain the headline teaching. Defenders call it the most expensive mistake and a plurality finding across hundreds of post-mortems. Critics call it a thought-terminating label, wrong about Khabardaar and Khilaadi both, producing practitioners who run demand tests where demand was never in doubt. This page takes the critics’ side without pretending the matter settled.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this recites the failure causes and runs interviews. Someone who has internalised it opens a project by naming the term they are most ignorant of and the cheapest decisive test of it, and will say when demand is not the risky term. They compute the buyer’s return, not their own, on the share of the problem removed, before the bill of materials freezes. They write the stopping condition down, date it and have it countersigned by whoever controls the money. And they separate kill from disposal, so a correct kill in a market that has not arrived leaves an asset, not a hole.

12. What each of them decided

Kanetkar did not ask the board to kill Khabardaar. She asked it to decline the ₹7.2 crore and fund instead an ₹85 lakh, twelve-week programme, a little under an eighth of the request, with two questions and a dated pass mark. Could a radio-only unit cut five-year ownership cost by two thirds, under ₹21.42 lakh a site? And would three of the eleven non-renewing sites pay for a statutory register alone? Version two, she argued, asked the board to win 223 sites — 83.2 per cent of every reachable site in India — when Khadaan had won 17 in twenty-six months.

Kamath’s decision was harder because her product worked. She stopped player acquisition outright, removing ₹21 lakh a month from the ₹71.20 lakh cost base, and took Jena’s ground team from four people to nine. The ₹299 pass stayed but stopped being the business; the thesis became that a ground owner with 128 players per booking has both the money and the scheduling problem. Joseph Kamau’s Nairobi pilot, run on grounds from the start, was the only cohort where commission exceeded cost. Joshipura agreed on one condition Kamath set herself: a pass mark written on 1 October, that 120 of the 1,410 listed grounds pay a monthly fee by 31 January 2027.

Discussion questions

  1. Khabardaar removes about a third of a ₹126 lakh exposure and costs ₹64.05 lakh to own. As Kanetkar, would you argue for a cheaper product, a different buyer or a different unit of sale, and what evidence would move you between them?
  2. Khilaadi’s ladder proved the ceiling, not the price. When is that a reason to change the payer, and when to stop? What must the ground-side pilot show by 31 January 2027 for the second?
  3. Jatan’s kill followed its own pre-registered rule and cost roughly ₹4.54 crore of gross profit. Design a pass mark separating “they do not need this” from “they cannot buy this yet” without becoming unfalsifiable.

13. Going deeper

What makes a good product idea is the next step, the generative counterpart to the five terms. What a product manager does matters because the arithmetic is useless unless someone owns it. PM myths versus reality unpicks the belief that the job is to ship, which produced Karnik’s feature list. Origins of product management explains why demand evidence sits with the PM. PM versus PMM versus TPM versus project manager versus founder asks who should have caught Khilaadi’s thin side. PM archetypes shows why a growth PM and a platform PM would diagnose it differently. How the PM job changes by company stage follows from section 7.
case40v1-pm.failure:
Ehsaas Sensor Labs: The Probe in Someone Else's Warehouse

A case on why products fail. Foundations — The PM Role & Foundations.

1. Sunday night, Pune

On the evening of Sunday, 29 November 2026, Sharvari Kalgutkar sat alone in the Ehsaas Sensor Labs office on Senapati Bapat Road, Pune. The board met at ten the next morning. Before her were two documents that could not both be true: a half-yearly summary from Dharohar Collateral Services claiming the Ehsaas system had prevented ₹367.80 lakh of grain spoilage across forty-eight warehouses between April and September, and her data scientist's reconciliation showing that at twenty-two of the forty-eight the probes had sent almost nothing since June.

Sharvari had joined fourteen months earlier as the company's first vice-president of product, out of a connected-car team in Bengaluru. She had spent October talking to warehouse managers, and had come back with a question her chief executive did not want asked four days before a term sheet lapsed: whether anybody using the product was the person with the problem it solved.

2. How Ehsaas got here

Abhay Tarkunde and Nilesh Gondhalekar founded Ehsaas Sensor Labs in Pune in February 2023. Abhay had run quality assurance for a Nashik grape exporter; Nilesh had designed industrial instrumentation in Nagpur for eleven years. Their observation was correct: much of India's foodgrain sits in privately managed warehouses whose moisture discipline depends on a man with a steel spear and a practised thumb, and damp grain heats, cakes and grows fungus long before anyone opens the stack to see it.

The Jaanch probe is a 1.4-metre stainless lance with capacitive moisture sensors at four depths, a temperature string and a low-power radio. Driven into a stack and left for a season, it reports every thirty minutes to a gateway and then to a dashboard called Nazar. The hardware worked. By September 2025 a NABL-accredited laboratory had calibrated it for wheat, maize, soyabean and chana, and the bill of materials allowed a probe at ₹4,500 and a subscription at ₹2,400 per probe per year.

The decision that shaped everything else was taken on 14 March 2025. Dharohar Collateral Services, a mid-sized collateral manager supervising pledged stock for lenders, offered a development-and-service contract worth ₹2.52 crore over twenty-four months — ₹10.50 lakh a month from April 2025 to March 2027. Ehsaas had eight months of cash. It signed. Three clauses came with the money: the firmware had to write into Dharohar's inspection format; Ehsaas could not sell to banks, non-banking lenders or rival collateral managers in India until 31 March 2027; and it could not approach Dharohar's warehouse operators without written consent.

That third clause is why, twenty months later, a company with 2,840 probes in the ground had never held one unmediated conversation with a warehouse owner.

3. The industry around the probe

Warehouse receipt finance in India rests on a chain of trust nobody owns end to end. The Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority registers warehouses and governs negotiable warehouse receipts; banks and non-banking lenders advance against pledged stock under Reserve Bank of India norms, and NABARD refinances much of it. Between the lender and the grain sits a collateral manager — Dharohar here, competing with Sohan Lal Commodity Management, Origo Commodities, NCML and Arya.ag — who certifies that the stock exists and is of the stated quality.

Each party has a different relationship with the truth about moisture. The lender wants certainty and prices its absence into the pledge margin. The collateral manager sells assurance, is paid per tonne supervised, and has an interest in appearing diligent while keeping inspection costs down. The warehouse operator earns a fixed rental per bag and bears spoilage loss only where his contract makes him liable, which at pledged-stock sites it usually does not. The producer organisation that deposited the grain bears the loss in the end but is rarely in the room. The processor who buys the lot pays on a gate assay and discounts hard for moisture. Struan Ferguson, hired in Glasgow in February 2026, believed such buyers would soon want a continuous storage record instead; his two prospects, a Busan feed importer and a Perth grain handler, had signed nothing.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Through 2025 the belief inside Ehsaas was that the warehouse operator was the customer: he has the grain, the staff and the loss. The Dharohar contract seemed to accelerate that thesis rather than distort it, because Dharohar's sites were warehouses and Dharohar paid to fit them out.

By January 2026 all forty-eight Dharohar sites were live, holding 2,400 probes between them, from about forty at a single-shed yard to near seventy at the largest. In April the company began selling to independent warehouses in Vidarbha and Marathwada at list price; eleven signed by August, taking forty probes each, which is 440. Of the 3,600 probes made, 760 remained in Pune.

The dashboard numbers looked healthy in the monthly pack. In September, Alejandra Portillo rebuilt the adoption funnel from raw event logs rather than the dashboard's summaries. Her version is Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1. Nazar dashboard adoption, 1 April to 30 September 2026

Thirty-eight of forty-five. The people acting on alerts were overwhelmingly Dharohar's own inspectors, measured on coverage and glad of a dashboard that spared them a climb up a stack. The operator in whose building the probes sat was not looking. That is a fact about demand, not design, though Marcin Kaczmarek had argued for six months that it was about design.

5. The two numbers that cannot both be right

Exhibit 4, Dharohar's half-yearly summary, is what Abhay intended to put before the board. It is Dharohar's own work and makes Ehsaas look indispensable.

The average rates of 2.10 and 1.46 are weighted by tonnes monitored; their difference of 0.64 percentage points applied to 1,92,000 tonnes gives the 1,230 tonnes in the same row. Alejandra's reconciliation, Exhibit 5, asks what the probes actually saw over the same six months. The registry accounts for 84,000 tonnes under monitoring at those forty-eight sites, not 1,92,000, and the tonnage with a reading on most days is 31,500.

The two exhibits cannot both describe the same reality. Exhibit 4 asserts 1,92,000 tonnes monitored; Exhibit 5 accounts for 84,000, which is 43.75 per cent of it. Allocate the claimed saving only to the 31,500 tonnes with readings on most days and it becomes 31,500 divided by 1,92,000, or 16.41 per cent, of ₹367.80 lakh — ₹60.34 lakh — and only then if the probe, rather than three good monsoon months, caused the improvement. Neither Sharvari nor Alejandra could tell which Dharohar had meant: tonnage supervised at a site, or tonnage with a probe in it. Nobody had asked, because asking would put the round at risk.

6. The people

Sharvari Kalgutkar, vice-president of product, Pune, owns the recommendation. Her position: Ehsaas has never tested who the buyer is, so every roadmap item is a guess. Her incentive is awkward, since she built that roadmap. Unsaid: she has discussed pricing with a Mumbai lender, which the exclusivity arguably forbids.

Abhay Tarkunde, co-founder and chief executive, Pune, wants approval for a scale-up: cheaper probe, more sites, a round closed on the Dharohar numbers. The lender channel, he argues, is worth more with 10,000 probes in the ground than 2,840. Unsaid: the lead investor has twice asked why independent renewals are weak.

Nilesh Gondhalekar, co-founder and chief technology officer, Nagpur, is proud of the hardware and right to be. The gateway failures behind Exhibit 5, he holds, need only ₹40 lakh of mains-independent gateways, after which the value will be undeniable. Unsaid: two of the nine continuously reporting sites are ones his engineers visit monthly.

Kavita Ambardekar, chief financial officer, Pune, joined in April 2026 from a listed auto-components firm. She will not let the board vote without a stopping rule. Her incentive is the audit: 70.9 per cent of revenue comes from one counterparty whose report she cannot verify. Unsaid: she has drafted a note on revenue concentration and not circulated it.

Yashwant Chikhale, head of field operations, Guntur, spent fifteen years in collateral management. Operators will never pay much, he holds, because at pledged sites they do not carry the loss; the money sits with whoever does. His incentive is his field team, which a pivot would shrink. Unsaid: his staff ran the panel A survey and knew what answer kept it funded.

Alejandra Portillo, data scientist, Guadalajara, is eleven and a half hours behind Pune, so her reconciliations land at breakfast. No dataset she has, she holds, can establish causation. Unsaid: she thinks the August survey unusable, and has not said so because Yashwant's team ran it.

Marcin Kaczmarek, firmware and design lead, Krakow, believes the product is not good enough for a man in a godown: the dashboard assumes a desk and English. He wants a vernacular, voice-first client. Unsaid: he has never watched a warehouse supervisor work, having visited India twice, only to Pune.

Struan Ferguson, head of partnerships, Glasgow, argues the real buyer is the offtaker who discounts for moisture at the gate. His incentive is commission on a first overseas contract. Unsaid: both prospects want a free pilot and have no budget.

7. Voices

Abhay Tarkunde to the leadership group, email, 16 October 2026, 23:14 IST

"Dharohar's report is signed by their quality head. It is the best validation we have ever had. We are not going to spend a month auditing our own best customer. Take it to the board, close the round, fix the gateways."

Alejandra Portillo, reply, 17 October 2026, 09:02 IST

"I am not auditing them. Our registry and their report disagree about tonnage by more than a factor of two, and I cannot tell whether that is a definitional difference or an error. If a diligence team asks which number is right, I will say I do not know."

Yashwant Chikhale, voice note transcript, 24 October 2026

"Madam, in Guntur I asked one owner why he never opens the dashboard. He said, the grain is not mine, the loss is not mine, and the Dharohar man comes anyway. He is not being difficult. He is correct."

Marcin Kaczmarek, team chat, 6 November 2026

"There is no demand problem. There is a terrible interface. Give me a Marathi voice client and the same operator will open it twice a day."

8. The options as Sharvari sees them

Kavita costed four, from the ₹284 lakh held on 31 October against a burn of ₹28.40 lakh.

Exhibit 6. The four options, costed from the 31 October 2026 cash position of ₹284 lakh
OptionMonthly burn (₹ lakh)Months to decisive evidenceCash used (₹ lakh)Cash remaining (₹ lakh)
A. Scale the warehouse-operator product30927014
B. Test the offtaker as buyer225110174
C. Shrink and wait for exclusivity to lapse16696188
D. Become Dharohar's hardware supplier18354230

Source: Ehsaas finance, 26 November 2026. Cash used is monthly burn multiplied by months; cash remaining is ₹284 lakh less cash used. November is excluded. Team sizes assumed: A 31, B 22, C 14, D 18. The options are alternatives, so no row is a total.

Option A builds what Nilesh and Marcin both want: mains-independent gateways, a vernacular client, a cheaper probe, 6,000 more probes in the ground. It is the plan the board expects. It leaves ₹14 lakh, a fortnight.

Option B tests Struan's thesis in India: pay two solvent-extraction plants and a feed miller to take a continuous storage record instead of a gate assay, and see whether they pay a premium or shrink the moisture discount. It breaches no clause, and walks away for five months from the only paying customer.

Option C cuts to a skeleton, lives off the Dharohar fee until 31 March 2027 and goes at lenders the day the clause lapses. It concedes two years spent building for the wrong buyer, and asks the board to fund patience.

Option D gives up on being a product company: sell probes and firmware to Dharohar and firms like it at a hardware margin, and let collateral managers own the customer. It is the safest cash outcome and caps Ehsaas at a supplier's size.

Sharvari was uneasy with her own framing. Each option names a buyer and asks how to sell to him; none asks the prior question of what the job is and whose job it is. A fifth possibility had surfaced twice in October: that the party who truly bears the loss is the producer organisation that deposited the grain, and that what it needs is not monitoring but a quality-linked payout, an insurance product Ehsaas cannot sell.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at ten on Monday, 30 November 2026. The Series A term sheet — ₹22 crore at a ₹88 crore post-money valuation — expires on Friday, 4 December, and is conditioned on 2026-27 revenue of at least ₹1.80 crore, against ₹103.66 lakh booked in seven months. Cash stood at ₹284 lakh on 31 October, ten months at the current burn. The Dharohar contract, the exclusivity and the no-direct-contact clause all run to 31 March 2027, with no renewal commitment. Thirty-one people are employed, nineteen in Pune and Nagpur, three overseas. The 760 probes in store carry ₹26.60 lakh of value. An insurance-linked product needs a partner licensed by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India; farmer-level data falls under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, for which Ehsaas has not designed.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, state what Ehsaas has evidence of and what it does not. Why is 2,840 probes deployed the least informative number in the investor update?
  2. Exhibits 4 and 5 disagree about how much grain the system monitored. What would you need to know to decide which is right, and what would you do if you could not find out in time?
  3. Panels A and B of Exhibit 3 tell opposite stories about willingness to pay. Which would you rely on, and what about how each was produced drives your answer?
  4. Among the common causes of product failure — no market need, the wrong customer, mistimed entry, running out of cash, building without testing — which best describes Ehsaas, and what is the strongest evidence against your diagnosis?
  5. The March 2025 contract bought ₹2.52 crore and cost direct access to users. Was that a reasonable trade with eight months of cash, and what should the founders have demanded in exchange?
  6. The four options each presuppose a buyer. Reframe the decision around the job to be done and who bears the loss, and say what changes. Then: what should Sharvari do when the board convenes, and what should she tell the directors about the ₹367.80 lakh in Exhibit 4?

Sunday night, continued

At a quarter to eleven Sharvari wrote on a sheet of paper the sentence she had been avoiding for three weeks: the person who looks at our dashboard is paid by the person who pays us, and neither of them owns the grain. Below it she wrote the four option names, then a fifth line ending in a question mark. Whatever she said about Exhibit 4, Abhay would hear as a vote against the round; whatever she said about Exhibit 5, Nilesh would hear as a vote against his hardware. The Dharohar report lay where it had lain all evening, signed, confident, impossible to reconcile.
case20v1-pm.failure:
Angadi Systems: The Bill Nobody Asked For

A case on why products fail

1. Opening

On the evening of Monday, 2 November 2026, Gitanjali Mahapatra sat in the Koramangala office of Angadi Systems in Bengaluru with forty interview notes spread across her desk and a board meeting fourteen days away. The meeting, set for 16 November, would decide how the company spent the next nine months of its life. Diwali was six days off, and her chief executive wanted a plan before the festival closed the offices.

Angadi's app helped small shopkeepers raise GST-compliant invoices from a phone. Fourteen months and ₹4.4 crore into the venture, it had been installed on 3,20,000 phones and was paid for by 1,600 shops. Mahendra Tiwari, the chief executive, believed the answer was more product: voice-operated billing in nine Indian languages, which would cost ₹2.4 crore. Gitanjali, the head of product, had spent October talking to people who had stopped using the app, and she was no longer sure the product was the problem.

2. Company background

Mahendra Tiwari founded Angadi in Indore in 2025 after a career selling accounting software to mid-sized manufacturers. His thesis was simple. India has well over a crore of small retailers, GST had made invoicing a legal obligation, and existing tools such as Vyapar, Zoho Books and Tally were built for accountants rather than for a grocer at a counter. A phone-first, vernacular, low-price product, he argued, would sweep the long tail.

The company raised a ₹8 crore seed round in September 2025 and hired quickly. By launch in February 2026 the team numbered fourteen, working from Bengaluru, Pune and Indore, with a designer in Lisbon, a data scientist in Nairobi and a customer-success lead in Melbourne. The roadmap, assembled from investor requests, sales requests and competitors' advertised features, held 112 items. Nobody had been asked to write down which shopkeeper, doing which job, would pay for which of them.

The market around Angadi was crowded and shifting. Khatabook had made the paper credit ledger a phone habit for millions of shops, and PhonePe for Business and Paytm gave merchants a soundbox and dashboards at no charge. A shopkeeper's attention was already contested before Angadi arrived.

The team's own record of the previous fourteen months is set out in Figure 1.

3. The situation

The launch had gone better than most. The Android app reached 3,20,000 installs in nine months, helped by a reseller tie-up and modest advertising. Mahendra quoted that figure in every investor update. The numbers beneath it, summarised in Exhibit 1, told a harder story.

Exhibit 1. Angadi funnel, February to October 2026

Source: Angadi product analytics, Nairobi data team. "Still raising invoices" means at least four invoices in the eighth week after the first one. A paid plan costs ₹1,800 a year, so 1,600 subscribers represent ₹28.8 lakh of annual revenue.

Faith Otieno, the data scientist in Nairobi, had flagged the pattern in July. The 48,000 users who raised an invoice and then lapsed (64,000 less the 16,000 who stayed) were not mainly people who found the app hard to use. Her cohort charts showed them dropping off at the same point, regardless of language or city. Tiago Pinheiro, the designer in Lisbon, had watched session recordings and seen shopkeepers finish an invoice and never return. For an invoicing product that was odd, and the team had treated it as an onboarding bug.

It was Harpreet Gill, in Melbourne, who suggested simply asking people. Between 12 and 30 October Gitanjali and Harpreet called forty of the lapsed users, picked across seven states, and Faith coded the answers. Exhibit 2 gives the result.
